#6389. A Superheated Plasma Zone Could Explain How Black Holes Launch Powerful Jets

By combining advanced X-ray and radio observations, scientists have uncovered new clues about how magnetic fields and superheated plasma enable supermassive black holes to generate powerful jets.

Some supermassive black holes consume enormous amounts of gas while blasting powerful jets of plasma into space at nearly the speed of light. According to conventional models, these two behaviors should be difficult to sustain together. Rapidly feeding black holes are expected to develop cold, flat disks of swirling matter that make it harder for powerful jets to form.

Scientists studying a supermassive black hole in the galaxy 3C 120 have now identified a possible solution to this longstanding puzzle. Their observations suggest that a region of extremely hot plasma near the black hole creates conditions in which magnetic fields can help launch a relativistic jet, even as large amounts of matter continue falling inward.

The research, led by Associate Professor Hirofumi Noda of Tohoku University and Associate Professor Kazuhiro Hada of Nagoya City University, combined X-ray measurements with detailed radio observations to investigate both the material surrounding the black hole and the jet emerging from its vicinity.

“By looking at the same black hole with state-of-the-art X-ray and radio telescopes, we were able to see both the hot plasma surrounding the black hole and the jet emerging from it,” says Noda. “This allows us to directly connect the extreme environment near the black hole with the formation of the jet.”

Located in the constellation Taurus, 3C 120 is an active galaxy whose central supermassive black hole is rapidly accumulating matter while producing a powerful jet. Observations from the X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission (XRISM) indicate that the black hole’s cold accretion disk does not extend all the way inward. Instead, its inner edge lies at a distance of approximately 20 times the black hole’s radius. Closer to the black hole, the disk gives way to a flow of plasma heated to hundreds of millions of degrees.

To investigate the structure of the accretion disk, the researchers examined an iron emission line detected by XRISM. The intense gravity near a black hole changes the energies of X-rays emitted by orbiting material, producing a characteristic distortion in the line’s shape. By analyzing this distortion using Einstein’s theory of general relativity, the team estimated how far inward the cold disk extends.

The researchers then used observations from the Global Millimeter VLBI Array, Very Long Baseline Array, and East Asian VLBI Network to examine the jet. These networks combine signals from widely separated radio telescopes, allowing astronomers to resolve structures too small for individual telescopes to distinguish. The measurements traced the jet’s narrowing structure back toward a launching region within the hot plasma flow close to the black hole.

Together, the X-ray and radio observations provide evidence that the black hole’s inner environment differs substantially from the cold, flat disk expected under rapid accretion. Rather than extending uninterrupted toward the black hole, the cooler material transitions into an extremely hot plasma flow in the region associated with the jet’s origin.

The hot plasma could help explain how a rapidly feeding black hole generates such an energetic outflow. Unlike a cold, thin accretion disk, this type of flow may allow strong magnetic fields to build up near the black hole. Those fields can potentially extract energy from the black hole’s rotation and direct it into a concentrated jet of plasma traveling at relativistic speeds.

This mechanism offers a possible explanation for the simultaneous rapid accretion and powerful jet observed in 3C 120. The measurements establish that the system has physical conditions consistent with the proposed process, although they do not directly demonstrate that rotational energy is being extracted to power the jet.

The findings also provide a way to examine how the structure of material surrounding a black hole relates to jet formation. By studying X-ray emissions from the accretion flow alongside high-resolution radio measurements of the jet, researchers can test whether similar conditions occur in other active galaxies.

The team is now extending its investigation to a more massive black hole using coordinated observations from XRISM and radio observatories around the world. They are also comparing the measurements with theoretical models and computer simulations to better understand how matter behaves under extreme gravity.

“Our next goal is to build a more complete picture of how matter, magnetic fields and black hole rotation interact in these extreme environments,” adds Noda. “Understanding this process may also help us better understand how supermassive black holes influence the evolution of galaxies and the larger structures of the Universe.”

Reference: “Disk Truncation Triggers Relativistic Jet Launching of a Highly Accreting Supermassive Black Hole” by Hirofumi Noda, Kazuhiro Hada, Hiroto Maruyama, Taishu Kayanoki, Kenji Toma, Taiki Kawamuro, Yoshiyuki Inoue, Tomohisa Kawashima, Soyeon Yeo, Ilje Cho, Keiichi Asada, Yasushi Fukazawa and Yoshihiro Ueda, 19 October 2026, The Astrophysical Journal Letters. DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/aeaa2c

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could capture images 30% sharper than — and remain operational for twice as long as — initially expected. Researchers say these "remarkable" developments could greatly enhance the volume and quality of the data they will analyze.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 new alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine ‪—‬ which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex ‪—‬ successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other important spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

Roman was launched into space on board one of SpaceX's Falcon heavy rockets. It lifted off Aug. 30 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is currently around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

First, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.

The team that designed, launched and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Roman is around the same size as a small truck and was packed into the nose cone of the Falcon Heavy rocket prior to launch.

Thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, said in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, said in the statement.

In total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

Given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the new space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins said. "That's a lot of science!"

Roman is now on its way to L2, where the gravity of Earth and the sun cancel out, allowing it to remain in one place without expending much fuel.

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking."

There is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

Roman's WFI consists of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror. It will be capable of capturing images with a field of view 100 times greater than Hubble.

We have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

After Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome."

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, said in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."

NASA released Roman's first photos on Sept. 15. Each small square represents one of the telescope's light detectors, and each blurry green spot is a distant star. (This is just a test image and does not represent how the telescope's proper photos will look.)

The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he said it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.

The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Roman has completed around 85% of its journey to L2 and should arrive at its final destination in the next few weeks. (The timeline in this image is a screenshot from Roman's commissioning process website, captured on Nov. 11.)

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.

All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us."

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6386. Glass Behaves Strangely When Stretched to One Atom Wide – the Discovery Could Transform Electronics

As engineers push to make electronics ever smaller, managing their heat grows harder, and a discovery about one-atom-wide glass could open new possibilities for miniaturization.

Glass is known for keeping heat where it belongs. It insulates windows, protects buildings from temperature changes, and helps keep electronic components separated. Yet when researchers reduced glass to a thread just one atom wide, they found it could transmit heat with remarkable efficiency, revealing an unexpected behavior that could reshape how engineers approach increasingly small electronics.

In a study published in Nature Nanotechnology, researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder observed heat traveling through an atomic-scale glass connection in discrete steps. Each step carried exactly 40% of the maximum heat a single channel can transmit under the laws of quantum physics. The observation marks the first time researchers have detected this kind of quantized heat flow carried by atomic vibrations.

The finding could help address a growing challenge in electronics. As components become smaller and more powerful, managing the heat they generate becomes increasingly difficult. Glass, in the form of silicon dioxide, is widely used as an insulating layer in computer chips, making its behavior at extremely small scales particularly relevant.

“We will eventually reach a bottleneck to design the next generation of electronic and photonic devices,” said Longji Cui, an assistant professor in the Paul M. Rady Department of Mechanical Engineering at CU Boulder. “Thermal management inside electronic devices is extremely important, but to do it more effectively, we need to understand how heat is flowing through these nanoscale devices.”

Ordinary glass is a poor conductor of heat because its atoms are arranged in a disordered structure. That disorder scatters the vibrations that carry heat through the material, making it difficult for thermal energy to travel efficiently. When researchers stretched the glass into a connection just one atom wide, however, there was no room for the same disorder. Instead, the atomic vibrations could pass through the narrow connection with much less interference.

“Glass is what we put in windows to keep heat in,” said Guilherme de Vilhena, a researcher at the Materials Science Institute of Madrid and a co-author of the study. “But stretch it into a thread one atom wide, and it does the opposite: it lets heat through with an efficiency we had never seen in an insulator.”

The team made the observation using a scanning thermal probe microscope (SThM), an instrument equipped with a glass tip and a built-in thermometer. It measures temperature and heat flow through extremely small contacts by detecting the behavior of atoms and molecules. Cui compares the instrument to a fingertip capable of sensing heat and texture, only scaled down to the nanoscale.

“When you put your own finger to touch a surface, you can feel the texture and the heat,” he said. “With this microscope, we shrink this finger to nanoscale, and it can read the temperature and heat flow through a single atom.”

To observe the phenomenon, the researchers pressed two pieces of glass together and gradually pulled them apart. As the contact stretched and narrowed, it eventually formed a thread only one atom wide before breaking. This allowed the team to examine how heat moved as the connection approached the atomic limit.

The unexpected behavior could extend beyond glass. Cui believes other materials may exhibit similarly surprising thermal properties when examined at the atomic scale.

“We will now be able to study any material we want with this microscope, and there could be constant surprises that come from this instrument,” he said.

The microscope can investigate thermal transport in virtually any material, including metals and insulators. Cui hopes to use it to develop increasingly sensitive sensors capable of measuring phenomena that conventional instruments cannot easily detect.

“I want to push the world record for thermal sensing, which means I need to build more and more sensitive platforms,” he said. “And people will use it to study fundamental thermal problems.”

Semiconductors are among the team’s main interests because they form the foundation of nanoelectronics. By examining how heat moves through these materials, researchers could better investigate problems affecting the energy efficiency and reliability of increasingly compact electronic devices.

“The materials we are particularly interested in are semiconductors that are the building blocks of nanoelectronics devices,” Cui said. “This new microscope we developed makes a great diagnostic tool to explore issues associated with energy efficiency and reliability of electronic devices at the nanoscale.”

Reference: “Thermal conductance of atomic-scale glass reaches 40% of quantum limit” by Sai C. Yelishala, Yunxuan Zhu, P. M. Martinez, O. Mateos-Lopez, Wan Xiong, Dishan Chooi, Sophie Kimura, Juan Carlos Cuevas, J. G. Vilhena and Longji Cui, 13 October 2026, Nature Nanotechnology. DOI: 10.1038/s41565-026-02308-9

The research was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation.

Within the framework of the Fluidized Absolute Space Theory (FAST), space or medium can be viewed as a dynamic background possessing the properties of an ideal fluid; meanwhile, the Topological Vortex Theory (TVT) places emphasis on vortices, spin, topological constraints, and geometric structure.

Your experiments demonstrate that atomic-scale glass junctions do not necessarily act as thermal insulators due to structural disorder; instead, they can enter a state of near-ballistic, coherent phonon transport. We suggest further investigating whether this highly efficient heat transfer is primarily governed by the interplay of neck geometric constraints, the available phonon spectrum, and topological connectivity. If predictable patterns of thermal conductance can be reproduced across different materials, varying neck geometries, and distinct topological perturbations, it would help distinguish a “pure Debye frequency explanation” from a more general geometric-topological transport picture.

Mathematically, as a physical entity, the ideal fluid characteristics and properties of space are the prerequisite for the sustained evolution of material systems, providing the foundation for their dynamical behavior.

Mainstream physics has developed a highly instrumentalized, terminologized, and project-driven research ecology: (1) Large-scale facilities need to continuously generate news, and therefore tend to adopt expressions such as “unlocking,” “hidden,” “strange,” and “quantum breakthrough”; (2) Peer review tends to reward publishable labels for new phenomena rather than deeper geometric unification; (3) “Quantum materials” have gradually become a tool for funding allocation and journal classification, with their conceptual boundaries being continually stretched; (4) Experimental precision keeps rising, yet much work remains at the level of phenomenological classification, lacking a fundamental reconstruction of phase fields, vortex topology, and fluid geometry. This has become a brazenly shameless state of affairs in mainstream physics.

Einstein’s sorrowful silhouette has faded into the distance. But his intuition, his persistence, his belief in “local realism”, has finally found its rightful home in the framework of Topological Vortex Theory (TVT). Einstein was not a failed prophet, but a true physicist misunderstood by his era.

—— https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2088659998394077633

The really fascinating part of this is how they bypassed melting the glass entirely—using room-temperature probe indentation and sub-angstrom retraction to stretch an amorphous network down to a single-atom bridge right before it snaps.

It shows that once you strip away the 3D structural disorder and force energy down a single-atom axis, lateral scattering disappears and heat travels through cleanly. Since a pulled glass filament is naturally fragile and temporary, the logical next step for real-world electronics would be applying this same single-atom dimensional confinement to an ordered 1D crystalline thread—giving you a permanent, mechanically stable minimum-scale channel to bleed heat or carry signals without scattering. Reference Link : https://docs.google.com/document/d/18eEHMNQQniZSL76SGxZ_DVeIqIADZC–Vzur36Vfjo0/edit?usp=drive_link

If we look at recent breakthroughs in nanoscale thermal transport and quantum error correction side-by-side, a single unifying principle emerges: we have to stop treating noise and uncertainty as fundamental “probability errors” and start treating them as unrouted mechanical friction—what is essentially probability trash.

In the material science domain, researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder and the Materials Science Institute of Madrid bypassed high-temperature melting entirely, using room-temperature probe indentation to stretch an amorphous glass network down to a single-atom bridge right before fracture. By collapsing 3D structural disorder into a 1D axis, lateral scattering vanishes and heat travels through cleanly. While pulled glass is fragile and temporary, applying that same single-atom dimensional confinement to a permanent, ordered 1D crystalline thread provides the ultimate lossless physical highway for micro-electronics.

In the quantum domain, researchers at the Shenzhen International Quantum Academy solved the measurement bottleneck by abandoning the brute-force habit of constantly stopping and measuring a qubit to fix errors. Instead, they engineered a surrounding microwave reservoir to act as a continuous impedance filter. Stray photons and phase drift—the very “probability trash” that mainstream physics treats as random dice rolls—are naturally siphoned out as entropy at the boundary, leaving the logical qubit locked in phase equilibrium without a single digital interruption.

Can they work in conjunction? Absolutely—they represent two halves of the same complete architecture. The 1D crystalline thread provides the ultra-narrow, low-impedance physical pathway to guide signals or energy across distances without lateral scattering, while the engineered microwave cavity acts as the active impedance sink at the boundary to bleed off any rotational phase shear. By pairing 1D dimensional confinement with continuous analog drainage, you eliminate probability trash entirely at the edges before it ever pollutes the core calculation.

#6385. Rewriting History: New Research Reveals Ancient Iron Age King May Have Been a Woman

A ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain may have been a woman, challenging centuries of assumptions about a pivotal figure in British history.

Research led by Dr. Miles Russell at Bournemouth University (BU) challenges the traditional identification of Verica as a male king. Drawing on the ruler’s name and coin imagery, Russell argues that a woman held a central role in the events leading to Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43.

Verica ruled the Atrebates, whose lands covered much of modern-day Hampshire and West Sussex. Driven from power around AD 40, the ruler fled to Emperor Claudius in Rome, seeking support. That appeal gave Claudius an opportunity to intervene in Britain and claim a military triumph.

Russell, BU’s Director of Archaeological Fieldwork, argues that Verica’s identity has been filtered through assumptions made by earlier historians. “Verica is assumed to have been male because of the patriarchal mindset of 19th-century classical historians. Verica was not only critical to the special relationship between Britain and Rome in the early first century AD but was indisputably female.”

One clue, he suggests, is the name itself. Its “a” ending also appears in the names of female rulers from the same period, including Cartimandua of the Brigantes (in Yorkshire) and Boudica of the Iceni (in Norfolk). Boudica’s revolt against Roman rule in AD 60 made her the most famous of the three, but Russell considers Verica the more powerful and influential figure.

The title on Verica’s coins has also shaped how the ruler is remembered. “People also assume she was a ‘he’ because of the term ‘rex’ on coins, but ‘rex’ is a non-gender-specific title; both male and female kings were recognized by Rome, Cleopatra of Egypt being the most famous,” Russell said. “The use of the Latin title ‘rex’ on coins shows that Verica ruled with the full authorization of the emperor.”

For Russell, the images offer another important clue: “Whilst other coin-producing British Iron Age leaders portray obviously male warriors, Verica is depicted as a slender, feminine, bare-breasted figure riding on horseback.”

Verica’s identity also changes how Russell interprets the Roman account of the invasion. Historian Cassius Dio claimed that Claudius crossed the Channel because Verica persuaded him to do so. That story fits a broader pattern in Roman writing, which portrayed Claudius as weak-minded and ineffective, with women and freed slaves directing his decisions.

“The story of Claudius committing to something only because a woman told him to fits the trope of this emperor as being submissive and henpecked,” Russell said. “In effect, Dio was saying that the campaign was undertaken solely because of the whisperings of a barbarian femme fatale. Verica’s role was rather more central to the British expedition. Having her onboard ensured the project was a success as she provided tactical information and support on the ground.”

In this interpretation, Verica offered both a political justification for invasion and practical help in carrying it out. As Russell put it, “The invasion was Claudius’ great triumph, it being the only chance he had to prove he was a successful military leader. Verica provided the excuse for regime change, and the emperor seized it.”

Russell argues that Verica deserves recognition among Britain’s earliest influential female leaders. “We should take the archaeological evidence at face value,” he said, “and remember Verica as a female king and one of the earliest and most important of British female leaders. Had she not been deposed and fled to Claudius for military support, Rome may never have invaded Britain in the first place.”

The work follows earlier BU research into women’s place in Iron Age society. Published last year, that research involved Russell and university colleagues and found evidence of communities centered on women, where husbands moved to live with their wives’ communities.

The argument about Verica is presented in Caratacus: Great King of Britain, published by Bloomsbury in January (ISBN 9781350477902), and discussed in the latest edition of Current Archaeology.

A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

"BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the new findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

Additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

The proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.)

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," said Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the new study.

Under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," said Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the new criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the new criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang said. She noted potential challenges in implementing both new aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

Providers also may struggle with the new distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

Rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts. Nature, 659. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11237-5

#6381. Earth’s Ancient Oceans May Have Fooled Scientists About the Rise of Oxygen

Some of Earth’s best-known oxygen milestones may belong to the oceans, not the atmosphere, reshaping our understanding of the conditions that allowed complex life to evolve.

For billions of years, Earth had almost no oxygen in its atmosphere, making it a vastly different world from the one that supports complex life today. New research suggests oxygen accumulated in three major stages, with the deep ocean taking hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

Two geochemists at Chengdu University of Technology argue in The Innovation that scientists may have misjudged the timing of Earth’s oxygenation by using ancient ocean chemistry to estimate atmospheric conditions. Ocean chemistry is also influenced by nutrients, biological activity, circulation, and basin shape, making it an imperfect record of the air.

Instead, the researchers examined an oxygen isotope signature preserved in sedimentary sulfate. Reactions involving oxygen, ozone, and carbon dioxide produce a distinctive shortage of oxygen-17 in the atmosphere. This signature enters sulfate when sulfide minerals weather, providing a record of atmospheric oxygen.

The first major increase, the Great Oxidation Event, occurred between 2.4 billion and 2.1 billion years ago, raising oxygen from less than one-millionth of today’s level to between 0.1% and 10%.

The next increases occurred between 1.3 billion and 1.0 billion years ago and between 440 million and 410 million years ago, earlier than traditionally thought. The better-known Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic oxygenation events, dated to 800 million to 500 million and 420 million to 360 million years ago, may instead reflect ocean responses that lagged behind atmospheric changes by roughly 200 million and 30 million years.

Oxygen nevertheless remained scarce. Models based on the isotope evidence place mid-Proterozoic atmospheric oxygen at just 0.1% to 1% of modern levels. Charcoal, which requires roughly three-quarters of today’s oxygen concentration to form during burning, first appears around 420 million years ago.

Atmospheric and ocean oxygen generally increased together over billion-year timescales, although they could move in opposite directions over millions of years. When oxygen entered seawater containing accumulated organic carbon and sulfide, chemical reactions consumed the gas and could lower atmospheric levels. Some geological signals previously interpreted as oxygen increases may therefore indicate declines.

Oxygen also spread unevenly through the oceans. Photosynthetic microbes created localized oxygen-rich environments as early as 3 billion years ago, or earlier. These dominated during the Archean, before oxygen supplied from the atmosphere became increasingly important. The ocean interior did not become fully oxygenated until approximately 410 million years ago.

For life, the transition was gradual. An oxygen-free atmosphere severely limited organisms dependent on the gas, while fluctuating levels during the Proterozoic opened new habitats as animals evolved. After the third atmospheric increase, greater oxygen availability helped support larger bodies, active predation, and expansion into deeper waters.

The researchers caution that the isotope record has limited time resolution, oxygen concentrations after 1 billion years ago remain poorly constrained, and additional increases may have gone undetected. Their findings suggest that Earth’s transformation into an oxygen-rich world was shaped not only by rising atmospheric levels, but also by the long delay before oxygen reached the ocean depths.

Reference: “Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth’s atmosphere and oceans” by Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, 17 March 2026, The Innovation. DOI: 10.1016/j.xinn.2026.101353

Financial support was supported by the National Key Research and Development Program of China (grant no. 2022YFF0800100 to C.L.) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grant nos. 42425002 to C L. and 42572129 and 42103072 to H.W.).

“…, oxygen concentrations after 1 billion years ago remain poorly constrained, and additional increases may have gone undetected.”

#6379. Arctic Bacteria May Be Using Sunlight and CO2 in a Way Scientists Never Expected

An Arctic bacterium’s genes hint at an unexpected way of using carbon dioxide, raising the possibility that similar survival strategies exist in oceans far beyond the polar regions.

In the Arctic Ocean, where nutrients and usable organic matter can be scarce, a tiny bacterium may have found a remarkable way to survive. Think of it as having a built-in solar charger and an unusual food supply. By capturing energy from sunlight and using a chemical called acetone, it may be able to turn carbon dioxide into some of the building blocks it needs to grow.

The bacterium, known as Porticoccus arcticus, lives in the frigid waters of the Beaufort Sea, north of the Yukon in the Arctic Ocean’s Canada Basin. At some locations, it accounted for up to 9 percent of detected bacteria, suggesting it is an important member of the region’s microbial community. In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers at Concordia University uncovered genetic evidence of an unusual metabolism that could help explain how these organisms survive in such a challenging environment.

One of the keys appears to be acetone, a chemical produced naturally by marine organisms, including microscopic algae, and through reactions between sunlight and dissolved organic matter. Scientists already knew that some marine bacteria could consume acetone, but P. arcticus appears to have a different way of putting it to use.

Its genes point to a process called acetone carboxylation, which combines acetone with carbon dioxide to produce compounds that can enter the cell’s central metabolic pathways. These chemical pathways allow cells to process carbon and make the materials they need to function and grow.

The researchers found the complete set of genes required for acetone carboxylation within the bacterium’s relatively small genome. They also identified multiple genes for proteorhodopsins, light-sensitive proteins that help cells capture energy from sunlight. Genes involved in both acetone processing and light capture were among the organism’s most active, suggesting that it may be able to use sunlight for energy while supplementing its carbon supply through acetone metabolism and carbon dioxide assimilation.

What makes this combination especially intriguing is that the researchers had not set out to look for bacteria with these abilities.

“The genomic composition of these organisms led us to reconstruct the different types of energy and carbon metabolisms that exist,” said David Walsh, a professor in Concordia’s Department of Biology and the study’s corresponding author. “That is how we found this very specific set of genes associated with the use of acetone, which was unexpected. We discovered that the organism’s genes were telling us about something we did not suspect was happening in an ecosystem. This was a surprise, as we were not actively looking for acetone-degrading bacteria that can use light.”

Walsh explained that the findings point to two distinct metabolic abilities, including a way of obtaining energy that researchers call photoheterotrophy.

“This study introduces two new discoveries,” he said. “The first is a group of organisms, P. arcticus, that has a unique metabolism that uses organic carbon while at the same time has the capacity to use light as an energy source. We call this process photoheterotrophy.

“The second discovery is the way the organism consumes acetone to also consume carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere. This acetone-mediated inorganic carbon assimilation combines what animals do — eating food, in this case, acetone — with what plants do: fixing CO2.”

The genetic evidence suggests that P. arcticus has developed a way to take advantage of several resources available near the ocean surface. However, the findings describe its potential metabolic capabilities rather than directly measuring how much carbon dioxide the bacteria take up.

Whether these abilities will help the bacterium cope with a warming Arctic Ocean remains uncertain. Walsh does not yet know how changing conditions will affect P. arcticus, although shifts in sea ice could alter the availability of sunlight and acetone, potentially changing where the organism can thrive.

The researchers also plan to investigate whether bacteria in other oceans and freshwater environments possess similar capabilities. Such investigations could help determine whether this unusual combination of sunlight capture and carbon assimilation is a specialized Arctic adaptation or a more widespread microbial survival strategy.

Reference: “Evidence of an acetone carboxylation pathway in photoheterotrophic bacteria from the Arctic Ocean” by Susan McLatchie, Sara Palestini, Asher Woodhead, Tony Gutierrez and David A. Walsh, 26 September 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78082-y

Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica, contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A tiny brown mushroom found in Florida's swamps is the first known fungus to contain both psilocybin, the chemical compound in psychedelic mushrooms; and amatoxin, the poisonous substance in the world's deadliest mushrooms.

The species, Galerina indica, has been nicknamed the "dark magic mushroom" and was characterized in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Current Biology.

"There is no species of mushroom anywhere, in any group, that has been known to produce both at the same time," study first author Andrew Kunik, a fungal biology researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "So it's quite remarkable."

Exactly why the dark magic mushroom has evolved to contain these two compounds is unclear, but the authors told Live Science that they may give the fungus a powerful defense against being eaten.

The ability to produce either psychedelic or toxic chemicals has evolved multiple times across fungal lineages. A process called horizontal gene transfer, which is widespread among fungi, has played a part in that process.

In horizontal gene transfer an organism passes new genetic material to another, as opposed to vertical gene transfer, in which a parent passes genetic material to offspring. It can lead to unexpected genetic combinations and, in bacteria, plays a key role in the development of antibiotic resistance.

The tiny mushrooms seem to have acquired both psychedelic and toxic compounds via horizontal gene transfer.

Some of the world's deadliest mushrooms, from the Amanita genus, stop cells from producing proteins and can cause death through liver failure. Past work has shown these mushrooms shared the ability to produce their poisonous amatoxins via horizontal gene transfer with mushrooms from the unrelated genera Galerina and Lepiota. Some mushrooms have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer as well.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But Kunik and colleagues weren't looking for specific chemicals when they began hunting for Galerina mushrooms in the swamps of Florida; they just wanted to learn more about the mushrooms' chemical makeup, as not all Florida Galerina mushrooms had been characterized before.

To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that.

They collected five specimens from Galerina, a genus that contains over 300 species worldwide, many of which are poisonous. Among the samples they collected were small G. indica specimens that grew on moss-covered palm trunks. The largest mushrooms were only about 0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) tall, with caps up to about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide.

Chemical analyses revealed that the dark magic mushroom contained both psilocybin and amatoxins, including one amatoxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. The new amatoxin wasn't wholly unexpected, given that other species of Galerina produce closely related amatoxins, Kunik said.

The production of psilocybin alongside the amatoxins was more of a surprise for the research team.

"To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that," study co-author Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "We were shocked."

To understand how the tiny, deadly mushroom acquired its mind-altering, liver-poisoning abilities, the team compared the genes of G. indica with those of other psilocybin-producing mushrooms, finding the genes shared a common evolutionary origin — even though the mushrooms themselves are distantly related.

Scanning electron microscopy image of the spores from the “dark magic mushroom”.

The researchers also found G. indica’s psilocybin-producing genes are arranged in a different order than in other psilocybin-producing fungi, which suggests the gene cluster was rearranged during its evolutionary history, a clue that horizontal gene transfer happened.

G. indica seems to have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi about 15.5 million years ago, based on reconstructions of Galerina’s evolutionary history from DNA analysis, Smith said. However, it’s possible that psilocybin-producing genes entered the lineage through two separate horizontal gene transfer events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, Kunik noted. Collecting and sequencing more Galerina specimens could help untangle their evolutionary history.

The findings are surprising, said Hannah Reynolds, a fungal ecologist at Western Connecticut State University who was not involved with the new research. "What was exciting about this paper was seeing both of these [compounds] present, seeing that this gene cluster jumped in, got rearranged, maybe came in twice — it's very cool," Reynolds told Live Science.

The ability to produce two types of incapacitating chemicals could form a powerful defense against being eaten, because organisms that would normally eat them would have difficulty evolving defenses against both, Kunik speculated.

But the idea that this duo of compounds prevents the mushroom from being eaten is just a hypothesis. To buttress that idea, further research might tweak the genes of the dark magic mushroom to observe how removing one compound affects the species' role in the food web, Kunik suggested.

Tropical and subtropical mushrooms are historically understudied, so there is likely much more incredible fungal diversity right under our feet, Smith said.

Kunik et al. (2026). "The 'dark magic mushroom' co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin." Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

#6376. New Drones Are Hard to Find Since the FCC’s Ban. Here’s How to Care for the One You Have.

Don’t let wear and tear keep your drone out of the air. Let this maintenance checklist be your guide to safe flight.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It’s been nearly a full year since the Federal Communications Commission banned the release of new foreign drones in the U.S. While you can still buy models from previous years, very few, if any, new drones have been widely released to the public. The majority of drones sold today are older models still sold by the drone companies or used models that already have a couple of years’ worth of flights under their belt. Without an obvious upgrade path for most pilots, maintaining the drone you own feels essential.

With so many moving parts and delicate sections, your drone needs a bit more care than just a quick wipe-down and recharge. While proper handling is always best—there are still computer components and a camera in there—there are things you can repair if they get damaged.

Doing some relatively simple upkeep to your flier can add years to its lifespan. If you’ve got a drone that’s past its warranty and you want it airborne for a few more years (or a used drone in need of some elbow grease before getting back up and running), I’ve compiled a few tips on the best routine maintenance you can do to keep it flying straight and steady.

The easiest way to make sure your drone doesn’t break midflight is to take a good look at it before you send it up. Make sure the basic components are in working order. Check for loose screws, cracks or abrasions in the chassis, and damage to the propeller or camera.

When you turn your drone on, check the battery level and make sure there is a clear connection between your controller and the drone before takeoff. It sounds obvious, but it’s easy to skip a step when you’re in a hurry, and that’s the worst time to have a small problem turn into a big one.

When you’re done flying and the drone has landed, give it another once-over before putting it away. Take the time to remove any sticks, leaves, or other debris that might have clung to the body. I’d also recommend taking some compressed air or a blower to clean off any dirt that has started to clump on or inside delicate parts of the drone, like between the hinges of the camera attachment or in charging ports.

If you want to be thorough, wiping down the body with a gentle cleaning wipe or rag never hurts. You should also clean the camera lenses and sensors using isopropyl alcohol and a cotton swab.

In general, you should always update your drone’s firmware when a new update rolls in. While it isn’t necessarily essential to start flying, security updates often fix bugs that could affect navigation, controls, or connectivity.

If your drone’s companion app or software does not download updates automatically, make sure to check the app store on your phone as well as the settings page directly in the app to make sure you aren’t missing anything.

While not necessary before every flight, it is good to get in the habit of regularly recalibrating your drone’s major visual sensors, which impact obstacle avoidance, its inertial measurement unit, and its compass.

The calibration process may vary depending on the make and model of your drone, but you should be able to find an option to initiate the process through its software or companion phone app. Most DJI drones, for example, have a safety section under settings on the DJI app where most sensors are listed and can be calibrated when the drone is connected.

Even if you don’t find any loose screws in your preflight checks, you should go in and tighten the screws occasionally to make sure the body doesn’t come loose.

If you keep a small screwdriver in your drone kit, going through and checking the screws around the chassis shouldn’t take more than a couple of minutes. Don’t force it or overtighten if it isn’t needed: Just make sure each screw is secure.

The propellers on most consumer drones are made from a much thinner material than the rest of the body. While they are often somewhat protected, they can get damaged midflight, or simply start to degrade over time. What’s more, you may not notice a slightly damaged or eroded propeller: It won’t stop your drone from flying, but it may start to move slower or less precisely, and its imperfect airflow control may impact its battery efficiency.

If you see any visible cuts or scratches on a propeller, or fraying around the edges, it’s time to swap that one out. Most drone brands sell replacement parts for active models. There are also a number of third-party brands that make replacement parts for popular brands on Amazon and other online retailers.

Likewise, all rechargeable batteries degrade over time. If you want to keep your drone’s runtime at peak performance over the long haul, swap out its battery every few years. Like with a phone or a laptop, you’ll know when it’s time because the battery drains and dies more quickly.

That said, there are steps you can take to maintain your drone battery’s health. Rotate two or three batteries to spread out the strain. As with other tech, take care to avoid overcharging them or, conversely, letting the battery fully die. (Ideally, you want to store your batteries at around 50 percent capacity if you don’t plan to use them in the near future.)

And if you only use your drones sparingly, take the batteries out and charge them every few months to keep them alive.

As silly as it may seem, troubleshooting a problem you don’t understand is often as easy as cracking your drone’s user manual. Many specific malfunctions have easy solves or specific instructions to handle them.

It’s also a great way to learn more about the unique capabilities of your specific drone model, which can help you build a greater skill set as a pilot over time (assuming you’re reading closely).

If there are any larger issues with your drone that don’t feel solvable, take it to a service center. There are a number of certified options around that specialize in certain brands or types, so do a bit of research before you choose a location.

#6375. Not All Physical Activity Protects Your Brain, Scientists Warn

Across 30 countries, researchers found that exercising during free time was linked to lower dementia risk, while physically demanding work was linked to higher risk.

After spending an entire day on your feet, going for a walk or bike ride might seem unnecessary. Yet new research suggests that being physically active at work may not provide the same protection against dementia as exercising in your free time.

A major analysis involving more than 4.2 million people found that those who were most physically active during their leisure time had a 24% lower risk of dementia compared with those who were least active. In contrast, physical activity performed on the job was associated with a 20% higher risk.

The findings, published in The Lancet Public Health, raise an important question about the familiar advice to move more. If physical activity is good for the brain, why might its benefits depend on where and how it takes place?

Researchers at the University of Southern California (USC) examined this question by combining evidence from 74 cohort and case-control studies conducted across 30 countries. The participants ranged in age from 45 to 93 and were followed for a median of 10 years. During that time, researchers tracked diagnoses of dementia from all causes, including Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia.

The analysis was led by David Raichlen, a professor of biological sciences and anthropology at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences. It is the first systematic investigation of whether the “physical activity paradox,” previously documented in cardiovascular research, also applies to dementia. The paradox describes how physically demanding occupations may fail to provide the same health benefits as recreational exercise and may even be associated with greater disease risk.

“The findings challenge the long-held assumption that ‘every move counts’ for brain health,” said Natan Feter, the study’s first author, a postdoctoral fellow in Raichlen’s Evolutionary Biology of Physical Activity Lab at USC and a researcher in the Graduate Program of Epidemiology at Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.

One possible explanation lies in what happens around the physical activity itself. Walking, cycling, running, swimming, and playing sports during leisure time are generally activities people can choose and adjust to their comfort level. They may also provide opportunities to socialize, relax, and reduce stress.

A physically demanding job often presents very different circumstances. Workers may spend hours standing, repeatedly lifting heavy objects, or completing strenuous tasks with little opportunity for recovery. Unlike a recreational workout, these activities may occur alongside workplace hazards and pressures that extend well beyond the physical effort involved.

Manual occupations, for example, can expose workers to greater psychosocial stress, less control over their working conditions, and higher levels of air and noise pollution. These factors have independently been linked to dementia risk. Workers may also struggle to find time or energy for recreational exercise, particularly when access to safe places for physical activity is limited.

For these reasons, the researchers believe the higher dementia risk associated with occupational activity is unlikely to result from movement itself. Instead, the working conditions and broader social environments surrounding physically demanding jobs may help explain the difference.

The relationship also changed depending on how much activity people performed. Higher levels of leisure-time exercise were associated with progressively lower dementia risk, although the association eventually leveled off. Occupational activity followed the opposite pattern, with dementia risk increasing alongside greater activity before reaching a similar plateau.

Not every form of daily movement could be evaluated with the same confidence. Household physical activity appeared to be beneficial, although that finding came from just one study. Active commuting was associated with a modestly higher dementia risk, but only two studies examined this relationship. The researchers emphasized that more evidence is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn about either activity.

There are also important limits to what the larger analysis can establish.

Because the studies were observational, the findings cannot prove that physically demanding work causes dementia or that leisure-time exercise directly prevents it. Nearly all the studies relied on participants reporting their own physical activity, which can introduce errors in memory and reporting. Most of the evidence also came from high-income countries, despite expectations that low- and middle-income countries will experience the largest increases in dementia cases over the coming decades.

Even with these limitations, the contrasting associations remained after researchers accounted for factors including age, education, and chronic diseases. Multiple sensitivity analyses, which test whether findings hold under different analytical assumptions, produced consistent results. Feter said this consistency strengthens the case for taking the relationship seriously.

The importance of context may extend beyond physical activity. In a related study published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia the previous month, Raichlen, Feter, and their colleagues examined how different sedentary behaviors relate to brain structure.

They found that mentally engaging activities performed while sitting, such as working at a desk, were associated with greater volume in regions of the brain’s cortex compared with more passive activities, such as watching television. These regions included areas involved in executive function, which supports abilities such as planning and decision-making. Like the findings on physical activity, these associations do not establish cause and effect.

The researchers stress that their findings should not discourage people from working physically demanding jobs. Instead, they suggest that dementia prevention strategies need to account for the conditions under which people are active, including the opportunities they have to exercise for enjoyment outside work.

“In other words, when it comes to protecting the brain, the context of physical activity may matter just as much as movement itself,” Raichlen said. “Improving access to safe parks, walking trails and recreational facilities, ensuring people have adequate leisure time for exercise, and reducing harmful workplace exposures may ultimately prove as important as promoting physical activity itself.”

Reference: “Domain-specific physical activity levels and risk of dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis” by Natan Feter, Paula Iso-Markku, Tiladia Markarian, Dylan M Luong, Jack Gunnink, Natália Schröder, Eduardo Lucia Caputo, Jayne Feter, Anamika Nanda, Sarah Hourihan, Gustavo S da Silva, Ashley Ventura, Daniela Benzano Bumaguin, Yann C Klimentidis, Gene E Alexander, Daniel Umpierre, Pedro C Hallal, Airton José Rombaldi and David A Raichlen, September 2026, The Lancet Public Health. DOI: 10.1016/S2468-2667(26)00142-8

#6373. FDA Approves Breakthrough Treatment That Helps Children With Type 1 Diabetes Keep Producing Insulin

For children with type 1 diabetes, managing blood sugar is a lifelong challenge, but a newly approved treatment offers hope of preserving their body’s ability to produce insulin.

For children newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, insulin is essential for controlling blood sugar, but it cannot stop the immune system from destroying the cells that produce it. A newly approved treatment offers a way to slow that damage and preserve more of the body’s own insulin production. However, families have only a short window after diagnosis to consider the option.

In June 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) expanded its approval of teplizumab to include children and adolescents ages 8 to 17 with newly diagnosed stage 3 type 1 diabetes. This is the stage when symptoms appear and insulin treatment becomes necessary. The expansion was granted through the FDA’s accelerated approval pathway, based on evidence that the drug helps preserve insulin production. Teplizumab was already approved for people ages 1 and older with stage 2 type 1 diabetes to delay progression to stage 3.

Type 1 diabetes develops when the immune system attacks beta cells in the pancreas, which produce insulin to help the body use energy from food and regulate blood sugar. Some of these cells usually remain when symptoms first appear. Teplizumab targets the immune cells responsible for the damage, potentially extending the “honeymoon” period when patients still produce some insulin themselves.

“Insulin is essential in stage 3 type 1 diabetes, but it doesn’t address the immune process that is destroying the cells that make insulin,” said Kimber Simmons, MD, MS, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine and a physician-scientist at the Barbara Davis Center for Diabetes. “Teplizumab gives us an opportunity to preserve some of the beta cells and insulin-producing capacity that a person still has. The goal is to intervene early enough to make a meaningful difference.”

Evidence supporting the expanded approval came from the PROTECT clinical trial, which involved 328 children and adolescents. After 78 weeks, participants who received teplizumab retained significantly more insulin-producing capacity than those given a placebo. Researchers measured this using C-peptide, a marker of how much insulin the body produces naturally.

Nearly 95% of children treated with teplizumab maintained a clinically meaningful level of their own insulin production, compared with about 79% of those receiving placebo. Separate studies involving people with type 1 diabetes have linked higher C-peptide levels with fewer episodes of severe low blood sugar, reduced insulin requirements, and a lower risk of certain complications, including diabetic eye disease.

The timing of treatment is particularly important. Teplizumab must be started within eight weeks of diagnosis, while participants in PROTECT began treatment within six weeks. Earlier research also suggested that starting treatment sooner may produce stronger responses.

Treatment involves two 12-day courses of daily intravenous infusions, typically six months apart. Potential side effects include rash, headache, nausea, and temporary reductions in lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. More serious risks include cytokine release syndrome, an inflammatory reaction, infections, and viral reactivation. Experienced medical teams and careful monitoring are therefore necessary.

Teplizumab does not cure type 1 diabetes or eliminate the need for insulin. Instead, it introduces another way to manage the disease by addressing the underlying immune process.

To help clinicians and families navigate these decisions, Simmons led a national group of clinical trial investigators and pediatric diabetes specialists in developing practical guidance published in Diabetes Care. Supported by Breakthrough T1D, the guidance combines clinical trial evidence with experience in everyday patient care. It covers patient selection, potential benefits and risks, shared decision-making, safety monitoring, and treatment planning.

Simmons, who also practices at Children’s Hospital Colorado, co-authored the published results of both PROTECT and PETITE-T1D, a study examining teplizumab in children younger than 8 with stage 2 type 1 diabetes.

“Once a treatment is approved, the question becomes: How do we actually do this in the clinic?” said Simmons. “The way patients are treated in the real world doesn’t always line up perfectly with a clinical trial protocol. We wanted to give clinicians practical guidance so they can have informed conversations with families and make thoughtful, safe decisions.”

The guidance also addresses a longstanding challenge in medicine: translating research advances into routine care.

“Research shows that, on average, it takes 17 years for landmark medical breakthroughs to become widely adopted in routine clinical practice. Closing that gap is essential to getting the best science to people sooner,” said Breakthrough T1D Senior Vice President of Medical Affairs Anastasia Albanese-O’Neill, Ph.D., APRN, CDCES. “Breakthrough T1D is focused on efforts that will close this gap in a way that is safe and supports shared decision-making between clinicians and families. This new clinical guidance serves as an important tool that will help guide timely care for children with a new stage 3 type 1 diabetes diagnosis. We’re grateful to the leaders who provided their expertise and time to develop it.”

The authors emphasize that teplizumab should be incorporated into existing diabetes care rather than delivered through an entirely separate treatment system.

“We don’t want to create a separate pathway that fragments care,” said Simmons. “This is an opportunity to be thoughtful about how we use a new therapy while keeping the whole patient in view. Our specialty needs to stay focused on providing the best coordinated care we can.”

Reference: “Clinical Guidance for Disease-Modifying Immunotherapy in Children and Adolescents With New-Onset (Stage 3) Type 1 Diabetes” by Kimber M. Simmons, Adriana Weinberg, Emily Breidbart, Carla Demeterco-Berggren, Stephen Gitelman, Kevan C. Herold, Shideh Majidi, Daniel Moore, Amara Ogbonnaya-Whittlesey, Neha Patel, Jennifer L. Sherr, Emily K. Sims, Kupper Wintergerst and Michael J. Haller, 11 November 2026, Diabetes Care. DOI: 10.2337/dci26-0061
