#6335. The 4 Best Laser Printers For Your Home and Small Office

If you print a lot of professional-grade documents, a laser printer is a worthy investment.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Laser printers, known for printing crisp, professional-looking documents quickly, are generally considered big, expensive machines designed for large offices. While some larger models live up to that reputation, plenty of compact options fit into your home office if you print files often.

While more expensive than an inkjet printer, most laser printers are a better long-term investment, with lower operating costs and designs built for heavy-duty printing. That said, choosing the right one at a glance can be tricky, and may vary based on your needs.

Printers aren’t the most exciting tech products, and many folks see them as frustrating, unreliable machines that require constant repair or replacement and are increasingly unnecessary for the average person in the digital age. While that may be true for some, they remain essential for workers who need to print contracts or create physical records, and students who need hard copies of their homework. With a little research, you can find a good laser printer that makes life easier and lasts a long time.

The recommended printers are based on my personal experience and knowledge of printers, as well as research from reputable publications, including PCMag and The Wirecutter. I looked for printers with performance and features that suit both home and small office users, with price and value in mind. I also spent months testing the best overall pick and using it as my everyday printer to ensure it’s a worthy recommendation.

I have been reviewing tech products for 25 years, including computing peripherals such as inkjet and laser printers. As an editor at Computer Shopper magazine, I helped develop the printer testing methodology used in the reviews. I then brought that expertise to publications such as Digital Trends and Business Insider, applying real-world usage that resonates with shoppers in the evaluation.

There’s no perfect laser printer, but if you’re looking for a reliable, easy-to-use unit that produces high-quality prints, the HP LaserJet Pro MFP 3101sdw fits the bill. I’ve been using this printer for several months and found that it’s an ideal fit for my home office. It also has plenty of advanced features that would make it a good fit for a small business.

With a 35ppm print speed, the 3101sdw is fast for its intended audience. When connected to a typical home Wi-Fi network, it takes about 5 seconds from pressing print to outputting the first page. Printed text looks good even at lower-quality settings, with small fonts staying sharp and legible. I found the scan quality more than adequate for everyday use, but 300 dpi is too low for designers, photographers, and other creative users. It also runs quiet, which is always a nice bonus.

Anybody who needs to make copies will find the ADF-equipped scanner handy, while the 2.7-inch touchscreen makes setup easy. It took me less than 10 minutes to get it up and running. Whether you connect via USB, Ethernet, or Wi-Fi, the printer responds quickly. It also has a USB port for quick prints or saving scans to a flash drive.

While the 3101sdw is small enough to fit on a large desk, it’s more practical to put it on its own stand. I wouldn’t call it “lightweight,” but I could carry it down five floors without much effort. It won’t win any design awards, either, which is too bad because HP generally knows how to make great-looking products.

The paper tray has an average 250-page capacity, but a notable drawback is that it has no manual feed tray. I didn’t find this an issue, but if you need to, say, print on envelopes, it could be problematic because you'd have to switch out the paper in the main tray. Another expert reviewer dinged the 3101sdw for lacking a fax function, but my workaround is to use the HP Smart companion app to scan and send (but not receive) faxes.

The 3101sdw offers stronger print quality, a better build, and ease of use. It’s hard to say how long mechanical devices like this will last, but HP’s printers are known for their reliability—I have a LaserJet from the 1990s that’s still going strong.

In my experience, Brother makes affordable laser printers that consistently deliver solid performance and text quality. At 36ppm and under $200, the HL-L2460DW is a strong basic option for a home or small office. Despite its barebones design, it has useful features like double-sided printing, Ethernet connectivity, wireless printing, a generous 250-page paper capacity, and a mobile app. Plus, it’s lightweight and doesn’t take up too much space.

The HL-L2460DW supports a 1,200-page standard-yield toner cartridge or 3,000-page high-yield toner cartridge, but comes with a starter cartridge that only yields 700 pages out of the box. (This is typical of printer manufacturers.) If you plan to print a lot, I’d recommend buying a high-yield cartridge right when you buy the printer.

This is a “budget” option, though, so this printer comes with a few caveats. I don’t love the small LCD display, which has a basic interface that doesn’t display much info and doesn’t feel as well-made. The basic operation means there’s no scanning, copying, faxing, ADF, or other multi-function capabilities. Plus, black-and-white graphics and images don’t look as good as text. User reviews have also complained about its reliability. Still, given its balance of price, speed, and print quality, the HL-L2460DW is a good value regardless of budget.

If it’s for personal use and you only plan to use it every so often, I’d steer you toward a different model, the HL-L2420DW, which has a 30ppm speed and every aforementioned feature except Ethernet. It’s perfect for casual printing, and it costs $50 less.

Most offices shy away from color laser printers because they are expensive to buy and maintain, and employees often use them to make wasteful prints. Likewise, at home, you’re probably better off going with a color inkjet printer. That said, if you truly need color prints, I love the HP Color LaserJet Pro MFP 3301fdw, which delivers excellent print quality and attractive features like glossy paper support. It’s a strong, if pricey, complement to any office.

Despite its compact footprint, the 3301fdw has a 50-page duplexing ADF and a 250-page paper tray. It’s not the fastest color laser printer, but its 26ppm speed is more than adequate for home or small business use.

Print quality is where HP’s laser printers excel. You can expect documents with crisp text and well-saturated, natural-looking color graphics and photos. Unlike most laser printers, the 3301fdw is compatible with select HP glossy paper, so you can make photo prints. They don’t really compare to inkjet photo printers, but it’s fine in most cases.

Like our overall pick, the 3301fdw is a breeze to set up via its 4.3-inch color touchscreen. For connectivity, it supports USB, Ethernet, and Wi-Fi, which covers most home and office networks.

You may have guessed the printer’s big con is that it’s pricey to operate. Whether you’re using the standard or high-yield toner options, the cost per page is high. If you’re looking to spend a little less, I’d look at the Brother MFC-L3380CDW, which has a comparable feature set to the 3301fdw and a lower operating cost. You’re compromising a bit on print quality and performance, though, which is why the HP leads the pack.

A true small-business laser printer needs to be a workhorse. It should offer a robust, office-centric range of features, print fast, support multiple users, hold enough paper, and have a high duty cycle. Experts agree that Brother makes some of the best laser printers for offices, and the monochrome MFC-L2900DW multi-function model is a particularly good option.

Imagine the L2900DW as an enhanced version of the HL-L2460DW. It shares a similar design, small footprint, and print engine, but features a high-capacity 50-page ADF for copying or scanning multi-page documents. The L2900DW also has a single-page duplexing scanner for two-sided pages. There’s even a fax function.

A large 3.5-inch touchscreen makes setup and on-device operation easy without a computer, while USB, Wi-Fi, and Ethernet give you options for connecting. Combined with a fast 36ppm speed, sharp text print quality, low operating cost, and the option to use high-yield cartridges, you’ve got a very capable all-in-one laser printer.

Graphics don’t look as sharp as text, but that shouldn’t matter if your office prints mainly documents. While its 250-page paper tray is adequate for a small business, expect to reload often if multiple users print often. This model offers no option for a larger or expandable paper tray.

The ADF has a scanner resolution of just 600 dpi, but that is plenty for text documents; the flatbed scanner has 1,200 dpi, which is fine for color images. The output tray’s 100-page capacity is low for heavy usage. One missing feature is a front USB port, which is handy for printing or faxing documents from a flash drive or saving scans to one.

If you need to support a large number of workers, consider stepping up to Brother’s MFC-L5915DW. It has a 70-page ADF and a 5-inch LCD, and you can expand its paper capacity beyond the standard 250 pages. With a faster 50ppm speed, support for 18,000-page high-yield cartridges, and a higher duty cycle, it’s an ideal choice for busy offices. It’s a big jump in price, which is why I went with the L2900DW, but it may cost less to operate in the long run.

Whether for the office or your home, a laser printer is a good option if you often print many multi-page documents. If you need a home printer for occasional printing, a more affordable inkjet printer may make more sense. Again, a laser printer costs more up front but pays dividends in the long run as a professional tool or a home tech staple. If you’re on the fence about what to buy, here are the things I look at when I evaluate laser printers:

Most prints from a laser printer are black-and-white text documents, and most models deliver decent print quality. If you need to print impactful pages with photos and charts, a color laser printer can print higher-quality graphics. Even the best monochrome printers we’ve tested and researched can’t match the detail and clarity of color ink toner. For example, if you have a multi-colored pie chart, a monochrome reproduction can only do so much to separate the different color shading.

Keep in mind, though, that even the cheapest color laser printer will be expensive, and its print quality may not rival that of higher-end models. They also do not support specialty media like glossy photo paper.

A basic laser printer’s sole function is to print documents, and that’s enough for most people. It’s generally compact and fits on a desk. But if you run a small business or work remotely in a home office, you may want a multi-function, “all-in-one” printer that scans and copies, too, among other tasks. Multi-function printers are far more useful, but they’re larger and cost more due to the extra hardware inside.

“Yield” refers to the estimated number of pages you can get out of a single toner cartridge. Most laser printers should get around 1,500 pages from a toner cartridge, while high-yield cartridges should last 3,000 pages or more.

Toner cartridges are expensive, especially for color printers, but they offer a better cost per page than ink. My rule of thumb is that high-yield toners will save you money in the long run.

Similarly, a laser printer’s “duty cycle” rating refers to the maximum number of prints per month that the manufacturer recommends to keep it in proper working order. Basic laser printers have a duty cycle of around 5,000 pages or less, while heavy-duty models have ratings of 10,000 or higher. Printing beyond the rated duty cycle can lead to breakdowns, more maintenance, or a shorter lifespan.

For personal use or small businesses that print occasionally, 25 to 30 pages per minute (ppm) should be fine. Small offices with a few employees that print often may want a faster printer with a speed of 35 to 40 ppm. In a larger office, I’d look for at least 40 ppm, if not more. Keep in mind that manufacturers measure speeds under ideal conditions, and real-world results may not always match. Expect a small discrepancy of a few pages.

Most printers rely primarily on a USB cable to connect to your computer, but a hard-wired connection alone isn’t practical in today’s world of wireless laptops, phones, and tablets. I recommend choosing a printer with a wireless connection compatible with your most-used devices, such as Wi-Fi or Apple AirPrint. Some laser printers also support Ethernet for a high-speed hard-wired connection. Office-focused machines may include a front USB port so you can plug in a flash drive with the files you need to print.

Most laser printers have a paper tray that holds 250 pages, which is enough for personal and small business use. Some compact printers may have a smaller capacity–around 150 pages. If you expect to print a lot, consider a model with a higher-capacity tray or support for multiple trays, and look for an output tray large enough to hold everything you print out. All printers also have a multi-purpose tray for manually feeding non-standard paper like envelopes.

In addition to the essentials, there are some features that I look for which are nice to have, but won’t make or break a printer:

Depending on the model, it can be basic or advanced. Depending on your use case, you may consider some or all of these essential. That said, they aren't universal, and some printers work well without them.

Laser printers use toner, a powder heated onto paper, while inkjet printers spray ink droplets. Laser printers are considered superior for their speed and print quality, but they are expensive to purchase and maintain. Inkjet printers offer color printing and affordability, but prints need time to dry, and the cost per page can be higher with heavy use.

However, the best modern inkjet printers today are fast and deliver great-looking prints, especially photos. They also support different paper types and sizes. Laser printers can also print in color, but they're pricey. Beyond speed, their advantages include consistent print quality and long-term reliability.

Which technology is better ultimately depends on your needs. Most people will find an inkjet printer sufficient and more versatile, but those who print often may find a laser printer more economical in the long run. In an ideal setup, consider an affordable laser printer for frequent print jobs and a good inkjet printer for color documents and photos.

Color laser printers can print photos and graphics on standard paper, but if you want to print on photo paper, an inkjet is the better choice, especially one that supports multi-color ink tanks. Laser printers aren’t designed for photo-quality reproduction, and generally don’t work with specialty paper. (As we discussed, some HP models are compatible with select glossy paper.)

Depending on usage and maintenance, a laser printer can last for many years. It’s a mechanical device, though, so there’s no guarantee that it won’t break down and require service. Here are a few tips to keep your printer running as efficiently as possible and maximize its lifespan:

Over 300 Live Science readers responded to a recent poll about whether they'd train themselves to lucid dream if they could.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."

Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.

#6333. Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

#6332. Man charged in spree of powder-filled letters that rattled Congress

Federal officials unsealed charges Tuesday against an Oklahoma man accused of mailing hundreds of letters containing suspicious substances to members of Congress and other officials last month and ahead of the 2024 election.

The court records, unsealed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma, show officials filed a complaint against Robin Martin with two charges: conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications. Martin is set to make his first court appearance Tuesday; information for an attorney was not immediately available.

The complaint alleges Martin sent more than 700 letters to election officials across the country as well as letters to members of Congress of both parties containing suspicious substances. The substances have so far tested as nontoxic and are believed to be yeast or flour, the complaint says.

The complaint alleges that Martin started sending letters with suspicious substances ahead of the 2024 election, addressing them to election officials in all 50 states. Some of those letters had messages written on them that could only be shown by exposure to ultraviolet light, the complaint says.

The mailings contained letters that claimed President Donald Trump won the 2020 election and raised concerns about issues with the 2024 count. Tests of the suspicious white substances included with the letters revealed they were nontoxic, the complaint says.

The 2024 letters had a return address of a business office in Maryland, while the 2026 letters had a return address previously tied to a Democratic Socialists of America office. Neither of those addresses were connected to the sender, the complaint says.

The complaint says that DSA provided officials with documents showing that someone identifying themselves as “George Livingston” contacted DSA officials in October and said they would be arrested for “TREASON AGAINST THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.” Those messages contained some similarities to the 2024 letters, according to the complaint.

Investigators later tracked down Martin’s phone to places where the letters were sent from and also tracked his car on surveillance footage. The complaint also says investigators tracked purchases he made, including turmeric and vinegar, that could have been used to create an ink that would be visible under UV light.

The case is separate from one announced last week against an Illinois man accused of sending threatening messages to members of Congress.

#6331. Mountain lions and other animals are set to get their own massive land bridge that crosses over 10 lanes of the 101 Freeway near Los Angeles

California's new wildlife crossing over the 101 Freeway is set to open in December 2026, reconnecting habitats for mountain lions and other animals.

The Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing is scheduled to officially open to wildlife on December 2, 2026. The planted bridge for animals spans the 101 Freeway in Agoura Hills, California.

It will reconnect wildlife habitat in the Santa Monica Mountains with the Simi Hills to the north. The freeway below carries more than 300,000 vehicles a day.

The late P-22, a mountain lion that lived in Los Angeles, helped inspire the project.

According to Caltrans, the state agency managing the project, the bridge over the freeway is about 210 feet (64 meters) long and roughly 174 feet (53 meters) wide.

It spans ten lanes of pavement: eight lanes of traffic and two breakdown lanes. A second structure carries the crossing over Agoura Road, a local road.

The crossing broke ground on Earth Day, April 22, 2022. The first stage, over the freeway, was completed in June 2025.

Caltrans costs for all stages are now estimated at $114 million, pending a final contractor estimate for parts of stage two. Public funds cover $77.7 million, or 68 percent, and private donations $37.2 million, or 32 percent.

Costs outside that budget, including the native plant nursery and wildlife research, are covered by additional private donations, according to the project’s official FAQ.

The top of the structure will be covered in nearly 1 acre (0.4 hectares) of native vegetation. The project will also restore more than 10 additional acres (4 hectares) of nearby habitat as coastal sage scrub and oak savannah.

The first stage of construction called for about 5,000 plants, the National Wildlife Federation said in 2023. Key species include coast live oak, toyon, ceanothus, sages, buckwheat and penstemon.

The plants are grown from seeds collected within 5 miles (8 kilometers) of the site. More than one million native seeds had been gathered by mid-2023.

Unlike most wildlife crossings, this one must deal with heavy traffic noise and light. The design tackles both with a large vegetated barrier and other design features.

Exclusionary fencing and vegetation cues are meant to steer animals toward the bridge. The site is already a natural funnel between open space to the north and south.

The National Park Service has studied mountain lions in and around the Santa Monica Mountains since 2002. It calls the 101 Freeway “the biggest barrier between the Santa Monica Mountains and other large natural areas.”

Biologists have documented at least 32 mountain lions killed by vehicles in the study area, part of a wider toll of roadkill on highways.

The isolated lions have the lowest genetic diversity ever documented in the West. The only population with lower levels was in south Florida in the mid-1990s.

In a 2022 study led by UCLA, sperm samples from five male lions that had died were on average 93 percent abnormal. The team also identified nine adult males from the Santa Monica and Santa Ana mountains with physical signs of inbreeding.

A 2016 modeling study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B put the local population’s chance of extinction within 50 years at 15 percent. When inbreeding depression was included, that probability rose to 99.7 percent.

In the simulations, at least one new lion arriving per generation was enough to largely maintain genetic diversity.

Park biologists first captured and radio-collared P-22 in March 2012, when he was estimated to be two years old.

To reach Griffith Park, he had crossed both the 101 and the 405, two of the busiest freeways in the world. He then spent more than ten years there, in the smallest home range ever recorded for an adult male mountain lion.

After scientists noticed a change in his behavior, he was captured on December 12, 2022. He was euthanized under general anesthesia five days later.

“P-22 was a fascinating animal to study,” Jeff Sikich, lead field biologist for the park service’s mountain lion study, said in 2023.

On October 28, scientists captured the first photo of an animal on the unfinished crossing, a coyote climbing its southern slope.

Bobcats, coyotes, gray foxes, mule deer and mountain lions already regularly use a trail next to the site.

Biologists from Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area planned to install remote wildlife cameras in early November. Their monitoring framework includes 14 objectives, from documenting use by mountain lions and mule deer to tracking genetic diversity, vegetation, light and sound.

“This is more than just about whether animals use the crossing,” said Seth Riley, wildlife branch lead at Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area. “We want to understand how effective it is in reconnecting an ecosystem that has been divided by the freeway for decades.”

“That is a much bigger scientific question and answering it will take years,” Riley added.

Images of animals using the crossing will be made public, but not in real time, for security reasons.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service.

A new AI model, called Brain-IT, can transform brain scans into images and reverse the process, turning images into what they'd look like as brain activity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool can use brain scans to recreate the images people looked at with eerie accuracy.

The system, called Brain-IT, uses data from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure activity in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes visual input. A computer model then predicts both the broad layout of an image and high-level information about its content. It then passes those predictions to an AI image generator, researchers explained in a study uploaded to the preprint database arXiv. The research was presented at the ICLR 2026 conference, held April 23-25, and publicized by its authors in September.

Brain-IT builds on an approach called the Universal Brain Encoder. That model begins with an image and then predicts the fMRI response that would be expected in individual "voxels" ‪—‬ small 3D units ‪—‬ in a brain scan.

"The key idea is that every voxel, a tiny cube of brain tissue, gets its own learned vector that captures what it cares about in images," said study first author Roman Beliy, a doctoral candidate in the Department of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel.

Some voxels may be tuned to relatively simple elements of an image, such as edges, textures or locations. Others might be responding to higher-level abstract categories, like faces, bodies or scenes.

Traditional image-to-fMRI systems have generally been custom trained for each participant and dataset. The Universal Brain Encoder is more flexible. It learns from data from multiple people and can transfer information across participants, datasets or different MRI systems with varying magnetic-field strengths, according to the study.

A voxel can determine which parts of an image are relevant to it based on its learned profile, essentially saying, "I recognize edges. Which parts of this image are edges?"

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The Universal Brain Encoder starts with an image and predicts brain activity; Brain-IT starts with measured brain activity and reconstructs the image the person saw. In other words,it asks "based on this brain activity, what was the subject looking at?". It sorts thousands of tiny brain-scan measurements from the visual cortex into 128 groups based on the kinds of visual information they tend to carry.

The system then lets those groups share clues with one another, allowing it to combine, for example, information about a scene's shape, color and possible objects, to build a more complete picture of the image, Beliy explained.

The decoder produces two types of visual predictions. One captures semantic information ‪—‬ the features associated with what is likely in a scene; for an image of a dog standing in grass, for instance, this would include things like the features of a dog and an outdoor, grassy setting. The other captures structural information, like the broad visual layout or how forms are arranged.

In the above example, this would be aspects like the outline of the dog or where it was positioned in the frame. The structural prediction gives the generator a starting point for the image, rather than beginning from pure noise, while the semantic info guides an image generator that removes the remaining static until the image emerges.

Although the new tool can recreate what people see, it can't reproduce memories or imagined scenes.

"We're not reading people's thoughts," study co-author Michal Irani, a computer scientist at the Weizmann Institute of Science, told Live Science. "The images we do manage to recover from fMRI require people's cooperation and full intended collaboration."

The original image of a baseball game (left) and the reconstruction (right) generated by the Brain-IT AI model based on the brain activity of a person viewing the image.

Brain-IT's synthetic images were compared with the images that participants saw. Brain-IT surpassed prior leading methods on standard objective reconstruction metrics and produced more faithful results, the study authors wrote. The system shined when limited fMRI data from a new participant was available, with just one hour of data from a new participant producing results as accurately as earlier approaches that had been trained on 40 hours of recordings.

A high-scoring or realistic-looking output should not be mistaken for a perfect copy of what someone saw, however.

In the final stage of processing, the system uses an off-the-shelf diffusion generator trained on massive numbers of images. Models like this generate plausible images and can smooth textures, sharpen facial features or fill in missing details.

Beliy said this "beautification" can make reconstructions more polished and convincing and introduce details that don't necessarily come from the brain data itself. In other words, the scan constrains the generated picture, but the AI model supplies some of its realism from learned patterns in photographs.

While the new system produces impressive results for seen images, it can't be used to reconstruct an imagined or remembered image.

"Brain-IT relies on how the brain processes a seen image," Irani said. "Information flows from the eyes to the primary visual cortex and onward through a series of visual areas that recognize objects and scenes."

In a controlled experiment, researchers also know precisely which image was shown, giving the model a target during training and evaluation. In contrast, memories and imagined images do not offer the same clean reference. They can be vague and shaped by brain networks involved in memory and thought, with only partial and weaker reactivation of visual regions, Irani said. One limitation that would prevent this technology from being widely deployed is that the only way to get reliable results is from fMRI scanning, which is cumbersome and expensive. The team is currently experimenting with using easier-to-collect electroencephalogram (EEG) data, which is obtained via electrodes on the head, but that work is in the very preliminary stages, according to Irani.

The new system could help brain researchers better understand which visual information is represented in different brain regions, how those regions interact and how individuals’ patterns differ. Such tools could eventually reveal differences in visual processing that could help clinicians spot neurological, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.

"There are numerous useful medical applications which we are currently striving toward," Irani said. "These include using our brain encoder/decoder to detect and analyze brain disorders such as MS, PTSD, autism and psychiatric disorders."

Beliy, R., Zalcher, A., Kogman, J., Wasserman, N., & Irani, M. (2025, October 29). Brain-IT: Image Reconstruction from fMRI via Brain-Interaction Transformer. arXiv.org. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25976

#6329. Daily smokers are growing more negative about vaping

Daily smokers report more negative views of vaping and less disapproval of smoking, a shift researchers say could complicate efforts to help them quit.

Smoking bans and health campaigns helped make smoking less socially acceptable. But adults who smoke daily now report less disapproval of the habit from people around them.

Daily smokers in four countries were surveyed between 2016 and 2022. Over those years, smokers reported less disapproval of smoking and more disapproval of vaping.

The researchers called the pattern concerning because smoking is the more harmful habit.

The analysis was led by Giang Vu at the University of Queensland. She is a researcher at its National Centre for Youth Substance Use Research.

Her focus was on social norms. These are a person’s sense of what the people around them do and approve of.

“Social norms are linked to whether people quit smoking or take up vaping, so these shifts matter for public health,” Vu said.

Only attitudes were examined in this analysis. Quitting and switching to vaping were not tracked.

The answers came from the International Tobacco Control Four Country Smoking and Vaping Survey.

It was carried out in 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022. Canada, the United States, England, and Australia took part.

Answers from 19,915 adults who smoked daily were analyzed by Vu’s team. Most of them took part in only one of the four survey rounds.

Participants were asked four questions about smoking and the same four about vaping. How many of their five closest friends smoke? What do the people important to them think about their smoking?

The other two questions covered the general public’s attitude and the smoker’s own overall opinion.

In 2016, 63.5% of daily smokers said the people important to them disapproved of their smoking. That share had dropped to 54.3% by 2022.

Less disapproval was also sensed from the wider public. In 2016, 83.3% believed the public disapproved of smoking. Six years later, 72.5% did.

Smokers’ own views shifted too. A negative opinion of smoking was held by 52.1% in 2016 and by 43% in 2022.

This decline did not start with the new surveys. An earlier analysis of the same survey program covered 2002 to 2015. It found that disapproval of smoking among daily smokers generally weakened in that period.

Taken together, the two studies point to a long-term shift, Vu’s team noted.

One measure showed no statistically significant change.

In 2016, 19% of smokers said more than half of their five closest friends smoked. The share was 17.6% in 2022.

For vaping, the answers changed in the opposite direction.

In 2016, 31.3% of daily smokers said the people important to them disapproved of vaping. By 2022, the share had grown to 41.4%.

Smokers also sensed growing disapproval of vaping among the wider public. The share who believed the public disapproved of vaping rose from 41.2% to 48.3%. Both shares were highest in 2020 and somewhat lower in 2022.

Smokers’ own opinions of vaping turned more negative as well. In 2016, 32.8% held a negative opinion of vaping. By 2022, 49.1% did, compared to 43% with a negative opinion of smoking.

Even so, vaping had not overtaken smoking on the other two questions. Smokers sensed more disapproval of smoking than of vaping from the public and from people important to them.

Vaping also became slightly more common among smokers’ friends. The share who said more than half of their five closest friends vape went from 1.6% to 2.8%.

Vaping is regulated very differently in the four countries. In England, nicotine vapes are sold in shops. They are also promoted through the national healthcare system as a way to stop smoking. Australia formalized a prescription-only system in October 2021.

Levels of disapproval differed by country. Smokers in England sensed the least disapproval of both products. Smokers in Canada sensed the most disapproval of smoking.

But the direction of change was largely shared. On seven of the eight measures, no evidence was found that trends differed by country.

The exception was negative opinion of vaping, which increased least in England.

“These trends were broadly similar regardless of smoking or vaping policies,” Vu said.

Her team suggested that international media coverage and major events may shape attitudes alongside national policy. One such event was a 2019 outbreak of lung injuries among people in the United States who vaped.

The outbreak was later linked mainly to an additive in illegal cannabis vapes. According to the team, it was wrongly blamed on nicotine vaping.

Concerns about lung health during the COVID-19 pandemic may have added to the disapproval, they wrote.

Vaping is not risk-free. But current evidence indicates that it poses substantially lower health risks than smoking, the team wrote. There is also evidence that vapes help people quit.

“A growing disapproval of vaping may discourage people who smoke from switching to a less harmful alternative,” Vu said.

The team is also worried by weaker disapproval of smoking. People who smoke daily would benefit most from quitting. Earlier research has linked disapproval of smoking to quit attempts.

Efforts to make smoking socially unacceptable may be losing their effect on this group, the team wrote. Approaches that build smokers’ confidence and address the barriers to quitting may be needed.

Vu called for public health messages that convey the risks of both products accurately.

“This would allow people who smoke to make informed choices, while continuing to protect young people who have never smoked,” she said.

The study can’t show that these attitudes changed what smokers did.

Every participant smoked daily, so the results do not represent the general public. The team also cautioned against applying them to young people.

Attitudes toward smoking and vaping have followed different patterns in that group.

The group of daily smokers may itself have changed over time. Smokers open to alternatives may have already switched to vaping or quit. That would leave a group with firmer opinions against vaping.

The vaping questions asked about approval and opinion. People were not asked how harmful they thought vaping was. Rising disapproval may therefore partly reflect its social image.

Public attention in those years centered on a rapid rise in youth vaping, the team noted. Vaping may have come to look less like a quitting aid for adults and more like a youth problem.

The answers were self-reported. The study also can’t show that any country’s policies shaped its smokers’ attitudes.

Future studies could follow smokers over time. They could test whether a change in attitudes predicts a quit attempt or a switch to vaping.

The full study was published in the journal Nicotine & Tobacco Research.

#6328. Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining

At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

The largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell says, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”

These new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”

#6327. ‘Hell chicken’ dinosaur had a bizarre jaw and an unexpected appetite

A rare skull reveals how the “hell chicken” dinosaur’s unusual sliding jaw may have helped it mash fruit, much like a living parrot.

A small dinosaur nicknamed the “hell chicken” had an unusual way of using its beak.

Its lower jaw could slide back and forth, potentially pressing soft food against the roof of its mouth. That movement may help explain what it ate.

The dinosaur, Infernogallus jamesi, appears to have worked its jaw much like a living parrot that feeds on fruit pulp.

The similarity offers one of the strongest cases yet that some dinosaurs had adapted to eat fruit.

Fruit-bearing plants spread late in the age of dinosaurs, but direct fossil evidence of those adaptations has been missing.

Gregory Funston, an assistant professor in the Department of Anatomical Sciences at Stony Brook University, led the study.

His team built its case from the skull’s shape and comparisons with living animals. No food preserved inside the fossil confirms the animal’s diet.

Scientists have debated what this dinosaur’s relatives ate for a century.

Early researchers thought they ate eggs. Later proposals included shellfish, meat, seeds, fruit and food extracted from cracks.

“For more than 100 years, we didn’t know what the skulls of these animals looked like,” Funston said.

“Now, we know they were even weirder than we could have predicted.”

Infernogallus belonged to the caenagnathids, a family of toothless, beaked dinosaurs that lived mostly in North America.

These animals had long, slender legs and air-filled bones that rarely survive intact in the rocks of the American West.

Researchers have had to piece together their lives mostly from scattered, broken bones. The new fossil gives them the family’s first complete skull.

David Evans is the chief curator of natural history at the Royal Ontario Museum (ROM) and the paper’s senior author.

“Complete remains of small dinosaurs like Infernogallus are very rare in the fossil record,” said Evans.

Collectors found the skeleton in Garfield County, Montana, in 2011. It lay in sandstone about 51 feet (15.5 meters) below the rock layer marking the end of the Cretaceous.

The team also studied jaw and skull bones from Montana and the Dakotas, including a set held by the North Dakota Geological Survey.

All the specimens came from the Hell Creek Formation. That explains the “hell” in the dinosaur’s name. Its small, birdlike body supplied the “chicken.”

Growth lines in its leg bones show that the animal had finished growing. It was at least six, and probably seven, years old when it died.

At about 26 pounds (12 kilograms), the adult weighed roughly one-fifth as much as a larger relative found in the same rocks.

Infernogallus jamesi belonged to the same broad branch of the dinosaur family tree as T. rex.

In most dinosaurs on that branch, the main jaw muscles pulled the lower jaw upward to close the mouth.

CT scans helped the researchers rebuild the Infernogallus skull on a computer and see how its jaw differed.

Bones in its palate, or the roof of its mouth, curved sharply downward. Large muscles attached there would have pulled the lower jaw mainly forward and back. The sides of the skull also had less room for biting muscles.

An opening in the skull behind the eye measured about 11% of the skull’s length. In Citipati, a well-known relative, that figure was 29%.

Together, these features suggest that Infernogallus had a much weaker bite than its relatives.

Its jaw hinge also allowed an unusual amount of movement. A rounded ridge on the lower jaw fitted into a saddle-shaped groove on the skull.

When the team fitted these bones together digitally, the lower jaw could slide back and forth by as much as 0.6 inch (15 millimeters). That is about 14% of the skull’s length.

Inside the mouth, two bones met to form a large knob pointing downward. When the jaw rested, this knob sat in a groove along the middle of the lower beak.

Ridges and grooves lined both jaws. As the lower jaw slid, these surfaces could have sheared, mashed or crushed soft food, much like a mortar and pestle.

A large attachment point for a tongue muscle also suggests that a strong tongue helped move food around.

The team found fewer signs that the dinosaur could handle tough food.

Other plant-eating dinosaurs on its branch used teeth or swallowed stones to break down fibrous plants. The stones ground food inside the gut.

Infernogallus had no teeth. Although its belly ribs survived complete, researchers found no stones in its body cavity while preparing the fossil.

It also lacked the sturdy jaw hinge and flat crushing surfaces that animals use to break nuts and hard seeds. These clues pointed toward soft food that still needed mashing before the animal swallowed it.

The researchers compared the direction of jaw-muscle pull in 19 dinosaurs and birds with different diets.

Most of the other dinosaurs grouped together because their muscles pulled mainly upward. Infernogallus stood well apart from them.

Its closest match was Pesquet’s parrot, which lives in New Guinea’s mountain forests. This bird depends on fruit, eating the soft pulp and discarding the seed.

Most parrots, including African greys, use powerful bites to crack seeds and eat what is inside. Their jaw muscles mainly pull upward.

Pesquet’s parrot also has a longer, lower skull and jaw than other parrots, with more pronounced ridges at the jaw hinge. Infernogallus differs from its dinosaur relatives in similar ways.

Thomas Dudgeon is a postdoctoral research fellow at ROM and a co-author.

“It’s pretty rare for animals to become specialized for a diet of fruit, so when it happens, it comes with some remarkable adaptations,” said Dudgeon.

“The anatomy of Infernogallus is bizarre among dinosaurs, and we quickly realized that we were dealing with something special.”

The comparison suggests that Infernogallus may have stripped flesh from fruit and left the seed behind. The researchers think it probably ate other soft plant parts as well.

The team also explored whether these dinosaurs appeared at a time when fruit could have supported them. They rebuilt the group’s family tree and estimated when its branches arose.

Their results place the family’s origin more than 100 million years ago, shortly after flowering plants began producing fruit.

Those fruits included stone fruits, which surround a single large seed with flesh, as a cherry does.

Microvenator, the family’s earliest known member, already had early versions of the palate and beak features found in Infernogallus.

The branch with the most advanced jaws appeared around 84 million years ago. After that, the family split into many more lineages, while stone fruits and other fleshy fruits were getting bigger.

Earlier studies found no broad match between the diversification of dinosaurs and flowering plants.

The team suggests that the closer timing between this dinosaur family and fleshy fruits may reflect a more specific ecological connection.

The skull makes a case for fruit eating, but it cannot settle the question on its own.

The team measured the jaw’s sliding range using bones alone. Soft tissues probably limited that movement in the living animal.

The skull had also been crushed, so researchers used better-preserved relatives to estimate where some muscles began.

Living fruit-eating birds add another complication. Some swallow fruit whole, some eat the seeds and others eat the flesh. Those different habits make it hard to identify a fruit diet from a skull alone.

The researchers also do not know whether these dinosaurs helped fruiting plants spread.

Their possible dependence on fruit raises a question about their extinction, too.

Small body size is thought to have helped birds survive the mass extinction 66 million years ago. Infernogallus was small, but its family did not survive.

The team suggests that diet may have mattered. Fruit flesh is seasonal and does not last like seeds, so relying on it could have left these dinosaurs vulnerable.

Fossilized stomach contents would provide a more direct test of what they ate.

The researchers also want to build more detailed models of their chewing movements and learn more about how living birds handle fruit. A full description of another specimen is still to come.

The study was published in Nature Communications.

A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have company this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is currently orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.

#6324. Eating a balanced diet that changes with your age is the real secret to a longer life

A review links longevity to food quality and nutrient balance for people at different stages of life; the proposed diets by age remain untested.

In laboratory animals, eating less reliably lengthens life, but people find such restricted diets hard to maintain. A recent review suggests that people may be able to live longer without eating less, by changing the mix of what they eat.

Across large human studies, the balance of carbohydrates, protein, fat, and fiber in the diet was linked to the risk of death, regardless of how many calories people ate. The review also proposes that the best balance is different at different ages.

More people are reaching old age. Scientists project that the number of adults aged 80 and older will more than triple between 2017 and 2050, reaching 425 million.

Jintao Huang and Ziyun Wu of Shanghai Jiao Tong University wrote the review. Their co-author, Dejian Huang, is at the National University of Singapore.

The three authors ran no new experiments. They drew on animal research and on more than thirty large studies involving humans; they pooled the analyses, some covering more than a million people.

Most of the human studies tracked people’s diets and deaths over many years. Such studies can link a diet to a lower risk of death, but they can’t show that the diet was the cause.

People who got about 50 to 55 percent of their daily calories from carbohydrates had the lowest risk of death. The risk was higher for people who got less than 40 percent of their calories from carbohydrates, and for those who got more than 70 percent.

Neither a very low-carb diet nor a very high-carb diet looked best in these studies.

What people ate in place of carbohydrates also mattered. Research has consistently linked low-carb diets based on animal foods to a higher risk of death, while it has linked those based on plant foods to a lower risk.

People who ate more fiber had a 10 to 23 percent lower risk of death than people who ate less. The link was stronger for fiber from whole grains and vegetables than for fiber from fruit alone.

For protein, the findings depended on a person’s age. In middle-aged adults, eating more protein – especially protein from animals – often correlated with a modestly higher risk of death.

In adults about 65 and older, eating a moderate or higher amount of protein appeared to be protective. Protein at that age counters muscle loss and frailty, the authors wrote.

One study followed 6,381 adults for about 18 years. The researchers linked high protein intake to a higher risk of death in midlife and a lower risk in older adults.

Plant protein was consistently linked to a lower risk. Statistical comparisons also showed an advantage for replacing animal protein, particularly processed red meat, with plant protein.

The authors attributed the midlife risk to growth-promoting signals in cells, which protein activates. In animal studies, reducing those signals has been tied to longer life.

With fat, the authors wrote, the type mattered more than the amount. People who had diets higher in trans fat or in saturated fat, the kind in butter and lard, had a modestly higher risk of death.

The unsaturated fats in nuts, olive oil, and fatty fish were linked to a lower risk. People who obtained most of the fat in their diet from those sources, did not show a higher risk of death.

Plant-rich eating patterns such as the Mediterranean diet were linked to a roughly 10 to 25 percent lower risk of death.

The reverse was true of ultra-processed foods, industrial products made mostly from food extracts and additives. People who ate the most of those foods had a 15 to 30 percent higher risk of death than people who ate the least.

Ultra-processed foods now supply more than half of the calories eaten in many high-income countries. The authors recommended limiting them at every age.

Lifespan gains seen in animal experiments can’t be applied directly to people, the authors wrote.

One example involves methionine, a building block of protein. Rats and mice fed a diet low in methionine lived 30 to 45 percent longer than animals on a standard diet.

The evidence in people is more limited. Trials of similar diets have typically lasted 2 to 16 weeks.

In those trials, levels of a growth signal in the blood called IGF-1 fell by 7 to 14 percent. A DNA-based estimate of how old the body is biologically didn’t measurably change.

The authors found a pattern across such comparisons. The longer a mammal normally lives, the smaller the gain in lifespan tended to be.

A second example is the ketogenic diet, which is very low in carbohydrates and high in fat. A long-term ketogenic diet lengthened the lives of mice.

Human studies, though, have linked very-low-carb diets to either no difference in the risk of death or a modestly higher risk, particularly when the diets emphasized animal foods.

The authors concluded that the ketogenic diet seems best suited to short-term use under medical supervision, and less suited to years of use for a longer life.

Existing guidelines, including the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, mainly aim to prevent chronic disease, the authors wrote, and weren’t designed with a long life as the central goal.

The authors proposed daily ranges for protein, carbohydrates, fat, and fiber at each stage of life. For adults aged 36 to 64, protein is set at 10 to 15 percent of daily calories, with more of it from plants.

Later in life, muscle loss and frailty become the main concerns. From age 65, the proposal raises protein to between 15 and 20 percent of daily calories, mainly from fish and plant foods.

For fiber, the midlife range is 40 to 60 grams a day, which is higher than the 25 to 30 grams in current dietary guidelines. The authors wrote that the higher range comes from animal experiments and isn’t established guidance.

The authors also graded their own evidence. They rated it as high for adults under 65 and as moderate for older adults. For older adults, the evidence rests mainly on measures such as muscle loss and frailty and on general dietary guidance.

A food pyramid, in the review, has water, sleep, and regular exercise at its base, beneath any food.

The authors named several gaps in the evidence behind their proposal. Three groups remain understudied: adults 75 and older, people of non-European ancestry, and people in low- and middle-income countries.

Males and females may also need different advice. In mice, a lifelong high-fat diet shortened the lives of males by about 144 days on average and didn’t significantly change the lifespan of females.

Diets may one day be personalized, the authors wrote, using data such as blood sugar readings from wearable sensors.

In one study they cited, blood sugar and blood fat responses to identical meals varied up to tenfold from person to person.

The next question is whether such personalized advice works better than standard advice. Does it keep people healthy for longer?

The authors wrote that future trials should last at least three to five years, long enough to capture changes in estimates of biological age.

Until those trials are done, personalized diet advice can’t be given “with the same confidence as recommendations for tobacco avoidance or physical activity,” the authors wrote.

As for the age-based ranges, the authors described them as testable hypotheses.

The full study was published in the journal The Innovation Nutrition.

While basic, this scrubber includes a few nifty features, including a built-in squeegee on the top of the brush to wipe away water or cleaning solution after you’ve scrubbed.

Take your cleaning to the next level with a floor scrubber that vacuums and washes at once. This maneuverability is also one of the key reasons many of the head attachments are smaller and shaped with fine points.

We recommend this scrubber for tackling messes in your bathroom, whether on tile, in the shower, on bathtubs, or in and around toilets. While it comes with a flat-head attachment that can cover more ground, this option performs best in tight spaces rather than larger areas like your living room.

This is another commercial-grade choice that works on almost any surface, including carpet. The dual scrubbing rotators have stiff bristles that break down heavy stains and set-in grime.

You can then attach the buffing or polishing pads to finish your tile or hardwood, leaving it shining smoothly. The commercial-strength design requires corded power, but the long plug means you don't need to buy an extension cord.

This option is a bit more expensive than others on the list, but it's from a reputable brand and one of the most versatile models.

Instead of relying only on cleaning detergents, the Shark floor scrubber includes a powerful steamer. Non-powered floor scrubbers are essentially heavy-duty push brooms with features that make cleaning easier, like telescoping poles and squeegees on the side opposite the bristles. They're far more affordable and compact than electric floor scrubbers, so if you’re short on space or don’t want to spend $100 or more on a new product, opt for the manual model we recommend.

#6322. The search for early signs of Alzheimer’s is looking beyond the brain’s memory center

Tracking shrinkage in two brain regions could help improve early Alzheimer’s detection, though the approach needs further testing.

Doctors searching a brain scan for Alzheimer’s disease usually look at the hippocampus, the brain’s main memory center.

A new study suggests that two neighboring regions, the entorhinal cortex and the amygdala, shrink faster than the hippocampus in older adults with memory problems.

If further research confirms that these changes precede symptoms, tracking the two regions could help identify people at risk before memory loss begins.

Michael Miller is a biomedical engineer at Johns Hopkins University and the study’s senior author.

Miller said shrinkage from the slow loss of brain cells can show up on scans as much as a decade before a person has symptoms.

“Imagine if we could start to treat the neurodegenerative changes at the 2, 3 or 4-year point rather than after 15 years when the changes are manifesting in memory symptoms,” Miller said.

“That’s the great promise here for your loved ones who are at risk.”

The study compared how fast each region shrank in groups of people at different stages of the disease. It didn’t time when the shrinkage starts, and the measurements can’t yet be used to diagnose anyone.

The findings were published in August and presented this week at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience.

In Alzheimer’s, a protein called tau clumps into tangles inside brain cells. A staging system published in 1991 mapped where those tangles appear as the disease advances.

The tangles show up first in and around the entorhinal cortex, a thin strip of tissue beside the hippocampus. They reach the hippocampus next and then spread across the brain’s outer layer.

The amygdala is a nearby region involved in processing fear and emotional memories.

The 1991 staging system doesn’t focus on the amygdala until the middle stages of the disease. Later tissue studies found tangles there relatively early too.

Tangles don’t show up on an ordinary MRI. An MRI can show a region getting smaller as its cells are lost.

But the entorhinal cortex is hard to outline on a scan. It’s thin, and it lies close to fluid-filled spaces that can confuse automated software.

Miller’s team used MRI scans from 1,149 people in two research projects that scan the same volunteers repeatedly over years. Every person had at least three scans.

Most of the volunteers, 1,019 of them, came from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, a multi-site project launched in 2003.

The other 130 came from BIOCARD, a study that began at the National Institutes of Health in 1995 and moved to Johns Hopkins in 2009.

The volunteers’ average ages at the first scan ranged from about 68 to 74. Some had typical memory for their age, and some had Alzheimer’s dementia.

Others had mild cognitive impairment, a stage of memory and thinking trouble that doesn’t yet stop a person from managing daily life.

Two people outlined the amygdala and entorhinal cortex by hand on 665 scans, with a neuroanatomist guiding the work. A deep-learning program learned from those outlines and then marked the regions across the full set of scans.

From those outlines, the team calculated how much volume each region lost per year in each person.

Among BIOCARD volunteers with mild cognitive impairment or dementia, the hippocampus lost 0.76% of its volume a year.

The amygdala lost 2.38% a year, and the entorhinal cortex, which the team measured together with a thin adjoining strip of tissue, lost 3.69%.

In the larger project, the order was the same. The hippocampus in that project’s Alzheimer’s group lost 3.23% of its volume a year, compared to 7.19% for the amygdala and 8.40% for the entorhinal cortex.

In both projects, and on both sides of the brain, the entorhinal cortex and the amygdala shrank faster than the hippocampus.

Volunteers with typical memory showed that order too, at lower rates. In the larger project, their entorhinal cortex lost 1.84% of its volume a year. The rate was 3.53% in mild cognitive impairment and 8.40% in Alzheimer’s.

So the order alone doesn’t separate healthy people from people with the disease. The pace of the loss was higher at each later stage.

Different hospitals use different scanners, and the team found that raw volume measurements varied between manufacturers. The yearly shrinkage rates were steadier.

Within each diagnostic group, the rates didn’t differ reliably between machines from GE, Philips, and Siemens.

The team also checked the shrinkage against PET scans, which use a radioactive tracer to show where tau has built up.

Among volunteers with mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer’s, people with a stronger tau signal in the entorhinal cortex were also losing volume there faster. The team found the same link in the hippocampus, and in both projects.

The team rebuilt the surface of the entorhinal cortex in more than 400 computer models to measure its thickness. The faster the region lost volume, the faster that sheet of tissue thinned.

Inside the amygdala, the loss was uneven. In one group with mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer’s, three subregions toward the middle of the brain shrank by 6.34% to 8.31% a year.

The subregion on the outer side shrank by 2.52%.

The outer subregion also had the fewest tangles in postmortem Alzheimer’s brain tissue that the group had mapped in an earlier study.

The scans show tau and tissue loss in the same places. They can’t show that the tau caused the loss.

The team also asked a practical question: Can these two regions help distinguish people with typical memory from those with early mild cognitive impairment?

To find out, they tested 346 volunteers with typical memory and 210 with early mild cognitive impairment.

A statistical model was first built using only hippocampus measurements.

It scored 0.635 on a scale where 0.5 is a coin flip and 1 is perfect. When the amygdala and entorhinal cortex were added, the score rose to 0.665.

The authors described that performance as moderate.

Most of the gain came from fewer healthy people being wrongly flagged. At the same detection rate, about eight fewer healthy people in every 100 were misclassified.

Scientists call any measurable sign of a disease a biomarker. A scan result is one example, and a blood test is another.

“As biomarkers and treatments become increasingly available, knowing who is going to have cognitive decline is going to be really important,” said co-author Meaghan Morris.

The new analysis didn’t measure how long before symptoms the shrinkage starts. The decade Miller described comes from a 2014 study by some of the same researchers.

The 2014 study estimated that shrinkage in this part of the brain speeds up almost 10 years before the symptoms of mild cognitive impairment begin.

The volunteers’ average ages were around 70, so the scans say little about what these regions look like in younger adults.

Miller reported holding equity in AnatomyWorks, a company that develops digital anatomy atlases. The team hopes to learn what is happening at the molecular level around the tau changes in the two regions.

“Once we know more about the molecular neighborhoods, we can develop therapies,” Miller said.

Future research could test whether tracking the two regions in people without symptoms predicts who goes on to develop them.

The full study was published in the journal NeuroImage: Reports.

Scientists are racing to restore people’s ability to communicate. Powerful AI-based methods to decode speech signals and predict words, along with advances in technology, promise success.

This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me takes listeners through the breadth of scientific efforts to restore words, emotions and even gestures to people who can’t move or talk.
