Jules: Conan is very special to me. Watching and listening to him helped me disconnect from the harsh reality of my life. And when I got to meet him and chat with him, it meant the world to me.

Maria Aleandra Fernandez: Having the most normal conversation with Conan O’Brien is something I will never get over.

[Audio] So he has a bunch of banked phrases. He’s going to play a few of our favorites. OK. I’m fine. I’m perfectly [beep] fine. [laughter] Come on man, are we doing this or not? Oh my God, oh my God. I’m destroying this marriage. MA: He really is so genuine and like, not only willing to talk to us, but really looks forward to talking. Like, I love talking to you guys. I’m not just doing it to be a nice person, which feels, you know, feels wonderful.

[Audio] You have my love, my respect and we’re thinking about you guys all the time.

Sanders: As you were talking earlier, it made me think about what it means to make somebody laugh and to entertain them, and like how actually very, very special that must be. Just kind of, at its heart, it’s, it is joy and humans connecting. And so, extra special.

MA: That’s the other thing I’ve learned mainly through Jules, about humor and comedy. And who were we watching yesterday? The NPR interview with Dave Chappelle. [Audio] Dave Chappelle says he is very clear about his role as a comedian.

MA: And Dave Chappelle said something that is so spot-on. He said that comedians are how people metabolize things.

[Audio] We’re like the nation’s kidney. We help everyone metabolize not just facts, but feelings around facts, or ideas. And jokes are just a shorthand for all of that.

MA: And I’m also a nerd and I’ve been reading some Greek tragedies and studying about how, you know, that’s also like the artists that help people metabolize feelings and emotions. And when he said that, I was like, that’s exactly it. And that’s what Jules has done.

It’s something that heals. And it’s not even like it’s self-deprecating. It’s not like, oh, let’s make fun. And the way he does it is so smart and genuine, but also not taking himself seriously. It just disarms everything. You’re just like, oh, OK. And that idea of metabolizing the really hard feelings that come around grief, mortality, losing a person, seeing how he’s trapped in his body, but he chooses not to be trapped in that really big way is so profound.

Sanders: Science is iterative. It builds. It may take a wrong turn or two, but overall, it’s moving toward a deeper understanding of our world and of ourselves.

By using their voices, by telling their stories, by telling their jokes, Jules and MA are helping me, and maybe you too, metabolize the pain – and the joy – of living. Welcome to The Deep End, Talk to Me.

[Voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi.

Sanders: I’m Laura Sanders and today, we’re going to look ahead to what’s coming next for the human voice and efforts to restore it.

Sanders: In some ways, this podcast is a story of progress, of figuring out, little by little, more about the brain, and more about technology and more about people. Today, Jules can type with his eyes, and his son can hear his dad’s voice say I love you. In earlier episodes, you heard from Casey Harrell. Casey can think about saying a word to his daughter, and boom, they’re off playing a game together.

Casey Harrell: So this has kept me still in touch with people and the world, and it is not hyperbole to frame it this way.

Sanders: Casey has ALS and can no longer speak. He volunteered for a clinical trial, and now he has a device implanted in his brain that detects neural patterns as he tries to say a word. This system has changed his life.

Casey: It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends. Timing is everything, and that is why having nothing, this is completely revolutionary.

Sanders: But there aren’t many people like Casey. Leigh Hochberg is the director of the BrainGate clinical trials consortium, the trial that Casey is participating in. I asked him how many people might have participated in similar sorts of research projects. How many people have electrodes in their brain that can help them speak?

Leigh Hochberg: In terms of actually decoding attempted speech, I’m almost sure it’s still less than 10. It may be closer to five or six, so far, and that number undoubtedly is going to increase fairly quickly.

Sanders: So this is a small but growing number. Growing, because we now have a solid scientific understanding of the brain’s speech signals, and other signals too. And neurotech companies are very interested.

Hochberg: About 10 years ago or so, the academic research had de-risked this field sufficiently that it allowed for the entry of now likely a dozen or more companies that are actively pursuing their own version of an implantable brain-computer interface.

What I anticipate will happen, what I guess I hope will happen, is that the companies will continue to very carefully, thoughtfully and in a very focused manner, create their systems, and test them rigorously. And hopefully they’ll be demonstrated to be safe and effective. And at the same time, the academic groups have the opportunity to continue to demonstrate what’s possible, to push beyond that, and to show hopefully what those medical devices, once they’re actually available to market, might be able to do next.

Sanders: I talked with Vikash Gilja, a neural engineer who works at a company called Paradromics. He sees this momentum that Hochberg describes too.

Vikash Gilja: And, you know, we can see all the pieces coming together. These tools weren’t available even five years ago. And what we’re seeing is like, you know, month over month, there are new tools available. So we’re able to leverage those and move faster.

Sanders: Paradromics has developed its own brain-computer interface for communication. The device is about the size of a dime, and it sits on the motor cortex. That’s the part of the brain that creates speech signals. The chip then detects these signals as a person thinks about saying a word.

Matthew Willsey: So the cortical module has 421 tiny little sensors.

Sanders: That’s neurosurgeon and biomedical engineer Matthew Willsey, of the University of Michigan Health. He’s describing the device from Paradromics here.

Willsey: They’re about one and a half millimeters long. And you know, it’s smaller than your thumbnail, like kind of all the way around. It’s like a cylinder. And at the bottom of the cylinder are the electrodes, is what we call them. And we get them really close to the brain. And then when we deploy it, what it does is it pushes those electrodes down into the brain.

Sanders: Those tiny sensors are listening to the nearby neurons that control the muscles required for speech.

Willsey: The principle is to try and get these things as small as possible to disrupt the least amount of tissue as possible, and then to get them really, really close to the individual cells, the neurons themselves that have the information we’re trying to record.

Sanders: The goal here is to restore a person’s ability to talk.

Willsey: So in the ideal situation, the electrodes would sit, you know, right next to those neurons. This type of technology that’s very intuitive, that can record activity from the brain in kind of a high-throughput way, can put the words up at a good speed and a good accuracy, allows them to kind of regain the ability to communicate with others close to how they maybe were before they had the illness. So that truly is very powerful.

Sanders: You might remember that Casey’s implant, called the BrainGate 2 system, requires ports on his head that are connected to external wires.

Casey: What is annoying about this device is really easy to answer. It is not portable, and it is not implanted only inside my head.

Sanders: Unlike Casey’s implant, the Paradromics device is fully implantable. That means it’s wireless. This summer, Willsey implanted Paradromic’s device in a volunteer’s brain. The brain belonged to a 68-year-old woman who lives in Michigan. She has primary lateral sclerosis, a disease that has taken away most of her ability to talk. So far, the Paradromics system is up and running, and the volunteer is testing her abilities out.

Here she is talking with Willsey and other researchers in a video provided by Paradromics. You’ll hear her natural voice, which is hard to understand, and then a digital voice speaking the words her brain implant decoded.

[Audio] I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. Yeah, it’s good.

Sanders: This volunteer has used the device to talk to her grandkids on the phone. But this is just the very beginning for this research project. There’s so much more to test.Casey is still working on his system, too — particularly, streamlining the process. When Casey uses his brain-computer interface, it decodes speech signals from his brain, then puts words on a screen. Casey then selects a button, using his eye movements or his brain-computer interface, to say these words out loud with a digital voice. Here’s Casey.

Casey: It is not fast enough to provide enough instant conversation with other people that need to slow down to talk to me.

Sanders: But scientists want to skip this middle part — the words written on a screen. They want instead to go straight to speech, and perhaps make conversations faster. Casey says this goal to go directly from brain signals to a speaking digital voice would be his top priority.

Casey: That one is the holy grail of what this will become in terms of speech. It will allow you to have a seamless conversation. I am talking about, yes, I will intend to talk, and then it will just translate that automatically into speech, like we do, and you are doing right now.

Sanders: In an earlier episode, we talked about attempts to do just this with Casey’s system, to push it to do what they call brain-to-voice. Early attempts were hard to decipher. But it has already improved, by a lot. In the latest tests, this brain-to-voice process produces words that are understandable – reaching about 95 percent accuracy for listeners. Here’s Casey speaking test sentences. It comes from a preprint manuscript posted on the website bioRxiv.

[Audio] The day is not over yet. Please come in with me.

Sanders: Scientists have another thing on their to-do list. And this one goes beyond the words themselves. Here’s Gilja, from Paradromics.

Gilja: Let’s say I identify whether a sentence is a statement or a question. Well, now you can pass that information on to speech synthesis, so that you get these two different versions.

Sanders: The same words could be a statement or a question. You see what he means. You see what he means? And that information can be pulled out from a person’s brain activity.

Gilja: If I’m decoding prosodic information, if I’m decoding speed, when a word is meant to appear, that can also be passed on to modern speech synthesis systems, so that you’re more accurately capturing the prosody that somebody intends. Same thing with loudness, right? So you can see how as that information becomes available from the neural channels, it can be provided to the AI speech synthesis to get closer to the intended voice in the moment that the individual wants to generate.

Sanders: All of these signals can be collected and used to build a more accurate voice — one that says things exactly how a person intends to say them, like a Minnesotan’s ooftah or a slow southern hey y’all. Now, today’s voice clones can add these emotional layers onto words already. Here’s what Jules told me when I asked him about whether his voice clone can do it.

Jules: Oh, there are plenty of things it does that are all the above. But one thing in particular is how it inserts tone and inflections on words. Sometimes my wife will get mad because my response can come off with some sass.

Sanders: So there’s loudness, emphasis, pitch — all of these things contribute to what words means. But imagine if a brain implant can pick up these cues directly — no typing required. Here’s Hochberg.

Hochberg: There’s a lot that can be conveyed through the emphasis, through the tone, through even the humor that can sometimes be conveyed by the way that somebody who’s able-bodied may speak a particular sentence. All of those, I think, really can be captured by these implantable brain-computer interfaces by harnessing the rich neural activity that’s available from the brain. We should be able to restore a lot of that.

Sanders: Sergey Stavisky is one of the UC Davis researchers working with Casey and Hochberg. He and his colleagues are working on some of these ideas.

Stavisky: And even now we’re continuing to improve that and actually adding additional layers. So we have one forward-looking project where we can maybe decode the kind of emotional valence of how he’s trying to say it. Is he trying to say something in an angry way or in a surprised way or in a happy-sounding way, to kind of further make it more expressive.

Sanders: They’re even trying  to decode singing. Well, OK, it’s really more of a hum at this point, he says. But those sorts of tone shifts could, in theory, be deciphered.

Stavisky: We definitely have our work cut out for us on the singing and melody side of things.

Sanders: All sorts of voice signals could be pulled from brain activity.

Stavisky: Ultimately, we want people to be in full control of what they’re communicating. This should come from their intent. So, yeah, we are trying to decode all of the aspects of his voice, whether it’s the pitch, the timbre, the loudness, the intonation, which word he’s stressing. All of that, ideally, we would decode from brain activity, including kind of all of that emotional nuance.

Sanders: Voice clones can speak with various emotions. You heard my voice clone do just that in earlier episodes. But the difference here is that a person wouldn’t have to type in the instructions. They would come straight from their brain, seamlessly. Other nonverbal signals can be pulled from the brain, too.

Samantha Brosler: In the past five years or so, there have been a lot of advancements in the field of BCIs for restoring individual functions to people with paralysis.

Sanders: That’s Samantha Brosler, a bioengineer at the University of California, San Francisco. Some brain-computer interfaces can pick up movements. We haven’t talked much about them, but these implants have their own very successful research history. They’ve allowed people to control a robotic arm, for instance.

Brosler: Most of these devices so far have been designed to restore one function at a time, whereas in reality, frequently people who are paralyzed are missing both the ability to speak and perform body movements. And so in this study, we asked whether a single brain implant could be used to decode both speech and movement at the same time.

Sanders: It turns out, it could. She and her colleagues were able to decode gestures for communication — things like thumbs up, or a head nodding yes — and words. This combo approach is a more natural way of getting a point across.

Brosler: We naturally use gestures alongside our speech. So for example, some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up. But they can also add or change the meaning of what we’re saying. So for example, if you say maybe combined with nod head yes, that has a very different, you know, meaning than if you say maybe and shrug or shake your head no.

Sanders: My kids know that a slow maybe with a skeptical eyebrow raise is much closer to a no than my fast upbeat maybe with a little head nod. There is so much subtext in our body language.

Brosler: So I think of, you know, gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech to add expressivity to what we’re trying to say.

Sanders: In the study, the output was a digital avatar who looked like the person. Success looked like the avatar moving and getting the word right.

Brosler: And the idea is that we enable the participants to use speech and gestures alone or together. So in theory, someone could say hello while waving.

Sanders: The researchers started simple, with just a few phrases — hello, bye, good idea, how’s it going, let’s go — and just a few gestures, like a shrug or a point, a fist pump, thumbs up.

Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

Sanders: The sheer number of different approaches to restoring communication is a sign that this neurotechnology is coming fast. Here’s Willsey.

Willsey: I think it’s good. There’s a lot of players that are entering into the field that have a variety of different ideas where they can run the clinical trials and see how these different devices stack up.

Sanders: There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about the future here, and it’s a future that isn’t even that far off. Here’s David Brandman, one of the researchers at UC Davis who works with Casey. He’s also the neurosurgeon who implanted Casey’s device.

Brandman: I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation, and saying, you know, Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate despite facing a future of paralysis. It’s a device that would be implanted. It’s fully wirelessly. It’s cosmetically invisible, and you’d be able to use it to communicate your needs and have a meaningful conversation with friends and family. So I think that kind of conversation is about five to 10 years away.

Sanders: It’s a beautiful vision. When you’ve been a reporter as long as I have, you’re skeptical when scientists say something big is just five to 10 years away. But in this case, I see it.

It’s easy to get drawn into the technical details here. Different types of implants, the decoding processes, AI-powered voice clones and what they can do and can’t do — what they should do and shouldn’t do. But if you step back and really look, you’ll see that this research is all propelled by a very simple and powerful fact: The human voice is too important to lose.

Casey: What does my voice mean to me? It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: So now we are here, in this moment, as Jules would say, right here, right now. And right now, the human voice is shifting and changing, expanding in ways that were completely unthinkable even just a few years ago. The future of the human voice and its many replicas is anybody’s guess.

Sanders: In one of Jules’ comedy sets, the one he did in November of 2024, he wheels out onto the stage as the song “Walking on Sunshine” plays.

As the crowd settles and finishes their clapping and woo-ing, Jules pauses. You can’t see this, but he wiggles his eyebrows — a lot. The crowd goes crazy every time. He hasn’t said a single word yet. After another pause, he deadpans with his voice clone: “That is all the time I have. My Make-A-Wish covered only a few minutes. Goodnight, everybody.”

And with that, Jules takes control and he’s off on a tear, ripping through stories of a weatherman who seems too happy about standing out in hurricanes, the exquisite guilt trips lovingly crafted by his Cuban parents, and the indignities of having body parts shaved with his sister right there in the room. Jules has the audience laughing so hard. It’s magnificent.

MA: And being backstage and then seeing him come out, like roll out in his wheelchair and everybody go nuts because they’re like, what is going on here? Like, this doesn’t make sense. And every time I was like, this is like life. This is love. This is passion. This is like, what else is there? Like, I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here and what I can help him do.

Sanders: I get what MA meant when she said that comedy is something that heals. When his set actually does come to a close, he tells the audience. [Audio] Now you have to watch me slowly get off this stage. Goodnight, everybody.

Sanders: It’s hilarious. It’s happy. It’s sad. It’s perfect.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast, tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

The Deep End is a production of Science News. It’s based on original reporting by me, Laura Sanders. This episode was produced and mixed by Ella Rowen. Our project manager is Ashley Yeager. Nancy Shute is our editor in chief. Our music is by Blue Dot Sessions. The podcast is made possible in part by the Burroughs Wellcome Fund, with support from PRX.

#6320. Do fitness trackers help people exercise more? The answer is complicated

Fitness tracker users were more likely to meet exercise guidelines, but a new study cannot show whether the devices made them more active.

Step trackers, health apps, and patient portals offer different ways to monitor and manage health.

An analysis of a national U.S. survey found that these tools were not equally associated with getting enough exercise.

In the analysis reported by Heejun Kim and colleagues, adults were sorted into groups based on the tools they used.

Among adults in the wearable-centered group, 31.4% met both federal exercise guidelines.

Among adults who used few tools, 18.2% met both guidelines, compared with 19.9% of those centered on a patient portal. No clear difference could be found between these last two groups.

A patient portal is a secure website where patients can view test results and exchange messages with their health care providers.

The results suggest that the mix of tools may reveal more about exercise habits than any single device.

Kim, who led the study, is a doctoral student in sport analytics at the University of Mississippi. Kim worked with Ju-Pil Choe, also a doctoral student, and Professor Minsoo Kang of the Department of Kinesiology and Sport.

Because participants answered the survey only once, the findings show associations and cannot establish whether these tools make people more active.

Choe described two people as an example. The first person has a smartwatch and checks the step count on it each day.

The second person opens a patient portal for lab results or a message to a doctor. That person has never owned a fitness tracker.

“Both are using digital health tools, but in very different ways,” Choe said.

Data came from the 2024 Health Information National Trends Survey, a nationally representative survey of U.S. adults run by the National Cancer Institute.

Wearable users had been compared with non-users in studies of the 2019 and 2022 rounds.

Among the users, the odds of meeting activity recommendations were found to be higher in both. Those studies could not show which other digital tools the same people used.

Kim’s team instead took 17 questions from the survey, each of which could be answered yes or no. All of them referred to the 12 months before the survey.

The questions covered wearables, health apps, patient portals, telehealth visits, online health searches and health-related social media posts.

There were 5,804 adults who had answered every one of these questions. Based on their response patterns, the team sorted them into four groups.

The largest of the four groups, which made up 34.3% of the adults, was the one centered on patient portals. Its members messaged providers and viewed test results online, but very few of them used a wearable.

The broad group, representing 32% of adults, used almost every tool covered by the survey.

A third group of 11.8% relied on wearables and apps, whereas portals were used much less.

The remaining 21.9% of adults were placed in a limited group, in which few digital health tools were used. Most of its members did, however, use social media and look up health information online.

Two targets are set for adults by the federal Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans. The first is at least 150 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity.

The second is muscle-strengthening activity, which is to be done on two or more days of the week.

Of the 4,930 adults with complete answers, 25.1% met both exercise guidelines. However, the rates varied between groups.

In the broad group, 32.7% met both exercise guidelines, compared with 31.4% in the wearable group. The rates were lower in the portal group (19.9%) and limited group (18.2%).

These differences remained after researchers accounted for age, sex, income, education, race, ethnicity, body mass index, smoking and other factors.

Compared with the limited group, the broad group had 2.8 times the odds of meeting both guidelines, while the wearable group had 2.1 times the odds.

The difference between the portal and limited groups was too small to rule out chance.

For strength training, the picture was not the same as for aerobic activity. Higher odds of meeting the strength guideline were seen in all three other groups, including the portal-centered group.

Those odds were about 2.6 times (broad), 1.6 times (wearable-centered) and 1.6 times (portal-centered) the odds of the limited group.

The share of adults who met this guideline was 32.5% in the limited group and 49.5% in the broad group.

For the aerobic guideline, it was only the broad group that clearly differed from the limited group.

The lowest aerobic rate of the four groups was reported by the portal-centered adults, at 34.5%. In the limited group the rate was 40.2%, but this gap too was small enough to be due to chance.

A possible reason for the difference was offered by the authors. Strength training may be a more deliberate and planned kind of exercise than aerobic activity is.

As such, it could fit the broader habits of health management which portal use reflects.

The authors wrote that aerobic minutes can be accumulated through both structured workouts and everyday movement. For this reason, aerobic activity may be tied less closely to any one set of digital habits.

Kang said that a person who has more digital health tools is not necessarily a more active person. What counts for more, in Kang’s view, is the way in which people use the tools from day to day.

In the limited group, 12.9% of adults had not finished high school. A household income of less than $20,000 a year was reported by 25.7% of the group.

Among the other three groups, the share that had not finished high school stayed between 1.1% and 4.2%. The share living in households below that income stayed between 8.6% and 11.7%.

The limited group was also set apart by age. Of its members, 10.2% were people aged 75 or older, and in no other group was this share so large.

The broad group had the most college graduates, at 47.3%. The broad group also had the most adults in households which earned $100,000 or more, at 49.8%.

More digital tools were not simply a mark of better health, however. Of the four groups, the broad one had the highest average body mass index (29.5).

Choe said that people may be missed when exercise programs are built mainly around apps and wearables. These, Choe said, are people who would benefit from extra support.

The survey cannot prove that trackers increase exercise. Active people may be more likely to buy them. Digital skills or health care access may also play a role.

An earlier review found that trackers can help when used in behavior-change programs, which this study did not test.

People reported their own exercise and may have overstated it. The survey also missed vigorous activity, possibly counting some active adults as falling short.

Of 7,278 respondents, 2,348 (32.3%) were excluded due to missing answers.

Among those excluded from the digital-use grouping analysis, 52.7% were 65 or older, compared with 17.7% of those kept. Those excluded also had less education and lower incomes.

A second analysis included people with missing answers. The same four groups appeared, with 97.7% staying in their original group.

In this analysis, the portal group had 1.5 times the odds of meeting both guidelines compared with the limited group. The wearable group also had higher odds of meeting the aerobic guideline.

The authors suggested different ways to help each group exercise more.

Tracker users could get feedback and goals, while portal users could receive reminders through messages or appointments.

People who use few digital tools might need more in-person or community support.

The study did not test these ideas. More research is needed to see whether this support helps people exercise more.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Physiology.

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.

#6317. Fossils found in Thailand reveal a giant rodent that weighed about 66 pounds

Two fossil teeth from Thailand reveal an ancient rodent estimated to weigh 66 pounds, offering new evidence of how early rodents grew large.

Most rodents are small or medium-sized, but fossils reveal that some ancient species grew much larger.

Scientists found a fossil tooth in a coal mine in southern Thailand that belonged to an unusually large rodent.

The researchers believe it weighed about 30 kilograms (66 pounds). They named it Yakamys sirindhornae.

Sixty-six pounds is about what a large North American beaver weighs. Yakamys lived about 34 million years ago. The giant rodents of South America are the largest ever found but they came long after it.

The find suggests that rodents grew large earlier than fossils had shown. It also suggests they did so in more parts of the world. For now, the evidence is two teeth.

Both teeth were found in a layer of clay inside the main coal seam of a mine in Krabi Province. They were collected by a Thai-French fossil expedition.

The project was designed by Yaowalak Chaimanee of the University of Poitiers in France.

The co-authors work in France and Canada and at Thailand’s Department of Mineral Resources. The fossils are now held by that department.

One tooth is a lower molar, which is a grinding tooth from the back of the jaw. The other is a broken piece of a lower incisor. Incisors are the long front teeth a rodent gnaws with.

The clay is roughly 35.1 million to 33.7 million years old. That age is based on other mammals found at the site and on magnetism preserved in the rock.

In the name Yakamys, the word yak is Thai for giant and mys is Greek for mouse or rat.

The species name honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn for her long support of science and fossil research in Thailand.

The molar is 0.46 inch (11.56 millimeters) long and almost as wide. That sounds small. It isn’t small next to the teeth of its relatives.

Yakamys belongs to Ischyromyidae, one of the earliest major families of rodents. Its molar is the largest yet described among early members of that family.

Until now, an animal called Hulgana was regarded as the largest Asian member of the family. Its molars are less than half as long and less than half as wide.

The closest in size is Manitsha tanka. This rodent was described from South Dakota in 1941. Its lower second molar measures about 0.32 by 0.35 inch (8.2 by 8.9 millimeters).

The incisor was cut lengthwise by the team to place Yakamys in that family. Its enamel was then examined under an electron microscope.

The banding inside the enamel is consistent with the pattern reported for other members of the family.

No bones of Yakamys have been found and so its weight had to be estimated from tooth measurements.

Bigger teeth go with heavier bodies in living rodents and this relationship has been turned into equations.

Virginie Millien is a biologist at McGill University in Canada. She applied seven published equations to the two teeth. The answers ranged from 47 to 104 pounds (21.4 to 47.3 kilograms).

The seven answers averaged 70 pounds (31.6 kilograms) and the middle value was 63 pounds (28.6 kilograms).

The team took the midpoint of those two figures and rounded it to 30 kilograms, or 66 pounds.

The weight reported by the team is therefore a rounded summary of answers that disagree. Millien called it “only a ballpark figure.”

Estimates of this kind are uncertain because the link between tooth size and body weight varies among living rodents. The estimates span roughly 24 to 152 pounds (10.8 to 69 kilograms) when each margin of error is included.

The weights of giant rodents have been revised sharply before. One South American giant was first estimated at more than 2,200 pounds (1,000 kilograms).

Later studies that included one by Millien in 2008 estimated about 770 pounds (350 kilograms).

Rodents include more species than any other group of living mammals. Their oldest fossils come from North America. Very large body size has evolved in only a few branches of the group.

The best-known giants lived in South America long after Yakamys. Large species were rarely documented among early rodents and Manitsha was one of the few examples.

The fossil record of the family in Asia was sparse. Most of it came from small animals in China and India.

Yakamys extends the known range of the family into Southeast Asia. It is also evidence that one early rodent line had already grown large by about 34 million years ago.

Yakamys and Manitsha are similar in estimated weight but their molars are built differently. To the authors, that suggests large size in this family wasn’t tied to one tooth design.

Giant rodents are commonly linked to life on islands. That explanation is hard to apply to Yakamys.

The authors wrote that the ancient geography of the Krabi area doesn’t point to an island. Neither do the other mammals found there.

The clay that held the teeth formed in a lake. Many other fossil mammals have been found in the coal around it.

One possibility was raised by the team. Yakamys may have lived along lake edges much as capybaras live near water today. Food there may have been plentiful.

But lake clay alone doesn’t show that an animal spent time in the water.

More complete fossils that include skull and skeleton bones would be needed to test the idea. More evidence from the rocks and the other animals at the site would be needed too.

Two teeth aren’t enough to establish exactly where Yakamys belongs within its family. The researchers could not run a formal analysis to identify its closest relatives.

Even the pairing of the teeth is tentative. The molar and the incisor were found close together in the same layer. The team assigned both to one species because both are unusually large.

A 3D model of the molar is available through MorphoMuseuM, an open online collection of 3D specimens. Other researchers can examine the tooth there.

Yakamys may not have been the first large rodent in the region.

An unpublished rodent incisor from older rocks in Myanmar is held by the same team. It is considerably larger than the incisors of other rodents described from the region.

The Myanmar incisor hasn’t been formally described or identified. Its size alone can’t show what kind of rodent it came from.

One question remains open. Was large body size a local event or a more widespread part of early rodent evolution?

More fossils from Myanmar and elsewhere in the region will be needed to answer it.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

#6316. Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

#6315. Protecting forest birds may depend on what happens outside park boundaries

Forest birds in small national park sites may depend as much on surrounding forests as on habitat within park boundaries, a new study suggests.

Drawing the boundaries of a national park on a map is easy. Trees stay where they grow, but birds don’t follow those boundaries.

Forest birds such as thrushes, warblers, and woodpeckers may build their nests inside national parks, but they often depend on the land outside those parks too.

Researchers examined eight small national park sites in the northeastern United States, comparing forest characteristics inside each park with those in the surrounding county.

Bird presence inside the parks was associated with forest characteristics across the surrounding county at least as strongly as with those across the park itself.

Small parks are therefore unlikely to protect forest birds without help from the land around them.

The analysis was carried out by Bruna Amaral, who is a doctoral student at Michigan State University. Her collaborator Elise Zipkin is an ecologist who heads the university’s Ecology, Evolution, and Behavior program.

Sixteen species were included in the work. The researchers asked only whether each species was present at a given survey point.

Bird numbers and nesting success were not followed. The results therefore describe a pattern and cannot be used to prove a cause.

Surveys were conducted each May and June between 2006 and 2023. Volunteers with the National Park Service’s Northeast Temperate Network visited fixed points in the forest of every park.

At each point, an observer spent ten minutes recording every bird within 164 feet (50 meters).

Roughly 91% of the records came from birds identified by their sound. Only those sound records were used in the analysis.

All 16 species are classed as forest birds. The wood thrush, the ovenbird, the scarlet tanager, and several warblers are included among them.

The parks were not created for wildlife. They are national historic sites and historical parks whose main purpose is the preservation of history.

The smallest park covers only 69 acres (28 hectares), which is close to the area of 50 football fields. About 2,860 acres (1,156 hectares) are covered by the largest park.

Acadia National Park was excluded from the study. One reason given was that it is more than ten times larger than the other parks.

Which forest was most closely tied to the presence of each bird? That was the question put to the data.

Three candidates were considered. The first was the forest within a quarter mile (400 meters) of the survey point. The whole park was the second, and the surrounding county was the third.

Five measures were used to describe the forest at each scale. Among them were conifer amount, shrub cover, and the number of large old trees.

Because a bird feeds, nests, and hides in the nearest forest, the team had expected it to matter most.

The researchers identified 40 statistically significant associations between bird presence and forest characteristics, involving 13 of the 16 species.

County forest accounted for 19 of the 40 links. Another 16 links were to the forest near the survey point. Only five were to the park as a whole.

So the forest averaged across a whole park showed the fewest links of the three. That is the very area a boundary defines.

The authors described the county result as surprising. These parks hold older and more varied forest than the land around them.

Three species were linked only to county forest. They were the wood thrush, the scarlet tanager, and the brown creeper.

Bark is where a brown creeper finds its food. The small brown-and-white bird climbs tree trunks in a spiral and pulls insects from the cracks.

Creepers were more likely to be present in a park when its county’s forests had more or bigger trees.

Fewer shrubs in those county forests were also tied to their presence. Inside the parks, no forest measure showed a reliable link to the bird.

“Species rarely respect human-made boundaries,” the authors wrote.

The forest close to each survey point was linked to ten species. Different species, however, were linked to different kinds of forest.

The black-throated blue warbler nests in shrubs. It was more likely to be present where shrub cover was thick and large old trees were fewer.

Downy woodpeckers dig their nest holes in decayed wood. These birds were more likely to be present where large old trees were plentiful and conifers were scarce.

Downy woodpeckers occurred in every park where black-throated blue warblers were recorded, suggesting those parks contain forest conditions suitable for both species.

Only weak, mixed links were found between park size and the birds. Five species were more likely to be present in bigger parks, and two were less likely. No pattern at all was seen for most species.

The team didn’t test why county forest would be tied to the birds inside a park.

One possible reason lies in the weeks after young birds leave the nest, Amaral said. Survival in that period depends partly on the land a young bird moves through before migrating south.

Earlier research on wood thrushes found that young birds do move this way. Mature forest is left behind for younger woods with dense undergrowth.

There the young thrushes eat insects and fruit and hide from predators.

Edges are another possibility. More forest edge is found in a county with broken-up forest, and nest predators are more active at edges.

Birds returning from migration may also pick a region first. A nesting territory would then be chosen second.

The land around the eight parks varies widely. Minute Man National Historical Park in Massachusetts lies in an open, broken-up landscape.

Marsh-Billings-Rockefeller National Historical Park in Vermont, by contrast, lies in a broadly forested county.

“We need to start to think beyond park boundaries,” Amaral said.

Benefits from bird-friendly backyards and farms can reach the parks next to them, Zipkin said.

Conservation easements were also suggested by the team. These are legal agreements that limit development on private land. They may be easier to arrange than enlarging a park.

The counts show whether a species was present. Once birds arrive, their nesting success may still be shaped by the park’s own forest, the authors wrote.

Only one park-wide value and one county value per forest measure came from each park. Estimates at those two scales are therefore less precise than the estimates for nearby forest.

What the measures capture is the kind of forest found in a county. How much forest a county holds was not part of them.

Every one of the eight parks is small, and about 60% of the surrounding region is still forest. No data on bird population trends in the surrounding counties were available to the team.

Trends inside and outside the parks could therefore not be compared.

The authors identified a next step: testing whether a park’s surroundings influence how birds respond to forest conditions inside it. This could help managers apply the findings.

The full study was published in the journal Landscape Ecology.

#6314. October broke a global heat record, and El Niño is still strengthening

October 2026 was the warmest October on record, as an intensifying El Niño added to global warmth and ocean temperatures reached new highs.

The global average surface air temperature in October 2026 was 15.35°C.

That’s 0.90°C above the 1991–2020 average and enough to make it the warmest October in the ERA5 record, beating October 2023 by 0.05°C.

It was also 1.75°C above the estimated pre-industrial baseline.

The data come from the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the European Union’s climate monitoring service. And the numbers keep stacking.

Before August 2026, the last individual month above 1.5°C was November 2025. Then August, September and October crossed it.

The last streak of three or more consecutive months above 1.5°C ended in April 2025.

The rolling twelve-month average – November 2025 through October 2026 – now sits at 1.51°C above pre-industrial levels.

January through October 2026 ranks as the second-warmest such period on record, 0.07°C below the same stretch in 2024 and 0.05°C above 2023.

A statistical model trained on 1979–2025 data gives 2026 a greater than 99% chance of exceeding 1.5°C for the full calendar year. That would make it only the second calendar year above that level after 2024.

There’s roughly an 80% probability it finishes as the second-warmest year on record and about a 20% chance it ties or exceeds 2024 for the top spot.

If 2026 does exceed 1.5°C, the four-year average for 2023–2026 would also cross that line.

An intensifying El Niño is adding to the global warmth. Sea surface temperatures across 60°S–60°N hit 20.95°C in October.

This is the highest October value ever recorded. The previous October record was set in 2023 during a developing El Niño. This one is considerably stronger.

The Niño 3.4 region – the patch of equatorial Pacific used to define El Niño intensity – averaged 29.94°C in October. That’s an all-time high for the region in any month, surpassing the record set just one month earlier in September.

The anomaly was +3.21°C, also a record, above September’s +2.99°C. For context, this exceeds the peaks of the monster El Niños of 1982–83, 1997–98, and 2015–16.

Across much of the central equatorial Pacific, temperatures ran more than 3°C above average. Along the Peruvian coast and west of the Galápagos, the anomalies reached 6 to 7°C.

The World Meteorological Organization expects this El Niño to peak in December 2026 and to persist through at least February 2027.

The ocean heat isn’t confined to the Pacific. Record October sea surface temperatures were also logged in parts of the northern Indian Ocean, the South Atlantic, and the subtropical North Atlantic.

Around Europe, records fell along the Atlantic coast and in the central and western Mediterranean.

The largest land-based anomalies on the planet were over West Antarctica.

There, temperatures ran more than 7°C above the October average and reached up to 11°C above normal in some areas.

The Copernicus report links this to high pressure over the Drake Passage and a wave pattern typically associated with El Niño. Siberia, the central United States, northern Canada, eastern Africa, and the Middle East also ran warm.

Cold anomalies showed up across much of southern South America, Greenland, northern Africa, parts of central Asia, and western Australia.

The warmth was not everywhere. But it was dominant.

European land temperatures averaged 11.08°C – 1.49°C above normal and the second-warmest October in the ERA5 record, behind only October 2022.

But unlike the record-breaking summer and September, the warmth was unevenly distributed.

Northern Fennoscandia and far-eastern Europe saw the most extreme departures, with Ukraine reaching up to 6°C above average.

Western Europe, by contrast, hovered closer to normal. Southern Italy, the southern Balkans, Greece, the eastern Mediterranean, and western Türkiye were actually about 2°C below average.

Individual months above 1.5°C are not the same as the sustained, multi-decadal average the Paris Agreement refers to. But the frequency with which individual months are crossing the threshold keeps increasing.

The first calendar year above 1.5°C happened in 2024. The second is almost certainly happening now.

A four-year average above 1.5°C would be another sign that the world is nearing the Paris Agreement’s long-term warming limit.

El Niño is expected to strengthen further before peaking in December, keeping attention on how this exceptional year will end.

#6313. Senate Democrats claim early wins in trio of key states

Senate Democrats scored a few early wins in key races Tuesday night, according to The Associated Press, flipping the open seat in North Carolina and winning critical races in Georgia and New Hampshire.

Democrat Roy Cooper, the Tar Heel State’s battle-tested former governor who has never lost an election, extended his streak Tuesday by defeating Republican Michael Whatley. He becomes the first Democrat to win a Senate election in North Carolina since 2008.

In Georgia, Sen. Jon Ossoff, who started the midterm cycle as the most vulnerable Democratic senator, concluded it with a thrashing of his Republican opponent, Rep. Mike Collins.

And in New Hampshire, Rep. Chris Pappas will succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen after beating back a comeback attempt from Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu and denying Republicans one of their best pickup opportunities.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip the Senate, and polls heading into Election Day showed the party competitive in several Senate races in traditionally Republican turf.

With his victory Tuesday, Ossoff heads into his second term with a growing national profile powered by clips of his searing critiques of President Donald Trump.

The Democrat raised an eye-popping $136.6 million through Oct. 14, swamping Collins, who brought in $10.7 million.

Georgia is a swing state that Trump carried by about 2 points in 2024. Four years earlier, Joe Biden had won the state by less than a quarter of a percentage point.

Before taking on Ossoff, Collins had to contend with a multicandidate primary, including fellow Rep. Earl L. “Buddy” Carter and former football coach and first-time candidate Derek Dooley.

Collins picked up Trump’s endorsement before the June primary runoff with Dooley, but a recent Atlanta Journal-Constitution/University of Georgia poll found the president with a 55 percent job disapproval rating.

Collins had been dogged by a House Ethics inquiry and reports that his son-in-law shared antisemitic and white nationalist social media posts.

Senate Republicans had initially hoped to persuade Brian Kemp, the state’s popular governor, to run for the seat, but he opted to endorse Dooley instead.

Cooper’s decisive win over Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee, is a political blow to Trump, who was heavily invested in the contest.

The president publicly urged Whatley to run after Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, a sometimes critic, announced his retirement last year. Trump visited North Carolina twice since Labor Day, holding rallies in Gastonia and Greenville to boost Whatley. And Vice President JD Vance also campaigned for Whatley and other Republicans.

But Trump, who carried North Carolina in all three of his presidential races, has seen his approval fall sharply in the Tar Heel State: A poll released Sunday by the Center for Survey Research at East Carolina University found 54 percent of voters disapproving of the president’s performance.

At the start of the cycle, the North Carolina Senate race was thought to be among the nation’s most competitive. But on the eve of the election, Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rated the race Lean Democratic.

Senate Democrats had long been eager to recruit Cooper, who won four previous statewide elections for state attorney general and two as governor. He launched his campaign in July 2025, shortly after Tillis announced his retirement, and his fundraising prowess and deep roots in the state proved too much for Whatley, a first-time candidate, to overcome.

Cooper was also able to withstand GOP attacks that sought to paint him as a soft-on-crime ideologue who embraced a radical, far-left agenda and promoted “transgender ideology.”

Instead of diving into divisive culture war issues, Cooper hewed closely to an economic message, which was summed up by his campaign slogan: “Make Stuff Cost Less.” He portrayed Whately as a rubber-stamp for the unpopular president and a former energy company lobbyist who grew wealthy while rates rose.

The Trump administration “promised that cost of living would be the Day One issue,” Cooper said at a campaign stop in Rocky Mount last month. “Not only has that not been the case, they have made it so much worse.”

Pappas’ victory makes him the first openly gay man elected to the Senate, although he didn’t emphasize the potential milestone on the campaign trail.

A fourth-term House member, Pappas’ family owns a popular restaurant in the state that claims to have invented the chicken tender. He cast his campaign as crucial for Democrats to hold the Senate.

With his win, Pappas also dealt a loss to one of the state’s most prominent political families. Sununu’s father and brother previously served as New Hampshire governor.

Sununu, who conceded before 8:30 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday before the AP had called the race, was trying to win back a seat he held for a single term before losing to Shaheen in 2008.

The Granite State hasn’t elected a GOP senator since 2010, but Republicans, including Sununu’s brother, Chris, have been elected to the governor's mansion every two years since 2016.

Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6311. Protecting cities from floods can come with a hidden cost for renters

Flood protection projects in Copenhagen may raise rents and water bills unevenly, placing a heavier burden on lower-income tenants.

A city can become better protected against flooding while becoming more expensive for its poorest residents.

New research shows how drainage projects can leave tenants paying disproportionately through higher rents and water bills.

The study, led by researchers at the University of Copenhagen, examined how flood protection costs reach households across the Danish capital.

Lead author Natalie Marie Gulsrud and her colleagues combined geographical analysis with a detailed look at the Hørgården housing development.

Their findings show why a policy applied equally on paper can feel very different depending on where someone lives.

At Hørgården, roughly 60 percent of residents have incomes below the Danish average. The development also appears on the Ministry of Social Affairs and Housing’s Prevention Areas list.

Its aging sewers need repairs, and a planned cloudburst route brings another obligation. Rainwater draining from roofs must be separated from wastewater and connected to the new system.

The paper projects rent increases of 17%–29% for the combined work. For a 75-square-meter apartment, that would add 967–1,292 Danish kroner to the monthly bill.

Stormwater separation accounts for about 22% of that increase, or 213–284 kroner each month. Most of the increase comes from sewer repairs.

The loans will be repaid over 30 years. Residents moving into Hørgården years after the work is finished will therefore help pay for it.

Copenhagen is investing in cloudburst tunnels and drainage improvements to keep heavy rain from overwhelming its sewers. Separating stormwater from wastewater is part of that effort.

The work protects the city, but apartment residents and not-for-profit tenants can bear a disproportionate share of its financing.

“Climate adaptation is not only about flooding and sewer capacity. It is also about rising rents,” Gulsrud said.

“Your type of housing determines how much of the bill you pay. Our case study shows that one-size-fits-all climate adaptation policies worsen urban injustice.”

“Stormwater costs fall disproportionately on not-for-profit housing residents, despite Copenhagen’s reputation for climate leadership.”

The researchers compared adaptation plans with data on housing types and tenure. They found that not-for-profit housing often lies closer to priority areas for flood management.

That proximity matters because properties along a cloudburst route may have to change their drainage systems at their own expense.

“We can see that not-for-profit housing is often located where cloudburst routes are typically established,” Gulsrud explained.

“The problem arises when properties along these routes are required to separate stormwater from wastewater on their own land to connect it to the cloudburst system. This makes sense from a water-management perspective, but it can also impose substantial costs.”

For an older development such as Hørgården, connecting to the new infrastructure involves extensive work. Those expenses ultimately reach households through their rents.

Water bills introduce a separate problem. Stormwater charges are based on drinking water consumption in each dwelling, rather than the rainwater leaving the property.

Imagine a detached house beside a four-storey block containing four apartments. Both buildings have a 100-square-meter roof.

If every household uses the same amount of drinking water, the apartment block pays four times the stormwater charge. Its roof is no larger.

This arrangement disadvantages buildings where many households share a roof. Not-for-profit developments commonly have four to six storeys.

“It would be fair if payment reflected the amount of stormwater each property actually discharges into the sewer system,” Gulsrud noted.

“At present, charges are tied to drinking water consumption instead. There is a fundamental inequity in the way water bills are allocated and in how residents pay for climate adaptation and cloudburst management.”

“As water charges continue to rise, the burden falls most heavily on the most marginalised members of society.”

The researchers also examined how these decisions are made. They found a divide between departments responsible for technical infrastructure and those dealing with social policy.

That leaves household finances poorly accounted for when drainage requirements are enforced. A project can satisfy engineering standards while putting residents under greater financial strain.

“In this paper we hope to introduce a human aspect to a highly technical topic involving stormwater pipes, housing tenure, and climate financing,” Gulsrud said.

In Hørgården, public records showed that officials knew housing costs would rise. Those costs nevertheless did not determine whether the separation requirement would go ahead.

The authors argue that closer cooperation between social and technical departments could help distribute costs more fairly. Housing circumstances and household resources would then become part of planning the work.

For residents, that would mean considering the rent bill alongside the drainage plan.

“Who gets protected as the climate changes, and who carries the cost? A just transition needs social and technical governance working together, not on separate tracks.”

“If we don’t fix this, we risk deepening socio ecological inequalities in the green transition. We hope this research moves us closer to a transition that is genuinely just and caring,” Gulsrud concluded.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6310. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

A.R. Kunik, et al. The ‘‘dark magic mushroom’’ co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin. Current Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

Tina Hesman Saey is the senior staff writer and reports on molecular biology. She has a Ph.D. in molecular genetics from Washington University in St. Louis and a master’s degree in science journalism from Boston University.
