#6284. Democrats flip House as Republicans confront ‘blue tsunami’

Democrats seized control of the House on Tuesday by safeguarding vulnerable incumbents and flipping districts in both battleground and deep-red terrain, delivering a sweeping repudiation of Donald Trump and Republicans that threatens to stall the president’s remaining agenda.

The Associated Press call came at 1:26 a.m. Eastern time Wednesday, hours after Democrats were projected to win a majority in the Senate, with a string of victories in deeply conservative states.

“The American people have spoken and made clear they've had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,’’ House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black speaker, told cheering supporters in Washington. “They want a Congress that's going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do.”

Recent polls had forecast a strong Democratic showing amid rising discontent with the president's policies and economic anxiety driven by rising prices and the Iran war. But the magnitude of the Democratic majority surprised even the most optimistic Democratic partisans.

The “blue tsunami” marked an extraordinary turnaround for a party that suffered withering losses in 2024, when Trump returned to the White House and Republicans won a governing trifecta in Washington.

Republicans had hoped that a mid-decade redistricting push driven by Trump would help them keep their majority by flipping House seats in Texas, North Carolina, Florida and Ohio, among other states. Instead, many of those districts remained in Democrats’ hands.

Trump put himself front and center of the midterm campaign, imploring voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” On Tuesday, he posted on social media that he “wasn’t on the ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

But in a later interview with CBS News, Trump congratulated Democrats on their rout. “My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country," he said.

Among the night’s Democratic pickups were seats in rural and Republican-leaning districts. Farmer Jamie Ager defeated Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to flip a Western North Carolina seat that was left open after Republican Chuck Edwards announced his retirement after facing allegations of sexual harassment.

In Kentucky’s 6th District, Democrat Zach Dembo, a Navy veteran and former federal prosecutor, defeated former state Sen. Ralph Alvarado for an open seat anchored in Lexington.

Democrats also swept perennial battleground districts, flipping seats in states such as New Jersey, Colorado and Wisconsin. And in Pennsylvania, Democrats were projected to flip all four seats they were targeting, including the Philadelphia-area district of GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.

Anger over Trump’s tariff policy drove discontent in farm country, with Democrats ousting Republican Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa and flipping the seat of Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson, who lost her bid to succeed retiring Sen. Joni Ernst.

Meanwhile, Latino voters, who were credited with helping propel Trump back into the White House in 2024, bolstered Democratic successes in Texas, scuttling GOP hopes of making good on the party’s mid-decade redistricting gambit.

Texas Republicans believed Latino voters would stick with the party this year when they redrew the state's congressional map to create up to five pickup opportunities. But anger over the president’s immigration policies, coupled with economic anxiety, has driven Trump’s approval numbers among Latinos to historic lows.

In South Texas, a pair of Democratic incumbents — Reps. Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar — easily held on to their redrawn seats, while former Bexar County sheriff's deputy Johnny Garcia prevailed over Air Force veteran Carlos De La Cruz in a district newly redrawn to elect a Republican. Democratic attorney and educator Katy Padilla Stout flipped the open 23rd District, which stretches across the state’s border with Mexico, and Tejano singer Bobby Pulido routed GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in another South Texas race.

The strength of the Democrats’ performance was evident in several under-the-radar races the party won in traditionally red districts, including Missouri’s 2nd District, where Republican Rep. Ann Wagner was ousted, and Indiana’s 5th, where Rep. Victoria Spartz lost reelection.

Speaker Mike Johnson, who crisscrossed the country to boost Republican candidates in the final weeks of the campaign, noted Tuesday night that history wasn’t on the GOP side: The president’s party almost always loses seats in a midterm election.

"From the first day of this election, we knew that to keep the House and sustain our majority we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history," Johnson said in Shreveport, La. "It looks like history will be kept tonight."

The new Democratic majority is expected to dedicate resources to investigating the activities of the Trump administration as well as the president.

The likely new Democratic chairman of the House Judiciary Committee is Maryland’s Jamie Raskin, while the Oversight and Government Reform panel is likely to be led by California Rep. Robert Garcia. Raskin and Garcia have already been busy making oversight requests of the administration.

For instance, the two lawmakers joined on a letter last week calling for the retention of conversations between the president and AI chatbots on matters of policy.

"The President and his advisors’ use of AI exposes the country to malign influence from unknown and unaccountable third parties. We already have ample evidence that AI chatbots can be manipulated to suit the commercial, political, or personal agendas of their designers​," Raskin and Garcia wrote.

Beyond the oversight, Jeffries outlined last month some of his legislative priorities for the next Congress.

"I think we need to put money in the pockets of everyday Americans by doing things like expanding the Child Tax Credit, as well as the Earned Income Tax Credit​," Jeffries told News12. "And, of course, we also need to end this war because the war has dramatically increased gas prices, fertilizer prices and diesel costs.​"

That was a reference to the military campaign against Iran, which appears likely to ratchet back up after the midterms.

I​n a pre-election interview with CNN, Jeffries said priorities that unite the Democratic Caucus include action on stopping the president's sweeping application of tariffs, as well as on reversing cuts to Medicaid and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits.

Ancient writers couldn't agree on how Egypt's last queen took her own life, and the famous snakebite story may owe more to her enemies than to the facts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The death of Cleopatra is among the most famous in history. In 31 B.C., the Egyptian queen and her Roman ally and lover, Mark Antony, lost the Battle of Actium to Octavian, who would later become Rome's first emperor, Augustus. The following summer, Cleopatra was captured during a Roman ambush inside her royal tomb in Alexandria.

According to Octavian’s account, rather than facing the disgrace of defeat, the queen allowed a venomous asp snake to bite her and quickly succumbed to its poison. Some Roman writers, such as the historian Velleius Paterculus, repeated that story without question.

But others were far less certain of this account, calling it Roman propaganda to cement Octavian's rise to power. And most historians today doubt that a snake was involved at all. So how did Cleopatra die?

Live Science spoke with experts, who told us that the queen's death is still shrouded in mystery.

"We cannot know for sure exactly how Cleopatra died," Prudence Jones, a professor of classics at Montclair State University in New Jersey and author of "Cleopatra: A Sourcebook" (University of Oklahoma Press, 2006), told Live Science in an email.

What historians largely agree on is that Cleopatra VII, the last queen of Egypt's Ptolemaic dynasty, took her own life and that she chose a method that left her body composed and dignified.

Physical evidence of Cleopatra's death is elusive. Much of Alexandria's royal quarter now lies underwater, and underwater archaeologist Franck Goddio, who has been excavating it, hasn't found the queen's mausoleum, Jones said. Even if Cleopatra's remains surfaced, bones would be unlikely to show evidence of snake venom, she added, noting that forensics is outside her area of expertise.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Divers celebrate as a crane pulls an artifact from the waters at Abu Qir bay in Alexandria, Egypt on Aug. 21, 2025.

The best witness may have been Olympus, Cleopatra's personal physician. "Unfortunately, nothing survives of Olympus' account," Jones said.

What does remain is a story told largely by Cleopatra's enemies. The earliest surviving account is a poem by the Roman poet Horace, whose patron was a close friend of Octavian, said Jane Draycott, a historian at the University of Glasgow. His Ode 1.37, written around the time of her death, celebrates Octavian's victory and already pictures the queen handling serpents — yet it ends with grudging admiration for a woman who refused to be paraded as a trophy.

Following her capture, Cleopatra was held under military guard. By then, she had already tried to end her life twice. Cleopatra had tried to stab herself when Roman soldiers broke into the mausoleum where she had barricaded herself, and she later tried to starve herself, stopping only after Octavian threatened her children.

To Draycott, those attempts leave little doubt that Cleopatra would rather die than live as a captive. "She does not want to be a prisoner; she does not want to be led through the streets of Rome in triumph as a defeated foe," she told Live Science.

In the Greco-Roman world, suicide didn't carry the stigma it later acquired under Christianity, she added. "It was a way of wiping the slate clean, removing any shame, any disgrace from yourself." After the defeat of his remaining forces at Alexandria and hearing a false report of Cleopatra's death, Antony was the first of the two lovers to die by suicide.

According to the Greek biographer Plutarch, who based his account on that of Cleopatra's personal physician, Cleopatra visited Antony's tomb, bathed, ate and sent Octavian a sealed letter asking to be buried beside Antony, signaling that she meant to die. Octavian realized what was happening and sent messengers rushing to her, but they arrived too late. They found her dead in her royal regalia, with her attendants Iras and Charmion dying beside her.

A statue depicting Cleopatra's suicide by asp, the most famous of several ancient theories.

Jones has compiled what ancient historians, biographers, geographers and physicians wrote about Cleopatra's death. Every source mentions a snakebite, but several also suggest other possibilities, including a poisonous ointment, poison hidden in a hollow hairpin, and snake venom poured into a wound the queen made by biting herself. Only one of these writers, the geographer Strabo, was alive when Cleopatra died, and the only people in the room with her died, too.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio wrote that the sole clue was a pair of faint pricks on her arm. That doesn't settle much, however. "A cobra bite can appear as two small puncture wounds, but not all cobra bites appear this way and not all double puncture wounds result from snakebites," Jones said.

Jones traces the snake version of the story to Octavian, who was in Alexandria when Cleopatra died. Plutarch reported that an image of Cleopatra with an asp clinging to her was carried in Octavian's triumphal procession in Rome. "Octavian, however, was Cleopatra's enemy and for that reason we may not want to accept his account uncritically," Jones said.

Draycott suggested another possible source of confusion: Snake-shaped jewelry was fashionable in Alexandria at the time, so Romans viewing an effigy of the queen may have mistaken a snake bracelet for a real snake.

Draycott doesn't think one snake could have killed all three women. Jones is less certain. Snakes don't inject the same amount of venom with every bite, and some "dry bites" deliver none at all, Jones said. "On the other hand, I don't think it is impossible, as the body of a cobra contains enough venom to kill multiple people," she added.

The general view among historians, Draycott said, is that Cleopatra took some kind of poison — one that worked quickly and didn't cause seizures or vomiting. The absence of these symptoms is telling: An asp is believed to be what is now known as the Egyptian cobra (Naja haje), whose venom causes a slow, agonizing death with respiratory failure.

A young Egyptian cobra (Naja haja) strikes a typical defensive pose in scrubland near Sidi Ifni, Morocco.

Cleopatra likely would have had other means, then. Alexandria was the Mediterranean's center of scientific study, and texts from the period, such as Nicander's "Theriaca," catalog venomous animals, Jones noted. Cleopatra's father, Ptolemy XII, even consulted the pharmacologist Zopyrus about antidotes. Plutarch claimed that Cleopatra personally oversaw experiments that observed the effects of deadly poisons on condemned prisoners.

Still, that claim and other poison stories should be read with caution, Draycott said, because they draw on Roman stereotypes about women. In the Roman view, "manly men will battle with swords," while women, seen as "deceitful and weak" at this time, were thought to kill in secret. "They'll sneak it into your food," Draycott said, summing up the stereotype.

Roman writers were equally suspicious. Poisoning allegations dogged the Hellenistic dynasties of ancient Egypt and the neighboring Seleucid kingdom, as well as Rome's own imperial family. Some were probably true, Draycott said, but others may have been foodborne illnesses or other health conditions people didn't understand.

The method may remain a mystery, but for most historians, the motive doesn't change: Cleopatra chose to die on her own terms.

#6282. These members of Congress are heading to the governor’s mansion

The number of governors who once served in Congress is set to grow next year after several lawmakers won gubernatorial races across the country.

The incoming governors include members who’ve served in Congress for decades and some with relatively short stints in Congress. But several Republican lawmakers were unsuccessful in their attempts to become the top executives of their home states on what was largely a poor night for the GOP.

Here are the lawmakers who won their governor’s races on election night:

It was a blast from the (recent) past in Alabama, where Republican Sen. Tommy Tuberville was elected governor after defeating Democrat Doug Jones, his Senate predecessor whom he defeated in 2020.

Despite the defeat, Jones — who won a 2017 special election to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Alabama in more than two decades — lost by a closer-than-anticipated margin to Tuberville, a staunch ally of President Donald Trump and the former head football coach at Auburn. With 99 percent of votes counted, according to The Associated Press, Tuberville was leading Jones 52 percent to 48 percent — the narrowest gubernatorial race in the Yellowhammer State since 2002.

The governor’s mansion in the Sunshine State will remain in GOP hands, with Rep. Byron Donalds narrowly defeating former Rep. David Jolly to become Florida’s first Black governor.

Donalds, who was first elected to Congress in 2020, will succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, himself a former congressman.

Jolly is a former Republican lawmaker who left the party during Trump’s first term and joined Democrats last year. He was vying to become the first Democratic elected governor in Florida since Lawton Chiles won reelection in 1994. Jolly’s running mate was also a onetime House colleague — former Rep. Gwen Graham, the daughter of former Florida Gov. and Sen. Bob Graham.

The Volunteer State also made history on election night, electing its first female governor in Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn. Despite Tennessee’s deep-red lean, Blackburn only scraped by Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis City councilwoman, with a self-funding independent pulling in a portion of the conservative vote.

Before her election to the Senate in 2018, Blackburn served in the Tennessee Senate and nearly two decades in the House. She is expected to be able to pick her Senate successor after she is sworn in as governor.

Democratic-Farmer-Labor Sen. Amy Klobuchar was another history-maker in Minnesota, becoming the first female governor of the North Star State. She defeated Republican state House Speaker Lisa DeMuth in the race to succeed retiring Gov. Tim Walz, the 2024 Democratic vice presidential nominee.

Like Blackburn, Klobuchar was also the first woman to represent her state in the Senate, where she has served since 2007. She is also expected to appoint her successor in the chamber.

Unofficial returns from the U.S. Virgin Islands showed Democrat Stacey Plaskett prevailing in the open governor’s race with more than 50 percent of the vote to avoid a runoff and become the island territory’s first female governor.

Plaskett was first elected to Congress in 2014 as the Virgin Islands’ nonvoting delegate and served as a House impeachment manager during Trump’s second impeachment trial. She faced controversy last year over her correspondence with sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, but narrowly avoided being censured and stripped of her position on the House Intelligence Committee.

Two former members of Congress who later served in Joe Biden’s Cabinet are also heading for their states’ governor’s mansions.

In California, Democratic former Rep. Xavier Becerra easily defeated Republican Steve Hilton to succeed outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom. Since leaving Congress in 2017, Becerra has served as California attorney general and as Biden’s secretary of Health and Human Services.

And in New Mexico, former Rep. Deb Haaland easily kept the governorship in Democratic hands with her win over Republican Gregg Hull, the former Rio Rancho mayor. She succeeds another former House member, term-limited Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham.

Not all members of Congress were successful in governor’s races this year. A trio of Republican congressmen lost gubernatorial bids: Wisconsin’s Tom Tiffany, Arizona’s Andy Biggs and Michigan’s John James.

They join Republican colleagues who lost gubernatorial primaries this year, including David Schweikert of Arizona, Randy Feenstra of Iowa, Dusty Johnson of South Dakota, John W. Rose of Tennessee and Nancy Mace and Ralph Norman of South Carolina.

Sen. Michael Bennet, a Democrat from Colorado, lost a gubernatorial primary in June to state Attorney General Phil Weiser, who was easily elected Tuesday. Bennet, however, will continue to serve in the Senate as he isn’t up for reelection until 2028.

Andrew Menezes, Daniela Altimari, Mary Ellen McIntire and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

#6281. In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho, the documentary dives into how oceanographers are racing to understand the world’s changing waters

Aerial imagery of research vessel Star Keys safe harboring in Abel Tasman, New Zealand.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

As NASA's Voyager 1 probe reaches one light-day from Earth, we look back at its legendary photos of Jupiter that changed our view of the solar system.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which launched half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

Just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation showed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

Taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons showed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency announced its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

#6279. Could planets that orbit other stars be nonspherical?

Could planets that orbit other stars be nonspherical shapes, such as ovals or pears, depending on composition?

Bodies large enough to be considered planets have enough mass that gravity molds them into a roughly spherical shape.

The key word here is roughly — other factors also come into play, such as a planet’s composition (rocky or gassy) and its rate of spin. The faster a planet spins, the more its rotation causes it to bulge outward at the equator. That’s because as a planet rotates, there’s a tug-of-war between the way material wants to fly off the planet due to rotation and the way gravity wants to pull all that planet’s material inward. The battle between these forces is most intense at the equator.

In our solar system, Mercury and Venus are slowly spinning rocky planets; therefore, they are the most spherical of the Sun’s worlds.

Earth and Mars spin a little faster, so they are about 0.3% and 0.6% thicker at the equator than the poles, respectively. This shape is called an oblate spheroid. However, because these planets have a solid surface that is higher in some places than others, they are not perfect oblate spheroids — they are minutely lumpy and bumpy, as data from orbiting satellites have detailed. In fact, the surface area of Earth’s Southern Hemisphere is very slightly larger than its Northern Hemisphere, making Earth marginally pear-shaped. It’s important to note, however, that despite these deviations, Earth is still almost spherical — if you used a basketball to represent the shape of our planet, its deviation from a perfect sphere would be only about 0.03 inch (0.08 centimeter) at the middle.

The gas giants Jupiter and Saturn bulge outward the most — Jupiter is nearly 7% thicker at its equator than its poles, and Saturn is 10.7% thicker around the middle. Ice giants Uranus and Neptune have smaller central bulges, only 2.3% and 1.7% thicker at the equator, respectively.

What about exoplanets, though? Some planetary systems we’ve found experience much more extreme conditions, with large, gassy planets orbiting very close to their stars (called hot Jupiters). One of these hot Jupiters is WASP-121 b, which orbits a blazingly hot star. In fact, this planet orbits so closely to its star that gravitational forces have stretched it out into a football shape. Astronomers believe that if the planet were much closer to its star, it would be ripped apart entirely.

In addition to its stretched-out shape, WASP-121 b and other planets, including WASP-69 b and KELT-9 b, appear to have puffed-up atmospheres and cometlike tails. These tails form as their host stars blast the planets with high-energy radiation, knocking gas particles into space.

As for pear-shaped exoplanets, astronomers haven’t found anything to suggest they exist to the extent you’re likely picturing. Other terrestrial planets likely have deformations similar to Earth’s — or perhaps slightly more extreme — but even “extreme” in this case probably translates to a planet appearing essentially spherical from a great distance.

#6278. These Remote Atolls Are Among the Last Places on Earth Humans Haven’t Touched. Here’s What Scientists Found.

Bikar and Bokak sit so far from people that they may show us what the ocean looked like before humans.

There are few havens on Earth as pristine as the Bikar and Bokak atolls. Formed from sunken volcanoes around which coral reefs grew, these atolls in the Ratak chain of the Marshall Islands teem with life and remain uninhabited by humans. Rainbows of fish swim among corals and sea anemones, while sharks glide silently through the water in pursuit of prey. Until recently, even marine biologists had rarely explored these habitats in depth.

That began to change when Alan Friedlander set out across an impossibly blue swath of ocean and led his team into paradise. Friedlander is a marine ecologist at the University of Hawai’i who served as chief scientist for National Geographic’s Pristine Seas program on the expedition, and he takes a special interest in remote and protected regions of the ocean. The people of the Marshall Islands have known Bikar and Bokak for generations, but the atolls had never been comprehensively surveyed when Friedlander and his team arrived. For the Marshallese, the ocean is home even more than the land is. Their survival depends on the health of the fragile reef ecosystems around the country’s 1,225 islands and islets, only some of which are inhabited.

The opportunity came in 2023, when Pristine Seas was invited to join the Marshall Islands Marine Resources Authority in surveying Bikar and Bokak, which are safeguarded by the Utirik Atoll community. Friedlander and his team received a traditional blessing and farewell on Utirik before sailing north to Bikar, which lies about 72 miles (116 km) from the nearest inhabited atoll. Bokak is even more isolated, about 239 miles (385 km) away. This remoteness is part of the reason the atolls have remained relatively untouched by human influence. Friedlander wanted to carry out an ecological assessment of everything from the land habitats to the reefs and the open sea. That meant studying the structure and biodiversity of these ecosystems, documenting how well they had been preserved and how the two atolls differed, and identifying the conservation measures they would need in the future.

“The remote northern atolls of Bikar and Bokak represent some of the least disturbed coral reef ecosystems remaining in the tropical Pacific,” Friedlander and his co-authors wrote in a study recently published in Frontiers in Marine Science. “Both atolls are uninhabited and geographically isolated from major population centers and industrial development. Previous expeditions documented portions of their terrestrial habitats, seabird colonies, sea turtles, and shallow coral reefs.”

The team’s first stop was Bikar, which curves across the water like a crescent moon. There, the researchers used a variety of sampling methods, including scuba surveys, photography, underwater video, deep-sea cameras, and a submarine, to record which species were present and in what numbers. Polynesian rats, which humans introduced, were sometimes seen scurrying through the island’s old-growth Pisonia forests. Even so, native species still thrive. Seabirds such as masked boobies, great frigatebirds, black noddies, and white terns filled the skies, while shorebirds like the migratory Pacific golden plover pecked at the sand in search of small invertebrates. Bikar’s beaches are also a nesting ground for green sea turtles; the team recorded 132 nest pits there. Its reefs are full of fish, including several species of snapper and grouper. Giant clams, which host photosynthetic algae, filter the water and are vital to the health of the reef.

Farther north and even more isolated, Bokak is an oasis that has seen very little human interference. Its drier, savanna-like landscape is covered in tufts of bunchgrass and tree heliotropes, which bear clusters of small white flowers. Many of the seabirds that soar over Bikar are also found on Bokak. Bokak’s waters are even richer than Bikar’s: its reefs are dominated by coral and hold more fish by weight. Friedlander dove in to investigate. He came across a school of humphead parrotfish, a threatened species once thought to have nearly vanished from the islands. He also saw an unusual reversal of the typical food pyramid. Reef sharks and black jacks outweigh their prey in total biomass. Because these top predators feed so often, they keep energy and nutrients moving quickly through the reef, which helps the ecosystem run efficiently.

After Bokak, Friedlander’s team had one more location to survey, and it offered a sharp contrast. From 1946 to 1958, Bikini Atoll was a center of U.S. nuclear testing, starting with Operation Crossroads. When the islanders were evacuated before the first tests, they took only a few changes of clothes, not knowing that they would never be able to resettle their home for good. The series of detonations devastated the atoll. From the ocean’s glassy surface, Bikini seems to be ringed by cities of coral. But divers who swam closer found that many of these formations, which had taken thousands of years to grow, were little more than skeletons. Still, Bikini Atoll is not without hope. After searching long enough, Friedlander found patches of live coral that had settled on the dead reef and were swarming with fish. It was a sign of how resilient life can be.

Even Bikar and Bokak can’t fully escape what is happening elsewhere. Their remoteness protects them from most direct human pressures, but climate change is slowly reaching them, too. When the water gets too hot, corals expel the symbiotic algae that feed them and give them their bright colors, a process known as coral bleaching. Leftover radiation from the nuclear-testing era is still a source of contamination in the region. Meanwhile, currents carry in trash from other countries, and plastics break down into microplastics. People are responding with conservation measures. In 2025, two years after the expedition, the government of the Marshall Islands designated the waters around Bikar and Bokak, about 18,500 square miles (48,000 square km), as the country’s first national marine sanctuary, as part of the community-led Reimaanlok conservation framework. Despite the threats that come from far away, Friedlander is optimistic.

“As relatively intact tropical marine ecosystems become increasingly rare worldwide,” he and his co-authors concluded, “remote atolls such as Bikar and Bokak serve not only as regional conservation priorities but also as globally important ecological reference systems for understanding the structure and future trajectories of tropical oceanic ecosystems in the Anthropocene.”

#6277. Nov. 16, 1974: Arecibo sends a message

On Nov. 16, 1974, a group gathered at Arecibo Observatory in the rainforest interior of Puerto Rico, there for a reopening celebration after upgrades to the facility. After the requisite speeches, scientists used the radio telescope to send what would be known as the Arecibo message: 1,679 bits of data in 73 lines, each 23 characters long. To the assembled crowd, the dispatch sounded like nearly three minutes of two tones. But encoded in those tones was message crafted by a team of scientists led by Frank Drake and including Carl Sagan: a rough illustration of a human, the structure of a DNA double helix, and a map of the Earth’s position in the solar system.

The communication was aimed at M13, a globular cluster about 25,000 light-years away in Hercules. Since it would take thousands of years for the signal to arrive there – not to mention time for a signal to be sent back by any extraterrestrial civilization that intercepted it – the Arecibo message wasn’t so much an actual attempt at communication as it was a demonstration of how we might do so.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6275. The 7 Best Electric Chainsaws of 2026

Cordless battery-powered chainsaws are quiet, light, and fast—everything you need for a spring refresh.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you own a home with trees on your property, an electric chainsaw is a must-have tool in your yard care arsenal. Electric chainsaws have come a long way and, in most cases, closed the gap to their gas-powered cousins—they’re easy to start (just push a button or two in most cases), generate little noise, produce no fumes, and simplify maintenance. We’ve tested electric saws as big as 20 inches and they’re powerful enough to bring down a mature tree.

Saws with 24-inch bars or more are still considered gas engine territory, but that’s overkill for most homeowners. For cleaning up after storms, felling small to medium-size trees, and regular pruning or arboreal maintenance, an electric chainsaw is the ideal choice.

We noted how well each chainsaw endured prolonged use. Making repeated cuts can cause a chainsaw, and its battery, to heat up. If it gets too hot, it will trigger a thermal limit and the saw’s overload protection will shut it down. We also considered comfort, vibration, saw balance, and ease of use to make our final recommendations.

Stihl’s new battery-powered MSA 260 C-O tops our list of chainsaws for two main reasons: run-time and constant, consistent power. These are the two most common concerns or complaints we hear from people when it comes to electric saws. The MSA 260 C-O made significantly more cuts on one battery charge than any other saw tested. But that’s only partly attributable to the saw—it’s also due to Stihl’s new AllPro 300.0 battery. Working in concert, the battery and saw deliver power at a constant level, maintaining a chain speed through most of the saw’s runtime.

Aside from run-time and consistent power delivery, the MSA 260 C-O has the ability to chew through big, tough logs. Note that Stihl positions the MSA 260 C-O “for professional applications” so the performance does come at a cost, $770 for the 18-inch model we tested, plus another $350 for the battery. While that might seem like a lot, it’s in line with other pro battery and gas saws. So, if you’re a frequent chainsaw user, the investment is going to be worth it.

Husqvarna may not have been the fastest-cutting electric chainsaw we tested, but it’s at the top of our list because it does just about everything well—it operates smoothly, cuts fast (enough), and is easy to use. With the boost button engaged, it blazed through our cutting tests, slicing through an 8-inch log in about 5 seconds. It also had the fastest windup speed of any electric chainsaw that I personally tested—it was ready to cut as soon as I pulled the trigger. Even with its impressive power, this chainsaw is surprisingly quiet, producing 67 decibels at 60 feet. The Power Axe isn’t particularly light at 14.5 pounds with battery, but it’s well balanced. I had no problem holding it steady even when making cuts at waist-level height.

The Power Axe also comes with a suite of well-designed, user-friendly features. The power button and boost button are located just above the handle so they’re easier to access on the fly. You also have the ability to adjust the chain tension by hand, loosening a dial to release the tension, then rotating a dial to tighten it back up. The whole process takes seconds. There’s also a built-in chain brake to protect from injuries. It’s a well-built, high-performing electric chainsaw that still manages to come in at a reasonable price.

Echo’s DCS-5000 gives you what you want most out of a chainsaw: raw cutting power. It may lack some of the bells and whistles you’ll find on pricier models, such as tool-less chain tensioning and power-saving settings, but its base performance is right up there with the Power Axe 350i. The DCS-5000 cut through 8-inch hardwood in less than 4 seconds. That's saying something considering that the DCS-5000 costs at least $100 less than any other saw that can do the same.

Along with its impressive cutting speed, the Echo is also relatively light at just over 12 pounds. I could feel the difference whenever I had to lift it up above shoulder-height to cut higher limbs, or while crouching down to cut a fallen 8-inch beech tree.

There is a trade-off with the DCS-5000, though, in that it lacks any kind of quality-of-life-related features. You won’t find tool-less chain tensioning or ECO settings that conserve battery life here. It’s pretty loud, too, producing 76 decibels at 60 feet. And, finally, while I appreciated the lighter weight, I could also feel the vibrations in my arm more than electric chainsaws with more refined builds.

Still, if you don't mind the rougher feel, higher noise level, and lack of a few user-friendly features you’ll find on pricier electric chainsaws, the Echo DCS-5000 offers exceptional value.

The newest saw from Makita, the 40V Max XGT 20-inch chainsaw, is a beast. The brand claims it offers the power of a 50-cc gas saw, and we’re inclined to agree. The first pull of the trigger surprised us with the speed and sound of the chain whizzing around. And it wasn’t just the noise that was impressive—in testing, it positively tore through logs.

Using the 40V Max XGT for practical tasks like felling trees, or cleaning up fallen trees after a storm, confirmed its power. I tackled logs as big as 18 inches, and the saw left nothing to be desired—it handled everything I used it on, without faltering. The 40V Max XGT chainsaw, at 20-inches, is among the biggest battery powered chainsaws we test. Our test unit came as a kit, with everything you need, including an 8.0Ah battery and charger. The kit isn’t cheap, but if you’re already on the Makita 40-volt XGT platform, you can save $500 and buy the chainsaw as a tool only.

The Stihl MSA 80 is an easy-to-use chainsaw that also packs impressive cutting power. Its compact build—the 14-inch saw weighs about 10 pounds—gives it a balanced feel in hand. It features a narrow bar that makes it easier to fit it into the crotches of trees for pruning than other electric chainsaws we tested like the Ego 20-inch chainsaw or Husqvarna Power Axe 350i. Likewise, it comes equipped with a thinner chain that cuts more smoothly through wood, producing less vibration. Lastly, its variable speed trigger allows you to adjust the speed of the blade to suit the job at hand.

There are several user-friendly features worth noting. Chain adjustments are effortless: Simply loosen a knob, turn the adjuster, and tighten the knob. There’s also a lubrication system to keep the chain moving with a minimal amount of bar oil.

Stihl’s chainsaws come at a premium price, and this one is no different. At $500, the MSA 80 is the most expensive electric chainsaw we tested, despite having a relatively short bar. Even so, it’s an ideal choice for homeowners who are looking for professional-grade build quality and performance out of an electric chainsaw.

If you already have other Echo tools, like a leaf blower or trimmer, then you can save a little cash and purchase the DCS-2500T as a tool only.

There’s a price for the CS-2005’s cutting power and capacity, though—its weight. While we liked its buttery smooth operation, it weighs an arm-burning 19.3 pounds with a battery. Making cuts on limbs above the head or below the knees was a far more challenging experience than with electric chainsaws we tested that were 4 to 5 pounds lighter. The Ego CS-2005 also lacks a tool-free chain tensioning system. If you don’t mind the extra heft, the Ego CS-2005 is the high-powered electric you’ll want for really big jobs.

As new models come out, we can’t keep all the models we test on our recommended list. But some of these older models and runners-up are still worth considering. Here are a few:

Milwaukee M18 Fuel 18V 16-Inch Electric Chainsaw: Don’t be fooled by the Milwaukee’s lower voltage, this saw has plenty of power for quickly cutting up large limbs or felling medium-sized trees. It’s a good saw, but we’d mostly recommend it to folks already on Milwaukee’s M18 platform, so you can buy it as a tool only and save some money.

Stihl GTA 26: While folks often refer to tools like this as “mini chain saws”, Stihl bills the GTA 26 as a garden pruner. Intended specifically for pruning shrubs and small branches, the GTA 26 combines light weight and a pistol-like configuration to make an easy-to-handle tool. Think of it as a power loppers, with greater size capability.

Worx Nitro WG385 40V 16-Inch Chainsaw: At less than $300, the Worx Nitro WG385 can get the job done. It’s lighter and easier to maneuver than other similarly sized saws, but it’s also a little less powerful, with a little less run-time. Still, with some patience we were able to find it useful for basic property maintenance. For the price, the Worx Nitro WG385 is a good cost-effective option for occasional use.

At the heart of an electric chainsaw is its motor and battery, which need to work in concert to perform well. The longer the chainsaw bar, the bigger the log or tree you can cut. So, the motor has to have enough torque and speed, while the battery has to be able to deliver the power needed to sustain that torque and speed. This is one reason why bigger saws can cost a lot more than smaller ones. Batteries are a significant factor in the price of a saw, and bigger batteries cost more. Battery size is typically measured in amp-hours (Ah), and larger saws will typically have 8 to 12 Ah batteries.

Mini chainsaws, made for pruning and other small jobs, feature a one-handed design with a small cutting bar—4 to 8 inches—and a small battery. If you need to break down large branches from trees, opt for a smaller full-size chainsaw with a 12- to 14-inch cutting bar. For something professional-grade, consider a large chainsaw with a 16- to 20-inch cutting bar and larger battery.

Among electric chainsaws with comparable bar lengths, those with larger batteries will typically have more ripping power, which means they’ll cut through limbs and logs more quickly, allowing you to get the job done faster. Just keep in mind that a more powerful chainsaw is also often a heavier chainsaw.

An electric chainsaw’s runtime depends on the capacity of its battery, in amp-hours. Broadly speaking, more capacity means more juice, but larger saws draw more power per second, so it’s not uncommon to find large chainsaws with large batteries getting comparable battery life to their smaller, more efficient counterparts.

Since your chainsaw only uses power when you’re using it to cut, its true runtime comes down to how many cuts it can make on a single charge. The Popular Mechanics test team tests runtime by checking how many times each model cuts through a 6-inch log on a single charge. Depending on battery size and chainsaw power, that number can vary quite a bit—from as low as 50 to as high as 300.

The “cutting bar” is the business end of the chainsaw—the long, rounded metal guide that the chain spins around to create a blade. The length of the bar, which is measured from the base of the chainsaw’s head to the tip of the cutting bar, determines the maximum thickness of the wood that your chainsaw can cut through in a single pass. Generally speaking, your chainsaw can safely cut through limbs with a diameter up to 2 inches less than the length of the bar. For example, a 12-inch chainsaw can cut through a limb up to 10 inches in diameter in a single pass.

For a long time, going electric meant settling for a chainsaw with a shorter bar, but that’s no longer the case. While gas engines offer more power, especially in larger saws, there are electric options with professional-length cutting bars. For instance, a 20-inch electric chainsaw has the power to bring down mature trees.

Need is an important distinction here. We don’t recommend picking the most powerful saw with the longest cutting bar within your budget. A longer bar will give you more cutting capacity, but it’s also heavier and more difficult to handle safely. We recommend buying the tool that’s just big enough for the cutting tasks you’ll perform regularly. If you’re looking to trim small limbs and branches, a pruning saw with a 4- to 8-inch bar such as the Stihl GTA 26 is going to be the best choice. If you’re taking down trees and breaking them down for firewood, you may need something longer.

It’s important that you feel comfortable handling the weight of your chainsaw. If it’s too heavy to hold at chest height, then you can’t use it safely.

With electric chainsaws, weight is directly related to the length of the cutting bar. The longer the cutting bar, the heavier the chainsaw. A mini chainsaw with an 8-inch bar will weigh around 5 pounds, while a large 18-inch chainsaw can weigh as much as 15 pounds.

One thing to keep in mind: Many manufacturers list the “bare” weight of their cordless chainsaws without the battery, so when you do add that in, it can mean an extra 1 to 3 pounds to the load.

Chainsaws are among the most dangerous power tools you can put your hands on: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), some 36,000 people ends up in the hospital with chainsaw-related injuries each year.

That is why it’s crucial to always take every step you can to ensure the safest possible conditions when using a chainsaw. A good electric chainsaw should have built-in safety features to minimize the possibility of an accident: First, look for a trigger lock, which requires you to maintain pressure on a button near the handle to keep the chain spinning. Most will also have a chain brake at the front of the handle, which disengages the chain if the chainsaw kicks back.

That depends on the size of the tree. Even the largest electric chainsaws with a 20-inch cutting bar only have the torque necessary to cut down moderately tall trees. You’ll want a gas chainsaw that brings the extra power to bring down an older, larger tree, or if you’re bringing trees down regularly.

Electric chainsaws don’t require much maintenance. Use a brush or cloth to remove sawdust and other debris that’s caught in the chain and sprocket area after each use.

You should also clean any debris that’s fallen into the air intake slots: Brush it away material on the outside with a clean paintbrush, then blow the valves out with compressed air.

Lastly, electric chainsaws have an auto-lubrication mechanism, but we recommend checking the chain oil reservoir before each use, and refilling it if necessary.

Many cordless electric chainsaws are water resistant and will work fine in the rain. Before you take one for a spin, check its Ingress Protection rating (IP), which measures dust and waterproofing. If your chainsaw features an “IPX3” rating, it can handle “sprays of water” and should be fine in light rain. An “IPX4” rating can withstand moderate to heavy rain.

All that said, we don’t really recommend operating a chainsaw in the rain. Even with work gloves, rain makes every chainsaw-related job less safe, so hold off until the sun comes out if you can.

You should never use a corded electric chainsaw in the rain. Doing so presents a significant electrocution risk. (It’s one of many reasons we generally don’t recommend them.)

#6274. Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Taking gender-affirming hormone therapy was the right decision for 97 percent surveyed

Demonstrators rally at the U.S. Supreme Court in 2025 in support of gender-affirming health care for transgender youth. The vast majority of transgender and gender diverse young people are satisfied with their decision to take hormone therapy, according the largest survey on the topic.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.

Almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date. Nearly 97 percent affirmed it was the right decision, researchers report November 9 in JAMA Pediatrics. Only about 3 percent, or 10 individuals, said they regretted the step, and of those, seven felt the experience was harmful.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

With concerns around youth well-being fueling limits on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the researchers write, “the results provide further support for the existing standards of care [and] do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access.”

Gender-affirming hormone therapy — with the masculinizing hormone testosterone or the feminizing hormone estrogen — allows a person’s body to better match their gender identity. Around 3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States identify as transgender.

Among the study’s 376 young people, who were former patients of a clinic for transgender and gender diverse youth, nearly 92 percent began hormones at 17 or younger. Thirty percent took estrogen and 70 percent took testosterone, with the amount of time since starting the hormones averaging five years.

As per clinical guidelines for transgender health care, young people interested in medical treatment, joined by parents or guardians, began with an assessment visit with a mental health professional. For the study, participants took a yearly survey, filled out anytime from one month prior to six months following the anniversary of this initial visit. The research team analyzed surveys submitted from 2023 to 2025.

The new research adds to growing evidence on the benefits of gender-affirming hormone therapy for transgender young people. Gender-affirming hormones improve the alignment these young people experience between their appearance and their gender, increase their satisfaction with life and reduce depression and anxiety.

But state bans have curtailed young people’s access to gender-affirming care, which can include hormone therapy and puberty blockers. As of November 2026 in the United States, 28 states have laws or policies that limit this care, according to the health policy organization KFF. More than half of transgender young people age 13 to 17 reside in states that restrict gender-affirming care. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming health care for young people and provide evidence-backed guidelines for treatment.

#6273. Falcon 9 flies national security doubleheader

On Wednesday, Nov. 18, China is expected to launch a Long March 2D from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in Shanxi province at 5:50 p.m. EST, according to NextSpaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later that night on Wednesday, Nov. 18, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 10:00 p.m. EST. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force has said what the rocket carries. The Falcon 9 booster will land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

On Friday, Nov. 20, a Long March 8A is slated to lift off from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on Hainan Island at 6:00 a.m. EST, per NextSpaceflight. The payload has not been disclosed, but is suspected to be a batch of SatNet low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites for Guowang — a state-backed broadband megaconstellation meant to rival Starlink.

Closing out the week on Saturday, Nov. 21, the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) will launch NROL-136 on a Falcon 9 from SLC-4E at 7:30 a.m. EST. Rather than heading for a droneship, the booster will fly back to Landing Zone 4.

Last week opened on Wednesday, Nov. 11, at 6:41 a.m. EST, when a Long March 2D lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center carrying CAS Pathfinder-1. The Chinese Academy of Sciences built the satellite to test key technologies for its planned Origins space science program, CGTN reported. Later that night, at 11:36 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-627 mission from Vandenberg after two postponements. The booster landed on Of Course I Still Love You.

On Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:47 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched Starship Flight 15 from Starbase, Texas, aiming to catch both stages with its launch tower for the first time. SpaceX was unable to catch the Super Heavy booster after its onboard guidance system made the call to abort the attempt. Instead it exploded over the Gulf of Mexico just before reaching the water. The ship, on the other hand, reached orbit, the second Starship ever to do so, and released 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

Then on Saturday afternoon, after 14 trips around Earth, the rocket’s upper stage slowed over Starbase, dropped between the tower’s mechanical “chopsticks,” and was plucked out of the air. The catch was a first for SpaceX and spaceflight in general — no other spacecraft has ever entered orbit and then been caught at its launch site.

Russia launched a mission from the Vostochny Cosmodrome at 8:16 p.m. EST on Friday, Nov. 13. The Soyuz-2.1b carried a pair of high-resolution imaging satellites and a dozen smaller payloads.

Rocket Lab marked a milestone just after midnight on Saturday, Nov. 14. At 12:30 a.m. EST, its Electron rocket flew for the 100th time on The Mountain God Rises, lifting off from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula. The rocket placed a synthetic aperture radar satellite into orbit for the Japanese company iQPS. Synthetic aperture radar bounces microwaves off the ground to build images, letting it see through clouds and darkness.

The week ended in a loss. On Sunday, Nov. 15, at 12:40 p.m. EST, United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station carrying 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the company’s broadband constellation. It was Vulcan’s return to flight after the USSF-87 mission in February — which experienced a minor booster anomaly despite successfully delivering its payload — and the first of several dozen Vulcan launches Amazon has booked. About 10 minutes into the flight, ULA reported an anomaly, and the satellites never reached orbit.

Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit. Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us…

On Monday, Nov. 23, Arianespace is targeting 5:12 a.m. EST to launch an Ariane 64 from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana with 36 more Amazon Leo satellites.

Later on Monday, Nov. 23, SpaceX is slated to launch the classified USSF-266 mission for the Space Force from Vandenberg at 11:04 a.m. EST.

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, China is slated to launch a Long March 12 from the commercial launch site at Wenchang on Hainan Island at 2:00 a.m. EST, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been confirmed, but is likely another batch of SatNet LEO satellites for Guowang.

On Thursday, Nov. 26, a launch window opens for the third flight of Isar Aerospace’s Spectrum rocket from Andøya Spaceport in Norway, according to European Spaceflight. Its payloads include AT-Astra, an Austrian technology-demonstration satellite built by Vienna-based R-Space. Spectrum reached orbit for the first time on its second flight in September.

On Sunday, Nov. 29, NASA and Northrop Grumman are targeting 10:47 a.m. EST to launch the NG-25 Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. Named the S.S. James A. Lovell after the beloved Apollo 13 commander, the spacecraft will haul several tons of supplies to the space station.

Recently, researchers used AI to "decode" segments of birdsong. In the wake of this, Live Science asks its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The idea of talking to animals like Dr. Dolittle might sound far-fetched, but researchers are making progress toward understanding how other species communicate. In a recent Live Science interview, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie explained how she used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the calls of zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata). For instance, Elie was able to determine which calls the birds used to communicate over short distances versus longer distances.

Birds aren't the only animals scientists are hoping to understand. Researchers with Project CETI are using AI to decipher the clicks and calls of sperm whales, while a separate team (with the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI) conducted what they described as the first "conversation" between humans and a humpback whale. The whale, named Twain, responded to recorded calls played by researchers over a 20 minute period, a "conversation" scientists believe could help us figure out how to communicate with extraterrestrial life someday.

Closer to home, cats have already figured out how to use meows to get their human's attention, whether they're demanding food, affection or simply that we open the door for them (again). Whether this means they understand the human language or not is still up for debate, but it raises an interesting question: If we could understand what animals were saying, which species would you most want to talk to? Vote in our poll and let us know what you'd ask in the comments below!

#6271. New Senate class includes experienced lawmakers, ex-governor

The new Democratic majority in the Senate will feature a number of top recruits with significant government experience both on and off Capitol Hill.

None is more familiar than Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown, who unseated appointed Sen. Jon Husted just two years after losing Ohio’s other Senate seat to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno.

Having prevailed in a special election, Brown is expected to be seated before the end of the year.

Brown, who rose to be the Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs chairman during his first stint in the Senate, does not reclaim seniority under Democratic caucus rules but will surely have influence above and beyond that of a typical newly-elected senator.

Speaking to supporters after his victory Tuesday night, he said he would make it a priority to ban members of Congress from trading stocks — one of the popular campaign messages of Republicans and Democrats alike in 2026.

“We will fight to end these tariffs,” Brown said of his other priorities. “We will end this war. We will fight to lower your costs, and increase your paychecks and open up paths to the middle class.”

Brown will be joined in the Senate by several first-timers with outsize profiles and experience, led by Sen.-elect Roy Cooper, D-N.C.

“I am determined that no matter the challenges that confront me, I will be an independent voice ready to work with anyone to do what’s right for this amazing state that has given me so much,” Cooper said in his victory speech.

With his history of winning statewide elections, Cooper was a top recruit for Democrats and expected Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., with Republican incumbent Sen. Thom Tillis opting to retire at the end of the current term.

Cooper’s the only former governor in the Senate freshman class, though he is not alone among the newcomers with significant public sector experience, being joined by several House members.

New Hampshire Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas will be the first openly gay man to serve in the Senate, blocking the comeback bid of former Sen. John E. Sununu.

Illinois and Minnesota are sending their Democratic lieutenant governors, with Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton set to succeed Minority Whip Richard J. Durbin and Minnesota voters choosing Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan as the successor for retiring Sen. Tina Smith.

Minnesota’s other Senate seat will be filled by an appointee after Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., won the state’s governor’s race on Tuesday.

“The American people have now entrusted Democrats to fight for them and to put a stop to the most corrupt administration in our nation’s history, and with this new majority, we are ready to turn the page,” Stratton said in a statement. “With a new majority in the Senate, Democrats are prepared to stand up to the Trump administration while fighting to lower costs, protect our rights and democracy, and deliver progress for the American people.”

The smaller Senate Republican Conference picks up new members from a number of particularly red states, with Alabama Rep. Barry Moore winning the open seat contest to succeed Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who was elected governor on Tuesday.

Rep. Julia Letlow, R-La., who had defeated Sen. Bill Cassidy in the primary, prevailed in the general election and will move over to the Senate. Also heading to the Senate is the at-large congresswoman from Wyoming, Republican Rep. Harriet Hageman.

“We are about to engage in a battle for the future of this nation, and as we all recognize, the looming fight with the left is about much more than just policy differences. It’s about the very survival of this country as it has been and as we know it,” Hageman posted on social media after her victory.

Rep. Andy Barr, R-Ky., won the Senate seat being vacated by the retirement of longtime Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell.

Another House member crossing the Capitol is Republican Rep. Kevin Hern, who won comfortably in Oklahoma. While his contest was not a special election, Hern is also likely to be seated early, after the state attorney general released an opinion last week that he can take over for appointed Sen. Alan Armstrong as soon as the results of the election are certified.

The unusual scenario came about because Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin vacated the Senate seat earlier this year to fill the spot in the president’s Cabinet.

Hern, speaking with reporters before polls closed on election night, highlighted a relatively straightforward set of legislative priorities, including government funding legislation, the annual defense authorization, a surface transportation bill and the farm bill.

“The Senate hasn’t really done anything since last July, and that’s one of the reasons I think the Senate’s in trouble right now. They really haven’t passed any bills over there,” Hern said.
