#6249. The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The virus, eliminated in 2000, has now been circulating for more than a year

Flyers provide information about a Pennsylvania Department of Health measles vaccination clinic in Lancaster County aiming to curb an ongoing outbreak.

After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.

The highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17. Analyses of cases dated from when the first outbreak began in 2025 in West Texas through part of 2026 revealed the virus has been spreading uninterrupted for more than a year. That benchmark signals measles is no longer under control.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The United States is not alone. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status, PAHO announced; Canada had lost it in 2025. “Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage,” PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa said in a Nov. 17 news conference. “And this global trend is also affecting the Americas.” Countries will need to not only stop ongoing outbreaks, but also prove that no one caught measles within their borders for a full year to regain measles-free status.

That won’t happen overnight. But there is a way, experts say. Vaccinating people across the country, particularly in areas with low vaccination rates, will stifle the virus’s spread. But so far, the U.S. federal public health response has taken a back seat to efforts from state and local health departments to curb ongoing outbreaks.

Measles’s return “is an enormous black eye on the reputation of the United States,” said epidemiologist Jennifer Nuzzo of the Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I., in a Nov. 9 webinar hosted by the university. The Americas led the global campaign to control the virus, and in 2016 the region became the first to eliminate measles transmission from all its countries.

“To lose [elimination status] means we’re going backwards… meaning decades of progress lost,” Nuzzo said. “It’s an indicator of our lack of protection. It is an indicator of our lack of preparedness for disease threats in general.”

PAHO’s verdict comes amid a surge of measles not seen in the United States since 1991. Health officials have recorded more than 7,000 cases since the beginning of the West Texas outbreak. That tally includes nearly 2,300 measles cases in 2025 and 5,412 in 2026 as of November 12, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over 90 percent of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated or whose status is unknown. States report that 13 people have died, although the CDC so far recognizes only nine of those deaths.

While mild measles symptoms include high fever, cough and a rash, roughly 1 in 5 people will be hospitalized with complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Children younger than 5 years and adults over 20 are more likely to get sick, as are pregnant women and their infants. At least 13 babies were born infected, called congenital measles, since the beginning of 2025, researchers report November 16 in NEJM Evidence. Those babies are at risk for developing dangerous brain swelling that is almost always fatal later on in life.

The measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine helped eliminate measles from the United States in 2000. After that, cases still sometimes popped up. Those cases were mostly in unvaccinated people traveling from parts of the world where the virus still widely circulates. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

But widespread misinformation, including a disproven claim that the vaccine causes autism, means fewer children are receiving the MMR shot and more people are questioning its safety. According to the CDC, roughly 92 percent of kindergarteners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019. And in 2025, 83 percent of U.S. adults viewed the MMR vaccine as safe, down from 86 percent in 2024, according to a survey from the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. Yet decades of evidence show the vaccine is safe and highly effective.

That measles made a comeback is not a surprise, says Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University School of Medicine. Until recently, outbreaks were largely isolated to communities with low vaccination rates and quickly contained. But now, outbreaks seem to be more likely to spill over into neighboring communities, Lo says. “There’s a lot of potential connectedness between the outbreaks.”

What’s more, some infected people aren’t getting tested, making them invisible to officials who are now struggling to trace chains of transmission. An outbreak that hit Arizona and Utah, for instance, was far larger than official numbers suggest, researchers reported July 15 in a preprint at medRxiv.org. The roughly 1,000 confirmed cases may represent just 20 to 30 percent of the outbreak’s true size.

A functional surveillance system is crucial to keeping outbreaks under control, Jonathan Temte, a family medicine physician at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, said in the Brown University webinar. Without good surveillance across the entire country, “we can miss pockets out there if people aren’t reporting, if people are hiding cases.”

But surveillance alone won’t stop the virus from “popcorning across the country,” Nuzzo said. “Measles has returned, and it’s going to take vaccination to stop it.”

Over the last two years, measles outbreaks have popped up across the United States, sickening thousands of people since mid-January 2025. Most of those cases, shown by county where they were reported, are in people who are unvaccinated. Colors on the map indicate the relative number of cases reported. Green represents the lowest and red the highest number of cases. Notable outbreaks have appeared in Utah, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

Michael Mitchell and Andrea Uhlig/Brown University School of Public Health

Efforts to boost vaccine uptake could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles, but not all. “Figuring out which ones are [high risk] can be a little tricky,” Lo says. “But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

Homing in on school districts or individual schools could also help. State health departments typically report vaccination rates among school-age children by county. But that broad metric can hide high risk schools with low vaccination rates, epidemiologists Siyu Chen and Ana Bento reported in August in Nature Medicine. Computer simulations relying on data that included 50,000 schools across the United States showed that school-level estimates best revealed where the virus could gain a foothold. That was true even if county-level vaccination rates were close to 95 percent.

Another element that influenced where measles took off was whether communities with cases were near other areas with low vaccination rates, the team found. The outbreak in Texas, for instance, may have ended faster because communities with low vaccination rates were farther away from one another compared with outbreaks in South Carolina and Pennsylvania, says Bento, of Cornell University. Neighboring areas where many are unvaccinated may face longer-burning outbreaks. “Which is what we are now seeing,” Bento says.

Measles elimination status can be regained. The declaration that the virus is endemic is “not a punishment,” Bento says. It’s a sign that something needs to change. That might include vaccine catch-up campaigns, community outreach or getting rid of nonmedical vaccine exemptions.

Local public health officials are “doing every last thing that you can imagine with limited resources,” health psychologist Noel T. Brewer said in a Nov. 12 webinar hosted by the Association of Health Care Journalists. But a cohesive plan at the federal level could bolster defenses before the virus arrives in new states, noted Brewer, of the University of North Carolina Gillings School of Global Public Health in Chapel Hill.

Such efforts could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles. “A subset [with low vaccination rates] are high risk,” Lo says. “Figuring out which ones are which can be a little tricky. But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

There’s also wiggle room in the childhood vaccine schedule to provide kids extra protection. Normally children don’t get their first MMR dose until their first birthday. But doctors can give infants an extra MMR dose at 6 months if there is an active outbreak in their area. Pediatricians can also offer the second dose a month after the first one, rather than waiting until around the time children start kindergarten. Adults, particularly those who received only one dose, can also get a booster. It’s unclear whether health officials will officially recommend such actions.

“The problem is that there’s no trusted source for this vaccine decision anymore,” Lo says. Previous vaccine recommendations were up to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which was disbanded in March after lawsuits blocked appointments made by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Now, there’s a lot of different medical societies and initiatives to try and fill that void,” Lo says. But it’s unclear which would be best positioned to lead.

CDC director Erica Schwartz has said the health agency will not be changing its response to ongoing outbreaks. “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” she told Reuters. The CDC did not respond to Science News requests for an interview, but shared in a Nov. 17 statement that the agency will “encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”

Eliminating measles again will take dedicated resources and more funding funneled to public health departments across the country, Lo says. “You see increasing measles outbreaks and a lot of time and resources to contain these outbreaks at a time where you’re slashing budgets,” Lo says, “that’s a really bad mismatch.”

Public health responses to measles are expensive. Officials in New Mexico spent an estimated $5.4 million — over $53,000 per case — responding to a 2025 outbreak that was linked to West Texas. The CDC has provided an additional $100 million to states to help fight measles.

Other countries have beaten back measles after an unwelcome return. Extensive vaccination campaigns helped Venezuela and Brazil regain measles elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019. The Public Health Agency of Canada also announced that its nearly two-year-long outbreak officially ended in October, though it’s unclear when the country might earn its status back.

“It is not hopeless,” Nuzzo said. “It can be done, and I hope it will be done [in the United States].”

This story was updated November 17, 2026, to include a quote from PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa and a statement from CDC.

#6248. Voyager 1 reaches 1 light-day from Earth

At 5:16 a.m. EST on Wednesday, Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will become the first spacecraft to reach a distance of 1 light-day from Earth. A command radioed from home will need 24 hours to arrive, and a reply another 24 to come back. NASA is asking the public to celebrate by sending the spacecraft a signal on the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17.

NASA launched the twin Voyager spacecraft in 1977 to tour the giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter and Saturn, while Voyager 2 went on to Uranus and Neptune and is still the only spacecraft to visit either one. Both then kept going. They’re now the only probes ever to study interstellar space directly, the region beyond the Sun’s magnetic field.

Each spacecraft runs on a radioisotope thermoelectric generator, the same kind of power source that drives NASA’s Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars. Plutonium-238, the fuel source, gives off heat as it naturally decays, and the generators turn that heat into electricity. But because the output fades by about 4 watts every year, engineers have spent years shutting off components and instruments to stretch the spacecraft’s lives. This year, a risky maneuver nicknamed the “Big Bang” turned off several devices in one coordinated move to buy the spacecraft and their remaining instruments several more years of operation. Today, Voyager 1 only runs two of its original 10 instruments, and Voyager 2 runs three.

Voyager 1 is closing in on 1 light-day from Earth (about 16.1 billion miles [25.9 billion kilometers]) — farther than any spacecraft has ever gone. Its twin is about 2 billion miles (3.2 billion km) closer to Earth, near enough that a signal takes about 20 hours to reach Voyager 2.

Voyager 1 lifted off Sept. 5, 1977, two weeks after Voyager 2 but on a shorter trajectory as it was traveling to Jupiter. After visiting Saturn in 1980, it drifted away from the solar system’s planets for good. A decade later, it captured the famous photograph of Earth known as the Pale Blue Dot. In August 2012, it became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space, and Voyager 2 followed in 2018. Voyager 2 won’t reach the light-day mark until November 2035. You can see both missions’ exact locations on NASA’s mission status page.

A light-day is a distance measuring how far light travels in 24 hours. At about 186,000 miles per second (299,792 km per second), that adds up to roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion km). For scale, the Moon is just 1.3 light-seconds away, the Sun about 8.3 light-minutes, and Neptune a bit over 4 light-hours. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, lies more than 1,500 light-days away.

At a speed of nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 km/h), Voyager 1 is anything but slow. Still, it needed more than 49 years to cover the distance light crosses in a single day.

Astronomy usually asks readers to dim their lights. But tomorrow night is an exception: To celebrate Voyager 1’s accomplishment, NASA invites everyone to flash Voyager’s call sign, V-G-R, skyward in Morse code on Tuesday evening. Use NASA’s automated flasher on your smartphone or tablet. Or grab a plain flashlight and do it manually: V: dot-dot-dot-dash; G: dash-dash-dot; R: dot-dash-dot. Dots are quick blinks of the light, and dashes are long flashes of about a second. Pause between letters.

A recent satellite photo captured an underwater cloud of fish sperm, or milt, appearing to glow green during a Pacific herring spawning event at a reproductive "sweet spot" along the coast of Canada's Vancouver Island.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada [48.95586624, -125.42994277]

What's in the photo? A green cloud of milt (fish sperm) and eggs during a Pacific herring spawning event

Which satellite took the photo? Landsat 9

This surprising satellite snap shows a giant underwater plume of fish sperm that seems to glow green beneath the waves. The colorful cloud appeared during a spawning event at a reproductive "sweet spot" along Canada's western coastline.

The striking sight was spotted in Barkley Sound, along a section of the southern coast of Vancouver Island in British Columbia, roughly 45 miles (70 kilometers) north of the U.S. border. The bright-green cloud is the most concentrated between Salmon Beach — the triangular town in the center of the image — and the smaller Forbes Island, which is also "glowing" along its northern coast.

The green cloud is around 4 miles (7 km) from end to end and is made of milt — a fluid containing sperm made by fish, mollusks and other aquatic animals — that was released during a Pacific herring (Clupea pallasii) spawning event. Like many other fish species, Pacific herring reproduce by congregating in large groups. The females lay eggs, which stick to kelp, sea grasses and rocky surfaces, before the males release their milt, which disperses over the area and fertilizes the eggs.

Pacific herring, which grow to around 10 inches (25 centimeters) long, often congregate in this spot off Vancouver Island in late winter or early spring, gathering for several weeks before releasing their gametes, or sex cells, according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

"The herring spawn is a really fabulous time to be out here," local resident Ryan Cutler, who used a drone to capture close-up photos of this year's spawning event (see below), told CBC News. "It's a really, really spectacular time to be around."

The cloud of milt arguably looks even more imposing up close, as you can see in this drone photo from resident Ryan Cutler, who described the spawning event as "fabulous" and "spectacular."

Spawning events can last anywhere between a few hours and several days, and scientists are increasingly turning to satellite images to help monitor these occurrences, according to the Earth Observatory. In this case, the milt cloud was visible for around 48 hours.

While the milky substance appears a striking green in these images, it is actually white. It appears green only because it is closer to the surface than the surrounding seafloor, meaning that less reflected light is absorbed by the water. This is also why shallow patches of water often appear turquoise when viewed from above.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The coastline alongside Salmon Beach is perfect for herring to spawn because it strikes the perfect balance between a number of important factors. "Herrings prefer spawning locations that are more protected, have rocky substrate, and allow them to select areas with reduced salinity," Jessica Moffatt, a biologist with Vancouver Island's Island Marine Aquatic Working Group, told the Earth Observatory. "Barkley Sound hits the 'sweet spot' in many of these regards."

The Pacific herring is an important species in this region; it is a primary food source for Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), which give Salmon Beach its name. The herring are also hunted by local First Nation groups, according to CBC News.

During the spawning events, a wide range of other predatory marine life — including large fish, whales and sea lions — are drawn to the area to feast on the herring, according to the Earth Observatory. And on land, eagles, wolves and bears are more likely to appear during the mass reproduction event.

The milt appears green from above due to how wavelengths are absorbed by water as light reflects off the the white substance.

Coincidentally, this exact patch of ocean was the site of one of the weirdest oceanographic events ever seen. In 2020, around 4 miles (7 km) off the coast of Ucluelet (located just along the coastline to the left in the photo), scientists detected a rogue wave that appeared in the open ocean seemingly from nowhere. The massive wave reached the height of a four-story building, making it the most extreme version of this phenomenon ever seen.

Farther offshore, around 150 miles (240 km) south of Vancouver Island, researchers also detected a surprise swarm of more than 2,000 underwater earthquakes in a single day in March 2024, hinting that a section of the seafloor was ripping apart.

A recent satellite photo captured a series of clouds sculpted by von Kármán vortices from a volcano on South Korea's Jeju Island. A giant multicolor plume, ejected by China's Yangtze River, is also visible in the image.

A recent satellite photo captured a gleaming halo of phytoplankton encircling the remote Chatham Islands. The stunning sight is the result of a hidden underwater structure, which has also helped kill hundreds of cetaceans.

A recent satellite photo captured a stunning scene of sediment swirling across the West Florida Shelf after an extreme cold snap that covered large parts of the eastern U.S. in snow.

#6246. Capitol Lens | Images from Election Day

The 2026 midterm campaign cycle came to a dramatic end on Tuesday with Democrats reclaiming control of both chambers of Congress.

In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear," author and environmental historian Peter S. Alagona looks at the models used to develop the U.S. grizzly bear recovery program, and how California could make an ideal home for a new population.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Computer models are widely used in ecological research and conservation, providing scientists with tools to predict how a given species might respond to a stressor or shift in conditions. These models can then be refined and built upon with real world data to get a better understanding of what's going on within a population and what the biggest risks are.

But models aren't perfect. In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet" (HarperOne, 2026), author Peter S. Alagona highlights how these models are built on the presumptions of their creators. Alagona examines the model of grizzly bear (Ursus arctos horribilis) habitats used by the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to inform its recovery plan for the species — and why California, despite its apparent suitability, was left out.

Most of the grizzly habitat models that were introduced in the 1990s and 2000s, and then improved in the 2010s and 2020s, make two key assumptions. They assume that conservation efforts should focus on the best remaining grizzly habitats, and that we can best understand those habitats by studying bears in the places where they still live.

The result has, indeed, been a far better understanding of grizzly habitat use. But this approach has also produced a circular logic with a structural bias toward the status quo. In most grizzly habitat models, past realities and future possibilities fade. With each new study, it seems more and more like the only possible places for grizzlies are the exact kinds of places where they currently live.

The six recovery areas identified in the 1993 Recovery Plan were all places where grizzlies still lived or had recently lived when they were listed as threatened in 1975. The plan argued that these areas "had the potential to provide adequate space and habitat to maintain the grizzly bear as a viable and self-sustaining species." But it also acknowledged the risks and uncertainties facing the bears, and it pledged to assess other areas in their historical range.

This process was expected to take five years. Twenty-eight years later, in 2019, the FWS settled a federal lawsuit in which it agreed to finally conduct this long-delayed analysis. It built a simple model based mainly on secure habitat, and then applied it to both the San Juan Mountains of Colorado and the Sierra Nevada of California. Other potential recovery areas — such as the North Rim of the Grand Canyon in Arizona, the Gila Wilderness in New Mexico, and the Northwest Forest of Northern California — were, for unexplained reasons, not included.

The current grizzly bear recovery zones with the proposed boundaries.

The model did its job. According to the FWS, neither the San Juans nor the Sierra Nevada contained enough secure habitat to support a viable grizzly population. Instead of subjecting the study to peer review, the FWS published it in an appendix on page 286 of a species status report. Having pioneered the idea of secure habitat, David Mattson now set out to explain why the FWS was abusing it. In his view, the service's models focused on artificially small areas, failed to consider several key factors described in the scientific literature, and neglected to conduct essential supporting analyses to explain its conclusions.

The FWS had dragged its heels for almost three decades, and then, after pledging in court to conduct a good-faith analysis, produced a study that seemed designed to reach a predetermined result: The only places capable of supporting grizzlies were the places where the FWS was already trying to recover them. When Mattson and his colleague Troy Merrill ran a more detailed model for the southwestern states, they found that Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah contained seven potential recovery areas with more than 45,000 square kilometers of suitable habitat that could probably support more than 1,000 bears.

For more than a century, the prevailing narrative in California has been that the grizzly's extinction there was inevitable and its recovery is impossible. But Mattson's results for the southwest, combined with California's unique geography, cast doubt on this story.

California is home to nearly 40 million people, and it has more miles of roads than any state except Texas. But its population is extraordinarily concentrated. California is the most urban state, with 95% of its residents packed into cities and 75% living on only around 2% of its land area. Much of California has a human population density lower than that of the Northern Rockies. Unlike in the Northern Rockies, the majority of California's farms are concentrated in broad valleys dozens of miles from core wilderness habitats.

Kings Canyon National Park in California has been identified as one of the locations where grizzlies could thrive.

Outside urban and agricultural areas, California has more protected land than any state except Alaska, including the largest areas of potential grizzly habitat outside the six current recovery zones. Some of these protected areas are in desert ecosystems not suitable for grizzly bears, but others are in mountain ecosystems with potential grizzly habitat.

California's national parks and wilderness areas sometimes strain under heavy visitation, but the numbers paint a complex picture. Consider the southern High Sierra. In 2024, Sequoia Kings Canyon National Park, which is around 865,000 acres and 97% wilderness, topped 2 million visitors for the first time, whereas Yellowstone, which is around 2.2 million acres and 90% wilderness, received almost 5 million visitors, meaning that both parks had about 2.3 visitors per acre. Yellowstone has more than double the total land area in wilderness, but both parks border large U.S. Forest Service wilderness areas and other public lands, and the High Sierra has fewer roads cutting across its protected areas.

In 2024, I coauthored a study, almost eight years in the making, looking at potential grizzly habitat in California. This project, led by Alex McInturff from the University of Washington, ran four computer models, and then compared them to assess the results each produced. One of these models focused on historical sightings of grizzlies in California, two used approaches developed in other regions where brown bears currently live, and one looked at the habitat use preferences of one of California's other large carnivores, the puma.

The Grizzly Bear Recovery Program was created in the 1970s to restore populations to self-sustaining levels.

Each of these approaches has its own strengths and weaknesses. None of them fully account for the distribution or abundance of food on the landscape or for possible conflicts with people. Together, however, they provide a first assessment of the amount, quality, and locations of potential grizzly habitats. Amazingly, about a third of California appeared as suitable habitat in all four models.

The biggest areas of high-quality habitat were in the southern Sierra Nevada, around Sequoia-Kings Canyon National Park, where some of the last California grizzly sightings occurred in the 1920s. The Northwest Forest, along the Pacific Coast near the Oregon border, also scored highly owing to its low human population density and rich forest habitats. The Transverse Ranges, in the state's southwestern corner, scored highly because of their rich chaparral habitats and density of historical sightings, but ranked somewhat lower than the other two because more people live, work, and grow crops, including extensive vineyards and avocado orchards, around its borders.

These results made intuitive sense, given the state's robust historical grizzly population, large areas of protected habitat, and healthy black bear populations. But they represented a departure from the conventional wisdom that dominated the circular logic of most habitat models. For the first time, it was clear how much potential habitat could be available in California for a grizzly recovery. But our approach still clung to the conservative assumption that the grizzly is a wilderness species. We had shown, with some important caveats, that California probably had enough wilderness to support one or more viable grizzly populations.

What we hadn't shown was whether Californians were willing to coexist with grizzlies that might, someday, wander outside the state's wilderness boundaries.

From the book START WITH A BEAR: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet, by Peter S. Alagona. Copyright © 2026 by Peter S. Alagona. Published by HarperOne, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Excerpted by permission.

Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.

A century ago, prevailing wisdom cast large carnivores as adversaries—pests and threats to be removed for human safety and prosperity. In North America, among the most targeted of these animals were brown bears, or grizzlies, whose population decimation has made them emblematic of this fear-driven approach to wildlife management.

In California, where they once roamed the land in the tens of thousands, grizzlys have not been seen in more than 100 years. Modern conservation has evolved, yet it often remains rooted in a separation from nature, a systemic opposition that keeps the wild at arm's length.

In Start with a Bear, historian, ecologist, and bear expert Peter Alagona suggests we must reimagine the very heart of conservation, inviting a new framework for sustainable, reciprocal relations with the wild creatures that remain.

Peter S. Alagona is an environmental historian, conservation scientist, and nature-culture geographer. His work explores what happens when people share space and resources (their habitats) with other species: how we interact with non-human creatures, how we make sense of these interactions, why we fight so much about them, what we can learn from them, and how we might use these lessons to foster a more just, peaceful, humane, and sustainable society. He is a professor of environmental studies at the University of California, Santa Barbara. He is the author of "After the Grizzly" and "The Accidental Ecosystem."

#6244. 9 Chefs on the Meals They're Traveling For in 2027—From Korean Soups to Peruvian Ceviche

Any professional chef can confirm that while menu development, staffing, interior design, and operations are all part of running a restaurant or kitchen, finding the time to travel in search of different flavors often feels like a rare luxury. But spending time in a different city or region is key to staying inspired. Even a quick weekend getaway can lead to incorporating new ingredients in familiar dishes, serve as an opportunity to learn a new culinary technique, help forge a connection with one’s own heritage, or connect with peers who are pushing the industry forward.

As the end of the calendar year draws near, we spoke with some of our favorite women chefs about where they’re most excited to visit in 2027—from a sushi counter in Tokyo to the oldest restaurant in Beirut—and what they’re hoping to eat and learn from those travels.

A table at ARREA!, Almuerzo Otoño's restaurant in Álava, Spain

“I went [to the Basque Country] for the first time in 2013, but it was such a quick, rushed trip that I left feeling like I’d barely scratched the surface. I’ve been wanting to go back and really do it right ever since. At the top of my list of spots is Arrea!, Edorta Lamo’s restaurant in Kanpezu, a small village in the mountains of Álava. I’ve heard such wonderful things about it. What excites me is that it’s not the Basque Country most people think of first—as in, San Sebastián with its coastline and all of its pintxo bars. It’s inland cooking, built on what’s hunted, foraged, and grown right there in the mountains. And I'll be eating my way through plenty of pintxo bars too, of course. — Katie Button, chef/co-founder of Cúrate Bar de Tapas in Asheville, and author of Spanish Accent cookbook

“I’m in love with Erin French’s new cookbook [Seize the Supper], and wildly enough, Maine is one of the few states I've never been to. So, I'm plotting something for next summer. I love that it's a mostly female crew, a standout (unfortunately) in our industry. Erin’s focus on local produce and connecting to the earth speaks to my own regenerative cooking and inspires me constantly to dig deeper and deeper. I also admire her ethos of humble simplicity, distilling dishes to their core, filled with soul and properly honoring ingredients, with a nod to her family's heritage. I dream of her play on sweet and savory—like the soft polenta with honey and ricotta.” — Camilla Marcus, chef and founder of Westbourne

The seafood platter at the new Casa Juani in Boulder

Casa Juani's Spain-inspired sea urchin dish

“I am most looking forward to traveling to Boulder to visit my friends Kelly Jeun and Eduardo Vallelobo at their restaurant Casa Juani. Both are accomplished chefs who are experts in Italian and Spanish cuisines, and they recently made Bon Appétit's Best New Restaurants list. I am most excited to try everything on their menu, which is entirely Spanish. Eduardo is very proud of—and from!—Madrid, and the menu celebrates Spanish cuisine and culture.” —Melissa Rodriguez, Chef & Partner at Crane Club & Bar CC in New York City

For cookbook author Rebekah Peppler, edomae-style sushi is a must-eat in 2027.

“[Sushi Meino], a six-seat counter in Tokyo’s Azabujuban neighborhood by Chef Mei Kougo, one of only a few female sushi masters in Japan, has been high on my list since it opened in 2023 and I haven’t yet had the luck of securing a very-difficult-to-get reservation. I'm heading back to Tokyo in the spring and hoping 2027 will be my year! If I don’t get in, I’ll still be heading to Makimaki, her takeout-only hosomaki shop that opened nearby earlier this year.” — Rebekah Peppler, recipe developer and author

Baekyangsa Temple, where Buddhist nun and chef Jeong Kwan hosts meals

Freshly foraged ingredients, including mushrooms, herbs, and greens, used by chef Jeong Kwan

“Eating at venerable Jeong Kwan’s table has been high on my list for years, and I was devastated to be out of town when she and Chef Esu Lee were cooking together at his excellent restaurant Orson in Paris recently. It lit a fire in me to finally prioritize booking a trip to Baekyangsa Temple [where she cooks] to attend one of her demonstrations in 2027.” — R.P.

Street bread Ka'ak is the reason chef Mary Attea will be headed to Lebanon in 2027.

“I'm dying to try manakish and shawarma straight from the source. Plus ka'ak, the ring-shaped street bread with sesame, along with all the spreads from the market. And [I want to pay a] visit to El Soussi, one of Beirut's oldest restaurants, famous for its Lebanese breakfast, especially msabbaha, the warm mashed chickpeas with lemon and tahini. I'd be sure to get an order of beid ghanam as well, which is lambs testicles cooked in lemon and olive oil, served with fattet hummus. Growing up in the US with Lebanese heritage, we often ate many Lebanese meals as a family. But the dishes we prepared and enjoyed were such a small sliver of everything Lebanon has to offer. I've been wanting to go for such a long time so I could experience the vastness of this incredible cuisine and the country's beauty. I was meant to travel there this past March, which was postponed, so it's top of my list for 2027!” —Chef Mary Attea, executive chef of Musket Room and Raf’s in New York City

A ceviche dish at Lima restaurant Al Toke Pez

“I’m especially excited to explore Nikkei cuisine and experience Peruvian ceviche firsthand. In Mexico, we make wonderful ceviches, but I believe Peruvians have truly mastered the art of preparing this dish. I want to experience their approach to seafood, acidity, and flavor in its place of origin, while exploring the broader culinary traditions of Peru. I believe there are many shared histories and points of connection between Latin American cultures that we don’t always recognize, and I want to explore those connections through food. I’m also drawn to the opportunity to experience traditional Mesoamérican markets that are still operating throughout Peru, not only in Lima but in other regions as well. Markets reveal so much about a place: its ingredients, its people, its traditions, and the ways food connects communities. I’d also love to experience Inca culture firsthand and better understand the country’s rich cultural and culinary heritage.” —Norma Listman, chef and co-founder, Masala y Maíz in Mexico City

Traditional Assamese food items on sale at the annual Bhogali Bihu Festival in Assam

“I’m particularly interested in Assam’s distinctive use of black sesame and wild greens. During a trip to Mumbai, I had the opportunity to taste Assamese food prepared by two sisters who cook and preserve traditional Assamese foodways. Their food completely blew my mind. I would love to travel to Assam to learn more about the region’s culinary traditions and experience its food culture firsthand. As a chef who cooks both Indian and Mexican cuisine, I feel a responsibility to keep learning and exploring the vastness and richness of India’s food traditions. India is incredibly diverse, and there is still so much for me to discover. Now, as the mother of a mixed child with Indian heritage, I feel an even greater responsibility to expose him to his culture. Traveling to Assam would be an opportunity to continue learning for myself while creating a meaningful connection between my son and his cultural roots.” — N.L.

“I hosted a pop-up at ADI last year, and was able to witness firsthand the ways in which chef Kanchan [Adhikari] is doing the most incredibly inventive things with food within the South Asian diaspora while also marrying it with a Japanese omakase-style sentiment. One of my favorite restaurants of the past year and I am counting down the days until I can eat a meal in that gorgeous dining room again!"” —Samah Dada, chef and creator of recipe platform DADA Eats

A bowl of pollock soup, a dish local to Inje in South Korea

“Inje is the smallest county in South Korea and is most famous for hwangtae guk (dried pollock) soup. You can find many restaurants clustered together there that serve this regional specialty, but my absolute favorite is a place called Song-yi Sikdang. The brief menu basically comes down to the hwangtae jungsik—a set that includes pollock soup, a whole grilled pollock, an assortment of 12 perfectly seasoned namul banchans, and a warm bowl of rice. Inje is located in the Taebaek mountains alongside rivers and basins, so when you get there, you’re surrounded by stunning landscape and flora, which is absolutely gorgeous year round—ranging from verdant mountains, to golden and crimson foliage, to snowy tree tops. Inje is a short and tranquil two-hour drive from Seoul and feels similar to that of driving upstate on the Taconic from Manhattan. The geography and climate makes it the perfect environment for preparing dried pollock and also foraging for diverse wild greens and herbs (namuls), rare ones that you can only find there and are seasonally available at local farmers markets. —Clara Lee, co-author of Korean Soups and co-founder of food company Queens

I have been wanting to travel to Italy for many years, and Puglia has been top of mind. It feels like a place where food is still very much connected to the culture and deeply rooted in the abundance of the land. Since the provenance of things is our ethos, this feels particularly aligned for me. Anytime I travel (but specifically Europe). “I am really drawn to the simplicity of the cuisine. A beautiful local grilled fish with olive oil, handmade pasta, regional cheeses—these are all things that truly excite me as a chef because their beauty is in how uncomplicated they are. Local, fresh bounty, cooked well: to me this is what makes food memorable.” —Abigail Dahan-Kramer, pastry chef at Provenance in Philadelphia

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

Physicists at the Large Hadron Collider have detected a rare, 1-in-10-billion particle interaction that opens a view into the 'zeptoverse,' the smallest distance scale ever measured.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Using the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's largest particle accelerator, scientists have gotten the first glimpse of the "zeptoverse" — the universe as it behaves within less than a hundred-trillionth of a wavelength of visible light, the smallest scale that researchers have explored to date.

The new findings may one day help to answer long-standing cosmic mysteries, such as why there is far more matter than antimatter seen in the universe, and what makes up the dark matter that constitutes about 85% of all matter in the universe, the researchers announced Nov. 3 at a seminar at CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research), the organization that operates the LHC. The study, available as a preprint, has not yet been peer reviewed.

At the LHC, located near Geneva at the border of France and Switzerland, researchers were investigating elusive particles called beauty quarks. These subatomic particles are cousins of the standard "up" and "down" quarks that make up the cores of all atoms in the universe.

When beauty quarks are created — in this case, when the LHC smashes atoms together at incredibly high speeds — they live for just one and a half trillionths of a second before they decay. There are a number of ways beauty quarks can break down; researchers hope that analyzing rare forms of these decays might reveal that they might not unfold as expected.

Such outcomes could then shed light on new kinds of physics found only at very tiny scales of zeptometers, or trillionths of a nanometer. (For comparison, a wavelength of visible light ranges from about 380 to 750 nanometers.)

An artist's visualization of a beauty particle decaying into two muons.

By exploring this zeptoverse, scientists hope to discover new particles that have escaped detection until now.

"We're confident there must be new particles to discover, and these could help explain mysteries like dark matter and the existence of matter in the universe," study co-author Harry Cliff, a particle physicist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Why haven't we seen these particles yet? One answer, and perhaps the most likely answer, is these new particles only become manifest at very, very short-distance scales. So by probing into the zepto scale, we give ourselves the best chance possible of finding these new particles that could explain these mysteries."

We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past.

Now, after hunting for more than four decades, physicists have found the first evidence of the rarest kind of beauty-quark decay seen yet. "Only one in 10 billion beauty particles decay this way," Cliff said.

In this form of decay, technically known as the B0 to mu+ mu− decay, a beauty quark collides with an oppositely charged beauty antiquark. They annihilate each other, generating a pair of smaller particles ‪—‬ a muon and an antimuon. Previous research suggested that this requires a complicated set of interactions, making this kind of decay extraordinarily rare.

An experiment at the LHC called LHCb was specifically designed to study beauty quarks. In 2024, a major upgrade to LHCb made it possible to distinguish different types of particles. Using machine learning techniques, the researchers suppressed huge amounts of background noise, which helped them detect the first evidence of the B0 to mu+ mu− decay.

"We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past," Cliff said. "And so we have this massive sample of beauty decays, and that is ultimately what allowed us to see this decay for the first time."

The new results suggest that the way this rare decay happens matches the predictions of the Standard Model of particle physics, the current best description of how the basic building blocks of the universe behave. As such, the researchers have not yet discovered signs of new particles or new physics beyond the Standard Model.

"For me, I think the most exciting thing about this result is the fact that we are probing these unimaginably short distance scales," Cliff said. "Seeing the evidence for this decay begins a new area of research where we can start to make precision measurements that will give us the best chance of finding new physics in the future."

The researchers would now like to upgrade LHCb to fully exploit the improvements to the LHC's luminosity that are currently planned for the 2030s.

"However, there is some doubt over that now because the U.K. recently withdrew funding from the project," Cliff said. "So we are really trying to figure out if we'll be able to continue this type of research."

In an ideal world, "we'll collect many hundreds of these decays in the future, make precise measurements and probe deep into the zeptoverse," Cliff said.

#6242. Lindsey Graham’s famous quote makes sense now

“If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed ... and we will deserve it.”

Reflecting on Tuesday’s midterm election results, a shellacking by Democrats that served as a rebuke to President Donald Trump, this quote deserves another look.

In 2016, in the midst of a heated Republican primary race, with assorted candidates jockeying to be the party’s presidential nominee, those words were posted by what now seems a surprising source: South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Of course, Graham himself had been one of the candidates in that bitter contest. Insults like “lightweight” and “jackass” were tossed back and forth, and Trump publicly shared Graham’s cellphone number. (Trump finally apologized for that stunt — at Graham’s funeral this past July. Better late than never, I suppose.)

By the time of Graham’s death this year, though, his earlier self would not have recognized the senator from South Carolina who had transformed himself into one of the president’s golfing buddies and closest allies.

In May of this year, after Sen. Bill Cassidy lost his Louisiana primary to a Trump-backed opponent, Graham reasoned on NBC News that Cassidy lost because he “tried to destroy” the president, and warned the same fate would befall any Republican who crossed Trump. “This is the party of Donald Trump.”

Why the switch? “He allowed me into his world. That’s great,” he told The New York Times.

Lindsey Graham stayed relevant, with a desired seat at the table — at a cost to his political reputation and legacy.

After he died, Graham’s sister was appointed to complete his Senate term and was then pushed to run for a full term by her brother’s onetime nemesis Donald Trump. The president’s endorsement pushed Darline Graham past a more experienced Republican, Rep. Ralph Norman, in the Senate primary.

That she played a part in the Republicans’ historic midterm loss is a full-circle moment that Shakespeare would relish.

Graham lost to Dr. Annie Andrews, as the state elected a Democratic senator for the first time in decades. It came as a big surprise, especially to those Republicans who, like Lindsey Graham, started out as skeptics of the inexperienced, cruel president before making peace with the man, his policies and his power.

MAGA swallowed the GOP, and voters who elected Trump in 2016 and 2024 followed.

What was the breaking point for the people who ignored millions of dollars in attack ads on their way to the polls?

In Ohio, was it the Vivek Ramaswamy ad that dredged up opponent Amy Acton’s childhood trauma, supported by Trump and Vice President JD Vance?

In the South, was it the seeming glee of Republican state legislatures as they gerrymandered districts with substantial African American constituencies, all with the blessing of a Supreme Court-weakened Voting Rights Act?

In Texas, did Hispanic voters who swung to Trump in 2024 realize that ICE’s definition of “the worst of the worst” included business owners, grandmoms and schoolchildren?

Did tariffs turn off farmers as it affected expenses and bottom lines?

Did Americans rebel when they saw their dollars buy less while the president gushed over gold trinkets, a ballroom and a reflecting pool his hand-picked contractors couldn’t fix, and made billions for himself and his family?

Did the Islamophobia and anti-Semitism, the racism and homophobia in the name of Jesus leave true people of faith or just plain decent people disgusted?

In South Carolina, Darline Graham didn’t explain her plans for the economy or for fighting corruption or foreign entanglements, except to say “national security is not my thing” on a debate stage.

But the candidate with a scant resume did manage at a South Carolina rally to call her opponent “bats — crazy” while standing next to an approving Trump, who coined his own anti-trans slur for Andrews.

Andrews responded by saying: “If name-calling would help lower gas prices and grocery prices, he can call me all the names he wants. But I don’t think that’s going to get the job done.” In a state with 14 counties “without a single OB/Gyn,” as Andrews has said, the emptiness of insults is hard to miss.

Whatever lessons they draw from Tuesday, Democrats should not get comfortable.

Angry, hurting voters expect results — fast.

But for now, it’s hard not to recall the warning issued and then forgotten 10 years ago, with the hope that Republicans realize the old Lindsey might have been right all along.

#6241. US Flights Have Been Grounded Nationwide

The United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, with all outbound flights from the US being directed to halt ground operations. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated in a press conference that there was “no indication as of yet” that anything “nefarious” caused the ground stop, and suggested that it was due to a broad was a telecommunications outage.

“There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted,” the FAA said in a statement on X. “Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.”

Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement that the ground stop was due to a "communication issue" and that “FAA technicians are investigating.”

The halt on take offs and landing is in place for both domestic and international flights operating within the US. United Airlines, one of the four largest airlines in the nation, said that the order did not apply to in-transit aircraft: “United Airlines is responding to a nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. United flights that are already airborne will continue. New domestic flights will not depart while the FAA ground stop remains in place,” United Airlines said in a press release. “United will work with our customers to get them to their destinations once this issue is resolved.”

The last time a nationwide ground stop occurred in the US was in January 2023 following a computer outage in the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) pilot notification system (NOTAM).

CNBC reported that the widespread server outages affecting telecommunications over the past 24 hours were to blame, citing internal information from Alaska Airlines.

According to Cirium, an aviation analytics company, there are 26,284 flights scheduled to depart on November 13 from the US. As of 5:50 p.m., 600 flights have been diverted so far, with 496 of those 600 flights (82.7%) returning to their origin airport and the other 104 diverting to a different airport. At this time 481 have been canceled or no fly nationally, representing 1.83%. This will grow today,” a company spokesperson said. “After 4 p.m. Eastern time today, there were still some 11,000 flight scheduled to depart from US airports today.”
